How do you think about that?

I think we often impose an unfair standard on LLMs or AI in general of perfection—absolute perfection. Whereas the counterfactual of the human beings in real-world settings with their own perverse incentives—if you did a real objective comparison, I would argue that LLMs, at least without the perverse incentives baked into them... for example, you can imagine in the future AI having its own set of perverse incentives in terms of advertising or prescribing certain medications or things like that. But at least as it stands now, an LLM probably provides more objectively accurate guidance given the same set of information than a human being would. And it's infinitely more patient; it provides a lot more attention to detail.

Imagine if you could plug in your entire health history into that and the quality of outputs that you would get over and above what you can get with just a prompt alone. People also don't explain their conditions particularly well. One of the key skills a doctor needs to learn is how to get the right information out of a patient, and LLMs are not particularly good at that right now. Often when we see the comparisons, it's in the context of perfect information. The task is: we've got all of the information, and then you're taking that and making correlations and suggestions.

I really like that you pointed out that along the continuum of even a consultation, this is one task, and it's remembering that there's lots of tasks along that chain. Some of them you need that skill and quality of care for. The task is making sure that someone's lived experience is taken in, heard, and computed— either by a human or a technology—but also bringing out through questioning and empathy other things that might be below the surface or not the real agenda of someone coming in. We can talk about accuracy, but how good a clinician is or how good an agent is—there's many layers to that. Extracting is a task as well.

So, I really like that you touched on that.

Yeah. Just going back to your question, I think different contexts have different counterfactuals. If you're talking about Baltimore—I live in Baltimore, I'm close to Johns Hopkins, and I could walk to the emergency room or see a MedStar or John Hopkins physician anytime I want, as long as I can get an appointment within a few months. The quality of advice I'll get is probably at the best level possible for humans.

But if you go to rural Bangladesh, the quality of advice you currently have is extremely poor. Even if you go to a formal-sector physician, you're getting 48 seconds of their time. So why would you not trust an LLM with the information that you can give it to provide you better advice than that? That's number one. Now, for different types of use cases, like you said, the evaluation needs to reflect what we're asking the LLM to do.

So if it's just basic question-answering, there is a test for that, which probably most of the QA- type benchmarks handle nowadays— essentially a question-answering process. But if you want to see how an LLM-equipped frontline provider—like a pharmacy or a community health worker—performs compared to a physician in that same environment, you'd need to run a different kind of test and evaluation. We're actually now funding an evaluation in India where we're testing what happens when you equip a nurse with an LLM and give the same amount of information to each of them and the physician in that environment, and see what is the treatment plan, triage, and differential diagnosis that you can get out of the LLM versus the physician. Those kinds of evaluations need to look completely different than the QA-type models. The standard for what you provide within a self-care environment...

right now, if you ask ChatGPT anything, it would spit out something. But there needs to be mechanisms for handoff. For example, if somebody in rural Bangladesh is asking a question about something that could potentially be cancer, there needs to be a handoff mechanism between ChatGPT and the local care provider to say, "You should go to this particular provider," and also alert that provider that there is a potential patient who might have cancer. Right now, we've not built those kinds of systems to hand off between health systems and AI. The guardrails that you need for a health provider equipped with AI also need to be completely different.

What I'm trying to say—maybe not very articulately—is that depending on the different kinds of use cases for AI, you need to design different benchmarks and different evaluations. You need to evaluate against the right counterfactual. Then you would know whether AI is ready for that particular thing and also set up the right risk mitigation mechanisms and guardrails. For example, we now know that ChatGPT is infamous for taking people down mental health rabbit holes. It's really bad for those kinds of situations.

If you're schizophrenic, for example, you'd be really ill-advised to use ChatGPT for your care. However, if there were mechanisms built in—guardrails such that if somebody is talking about things that the AI might hallucinate or provide bad responses to—there is kind of an external oversight mechanism, right? Somebody is checking in on that conversation and making sure to escalate at the right time. That's the right kind of guardrail that we need, which we are not thinking about enough.

Regulation, health systems, and clinical contexts are at variable levels of engaging with and thinking about those guardrails, while people are using these with great benefits and some of the challenges that you've talked about.

Just one last point on that—I think between different environments, because of the regulatory environments and also the counterfactuals, I'm pretty certain that the most exciting use cases and the most exciting impact of AI we'll see, at least in the first five years, will be in the low-resource context where the alternatives are just really poor. In the US, all of the talk is about ambient clinical scribes, which is great from the perspective of reducing the documentation burden on physicians and giving them more time for patient care, but it's marginal in terms of health impact. Whereas in low-resource settings—like the Indian context that I'm mentioning—there are no doctors. So if you equip a nurse or a community health worker with AI, the kind of improvements you can see in health outcomes can be quite transformative. So I'm really excited.

Then I guess it comes to other existential questions around when we will see the flip where we don't only get the health outcome benefit, but suddenly everyone's looking at solving those big upside problems because that's where the dollars are. The reason people are going for these marginal types of gains in the US and high-income settings is because that's where the money is and that's what people are paying for. Do you see that flipping, and when?

Thank you for having me.
episodes.pullQuote: Most of what we call healthcare happens outside clinics. If we ignore that, we miss the biggest opportunity for real impact.
episodes.title: Evolving beyond verticals and funding what matters in healthcare
episodes.description: A systems thinker, entrepreneur, and now investor, Rubayat Khan brings the rare perspective of someone who has been a patient, builder, and funder. We unpack what it means to move beyond vertical health solutions, how to prioritise innovation in an era of shrinking aid budgets, and how LLMs might unlock integrated, people-centred care in low-resource settings - including why a 48-second doctor consultation in Bangladesh makes the case for AI more powerfully than any paper.

episodes.bio: Dr Aral Surmeli is the Founder and CEO of HERA Digital Health, a nonprofit that helps refugee women and children access local healthcare through AI-powered digital tools. HERA has served over 300,000 users across Turkey, the Middle East, and Africa, providing immunisation reminders, prenatal care tracking, and digital health records accessible via WhatsApp and offline apps. The platform is open source, co-designed with local healthcare workers and refugee communities, and integrates with national health systems and NGO services. Dr Surmeli holds an MPH from Harvard and is pursuing a DrPH at Johns Hopkins. He is a former Innovation Fellow at the Harvard Humanitarian Initiative and has been supported by Google.org, Grand Challenges Canada, MIT Solve, and Harvard iLab.
episodes.guestRole: Founder and CEO, HERA Digital Health
episodes.transcript:
It was 2021 when we applied for the USAID grant. It took one and a half years of back and forth before we were approved. And these were not short back-and-forth sessions. Every time they sent us questions, we responded, and they responded. And honestly, it was a long process.

Yeah. And the size of the grant is not amazingly huge. But we also know that having the USAID name is the bigger thing because they do all kinds of due diligence. You being able to go through their due diligence means you have a high chance with other funders because they're like, "Okay, they have checked everything they can." So these guys are probably trustworthy.

We know that investors do that as well. In January, I think, we received the note of a stop-work order, which I was —I went onto LinkedIn and said, "I'm not stopping. You can choose not to fund me, but I'm just not stopping," obviously.

Mhm. But the biggest thing that people may sometimes forget is how much work you did to get to that point, which is a lost opportunity of working with other funders and everything. Because one thing is when USAID pulls out, a lot of other funders also pull out.

You're tuned in to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. We have a new vague background. We have a snazzy new website which you can check out at gpodh.org. This is the podcast sharing the insights and stories of people implementing digital health solutions and AI with underserved communities around the world. The goal is really to foster learning between different contexts for people who care about ensuring we don't leave anyone behind. With that in mind, we have a very relevant guest today.

We have Aral Surmei. He is the founder of Hera Digital Health, creating digital tools and solutions for displaced people, for refugees. We're going to be hearing about their journey and their challenges. I'm really excited about this one because I've talked to a few people—I've had a few meta-conversations recently about things like regulation, evaluation, and policy with Anna Librick from the WHO. But ultimately, all of that needs to translate down to the actual building, the actual implementation, and the actual impact for people, particularly vulnerable groups. So let's get into this discussion.

Aral Surmei, it's such a pleasure to have you on the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. Thank you for taking the time to join us. I'm excited because you are doing, you're creating, you're building, and it's always good to talk to people who are in the weeds and building. So, I'm really excited to get your insights. Welcome to the podcast.

Well, thank you so much for inviting me. I'm really happy to be here.

Yeah. Aral, why don't we start with you telling us a little bit about yourself and your background.

Yeah, so I am a physician from Turkey. I worked mostly in emergency rooms, ambulances, and humanitarian settings. The first nonprofit I founded back in 2013 was a medical rescue association. So we worked in disasters, worked with search and rescue teams to provide the medical side of the response. Then I moved to the US to do my Master's in Public Health at Harvard and am now doing a PhD in Public Health at Johns Hopkins. But my work started with the Syria crisis when the refugee influx started to Turkey.

I was working in the border cities and Istanbul, where there are more than a million refugees, and really seeing what they were experiencing. The good thing in Turkey is that we have free healthcare for refugees, which is amazing, but we also know that doesn't always mean that they have full access to healthcare. And that's what I was seeing in the emergency room and in the ambulance: children coming to my ER with vaccine-preventable diseases that we know how to prevent, but they just didn't know where to get the vaccine; or a pregnant woman bleeding in my ambulance because she didn't know if she could get pregnancy care. She didn't know where she could go, when she could go, which hospitals would accept her, and everything. So that's how we kind of ended up working on Hera. We realized that this is a very tech-savvy population.

So we thought, "You know what? We can use digital health solutions to help them get connected with healthcare." And that's how my work started. Yeah.

That's such a great origin story. So many stories start from you living or seeing people living the problem, and you saw it in the back of ambulances, you saw it in your ER. You mentioned—I wanted to pick up on something you mentioned. Can you elaborate? You mentioned that often these populations, although vulnerable, are tech-savvy.

Yeah, that is—I don't know if I should say counterintuitive for some people, but mobile phones, especially smartphones, are a lifeline for them. If you imagine you left your home and all your family and friends are dispersed around the world, the only way to get connected is your phone. So we often find that mobile phones are not a luxury but rather a lifeline for them and something that they really value. They may change phones or phone numbers, but especially in the case of Syrian refugees, that is their primary way of getting information. So that's how we went this route, I would say.

So let's continue on this path then. You had this insight that we've got a population that is suffering because they're not able to get the access and the information that they need. Although the healthcare is there, they're not seeking it at the right time. Yet they are engaged with their mobile phones and technology. How did you put those together? How did you then approach doing something about that?

Yeah, so actually the interesting thing was, I think it was my last year of medical school, and I had the opportunity to intern at Harvard's Global Health Delivery Center in Dubai, which was led by Salman Keshavjee, the head of Global Health and Social Medicine at Harvard, and Subhash Chandir, who was one of the leaders of the center there. He was working on digital health, especially vaccine reminders using Short Message Services. While I was interning, he was like, "Okay, you need to learn about this." So he made me read everything digital health on PubMed. Luckily, there weren't that many papers back then—it's not like now. But when I went back to Turkey, I thought, "Wow, this could actually work here." That's how I made that connection. Then the first step—which I think is very important whenever you're innovating or creating something new—is, even before that, just talking to the population.

So we started doing formal and informal meetings with potential target groups. But one other thing that we did, which I think is extremely valuable, was working with the Syrian doctors who—they could be formally working in Turkish hospitals or informally working—but they knew the population very, very well. So we went to them and asked, "Hey, what do you think about this?" But more than that, "What would be helpful? What would be the pain points that we can solve?" has been super helpful. So the first thing we did was really just doing a deep dive into the issues and how we can solve them.

So you sat down and listened to people who needed the care and the people who were at the front line of delivering that. And I think that's great that you engaged the Syrian doctors who really understood the nuances of particular types of problems that the people they were looking after faced as well.

Yeah. And there is also the cultural difference, right? You need to kind of understand people's health-seeking behaviors: when they want to seek help when they have the opportunity to do that. As a mother—they have one, two, or more children, which means they can't really just say, "Oh, I feel bad; I should go to the hospital." There are barriers to healthcare that are socioeconomic, cultural, and obviously being a refugee brings a whole lot of issues with it that you need to deal with, where it may lead you to not prioritize your health.

So yeah. What happened next? How did you go from that to then creating something that would solve the problems that they were facing?

Yeah. I'm not a technical person, and my co-founder wasn't either—he was a friend from medical school. So, we were two medical people who knew nothing about coding and wanted to do this, which was not something I recommend. Have a technical co-founder, for sure. So we had to learn it the hard way. But we started talking to companies and also some friends that had technical backgrounds to understand how this would work, what we could do, and everything.

It was a long process coming up with an MVP and trying different things.

And when was this?

2017, I think we started in 2017. Yeah. But the live product came out—the first version came out in 2019, I think.

Yeah.

But yeah, it was a long process of trying to decide on everything. Now, with AI, obviously, it's made things much easier. At one point I was like, "I'm just going to learn coding off YouTube for six months," which didn't work. But yeah.

I'm curious to know now, if you were starting now—I mean, with the proliferation of tools that help you, where generative AI is helping you create code—I mean, people are quite polarized about this. Often people say it's just a faster way to get technical debt, actually. What are your thoughts? Do you think—having gone through and worked with technical founders and realized the deep technical work that you needed to do—how much do you think if you were starting again, you could try and kind of spin up yourself?

Yeah, I mean, I don't have the technical expertise to say what can replace what, but what I would say or I would do is a quick and dirty pilot with an unfinished product using any kind of AI tool I have. My understanding is that, again, the finished, polished tool is not—at least most of it cannot be done with what we have right now—but I think it would be useful for compiling something and trying new things, new features. That's kind of how I would go because for us it was a painful process. But the bigger issue there, which we are trying to solve now, is you have technical people who are highly experienced and experts in the technical stuff. They know which language to code in, what to code, the UI, and everything. And then you have these field people, which is us, who know the context really well, but there's a miscommunication between the two because

they're not used to people coming to them and saying, "We want this to work on the worst phone possible." They're more like, "Well, I can make this work on an iPhone 15." It's like, "No, no, I want it to work on that brick." Yes. Yeah. So that was the painful part which I think, now that we have our own tech team, has been much better for ourselves and we're helping other organizations build their tools as well. But yeah.

And I think just in general, in my experience working at Ada and bridging the technical, product, and design with the clinical domain, your job there is really to help understand the context: where you need to go slow, where you can go fast, and how to think about something so our technical colleagues can turn that into, "Okay, I understand now the constraints in which I need to work; I understand the risks and understand we can work together on how to mitigate them. We understand now what the technical requirements are. We have, therefore, some clinical or field requirements from you." That sounds like a similar journey that you've been on.

Yes, definitely. And the context of refugees is much different than everything else we have.

Yeah.

And it's not a static condition or a static context. So you constantly have to adapt and change what you're doing. For example, right now we are discussing whether we can implement Hera inside Syria for the people who are going back.

Wow.

We've been talking to teams and people on the ground who are like, "Yeah, this would be super helpful." That's great. But also, WhatsApp Business doesn't work there yet. Facebook works, but Facebook ads don't work. The App Store— if you're connecting through 4G, it works, but if you're on wireless, it doesn't work. So there are things like that. If you design around those and they don't work, then...

And it's not the same as in Turkey. So that dynamic and ever-changing context is really important to keep your eyes on.

That's a really good one. I like that. And just backtracking a little bit, can you just explain exactly what Hera Digital—this app for women and children—exactly does?

Yes, definitely. So, right now the main goal is to connect refugee populations with available healthcare services wherever they go. We do this with an open-sourced mobile app coupled with an AI-powered chatbot on WhatsApp. What it can do is, first, help them carry their health records. It's as simple as taking a photo of it, and whether you lose your phone or your phone number, we still have access to those. Because as a doctor, when people come to my hospital, I don't need the whole medical history; I just need to see if you have these vaccines and stuff.

Another feature is helping them find the nearest health center. Because if you imagine, even as a tourist when you go somewhere, you don't know where the hospital is, right?

So imagine living in a new country with another language. Another feature is calling 911 services, especially if you don't know there's a free ambulance service. Most importantly, and where we think the biggest impact is, is helping them schedule immunization appointments for their children or prenatal care checkup appointments for pregnant women. We know these are the most cost-effective interventions we have in public health, and they're often free, but we need to help them prioritize and let them know when they can go and where they can go. This is essentially what we do. Over the last year, we have been focusing more on the AI-powered chatbot.

The reason is you can actually do everything that an app can do over that WhatsApp bot. If you adapt it culturally and make it context-aware, people actually prefer that, which is interesting because we spend so much time on the app, but it turns out people just want to chat with a WhatsApp phone number. So those are what we have right now. They're all open-sourced, so others can take them, make them their own, and use them. We have no problem with that, which is actually something I wanted to share later in the episode about how to become sustainable and everything. But yeah.

Super. Let's definitely get into that. So I'm curious to know—you've seen this problem, you've built something that helps serve particularly mothers and their ability to look after their children or their unborn children, to seek care when it's needed. You mentioned—what are you observing as the most common type of conversation on the WhatsApp tool? What are they finding useful?

Yeah, that's actually really interesting because we're always looking at the history of the chat: what people are asking, what people want to know, and everything. One thing that's been super helpful is questions about sexual reproductive health because these are culturally hard to discuss with another person, even if they're doctors or nurses. So that's something that people ask a lot about; they want to learn. Another side of it is, when you say "AI chatbot," everyone compares you to ChatGPT. So we get questions like, "Should I invest in Bitcoin?" to which we just say, "Hey, this is not what we do." But we do get those. But the most interesting part has been seeing the sexual and reproductive health questions, and questions they want to ask like, "Does this vaccine hurt my children?

What are the risks?" and everything like that. People not only use it as a tool but also to converse around health topics, which is what we aimed for.

And is this an off-the-shelf solution that you've then fine-tuned? Is it something you've developed yourself? What's the solution you're using in the back?

Yeah. My CTO would be better at answering that, but my understanding is that we use a couple of off-the-shelf solutions, put them together, and then fine-tune them and make them more context-specific.

Because none of the LLMs are trained with refugee data,

let alone in Arabic. You really need to

kind of train it and give it one-shots or off-shots

for it to understand the population and everything. But yeah, that's the thing to do because LLMs are pretty good right now. You don't need to develop yours, but making it work for your population—

which is not represented by the training data that these models are on—is the important part. Yeah.

And I'm curious as well about the cultural nuances. What's the type of work that you do to make sure that's relevant? Obviously, you're Turkish and speak Turkish. So are you involving the Syrian doctors in the fine-tuning as well, in terms of the Arabic, to make sure the health information is relevant not just broadly in the whole Arabic-speaking world, but actually for what's pertinent or relevant within this population?

On top of working with field organizations, grassroots organizations, and the Syrian healthcare workforce, one thing that has been very important and valuable for us—which I would recommend for anyone in this sector—is that we hire refugees. Our senior developer is a refugee himself. Before him, we also had a refugee. Our field team is mostly refugees or disaster-affected people. That's how you make sure that you have representation. And one thing with our senior developer that I love is that he has two kids and a wife.

So anytime we talk about features, he's like, "Hmm, let me go and ask my wife, because she is from the target population."

So you've got a fast feedback loop right there. Exactly. Perfect.

That's how you make sure there's representation and that what you build makes sense. He was recently in Syria to see if we can work with populations there, talk to people, and everything. So that's how we make sure what we do makes sense to the population that uses it.

Super. That sounds awesome. Do you have any data on the impact you've had that you can share with us? Any individual stories of lives that you've affected? I think that'd be really helpful for people to understand the type of impact you've had.

Yeah, definitely. I think the most striking numbers are: I think we have more than 40,000 people using our technologies—the WhatsApp chatbot, the app, and other technologies that we've created. On top of that, with the trainings and the fieldwork, our work has impacted 310,1285 people, if I remember correctly, both in the refugee population and in the earthquake zone in Turkey and Syria, which I'm really happy about because, considering the funding we've had until now, it's been highly cost-effective. Story-wise, one story that I like is about one of the Syrian doctors we work with, a pediatrician who is an amazing pediatrician and has been helping us build this from the beginning. One day he texted me—and he works as a pediatrician with children, right? He vaccinates them and everything.

One day he texted me, "Hey, I totally forgot about my own child's vaccines. And I received a reminder from the app, and that's how I remembered I need to..."

His own child.

Yes. And it's someone who routinely vaccinates kids. It's funny, but it also shows the life as a refugee—that you have so many things to do: get education for your child, learn your rights, and everything. And health loses its priority. But we know that vaccines are super helpful. So I like that story a lot, and also it's someone I know closely and am comfortable sharing about.

But yeah, that was one of the stories that we always find super interesting.

And that takeaway you have—that if you really want to understand that context... It's easy for us to sit here and do our desk research and get a very superficial understanding of what life is actually like. But that's a really great story—there are so many difficulties to juggle if you've been displaced. Even if you're a doctor who understands this, that falls off your priority list because there are just so many important things going on that you have to manage.

Yeah. I think that's a great reminder that if we really want to impact people in the right way, we really have to understand what they're going through. So that's a really good one. Do you have any stats in terms of health outcomes, lives impacted, or preventive successes that you've had?

Yeah, we are actually just finishing up a study that we did with the Ministry of Health. I think the biggest highlight, which will be published soon hopefully—I need to get on it—is the increase in uptake for pregnancy care appointments by 20 to 25%. Which is huge, because that would mean one extra prenatal checkup, where the baseline was 0 to 1 out of... Turkey still uses eight appointments during the pregnancy. So that scaled up would be a huge impact. I think that's the most striking one that we have some evidence for.

Yeah.

But other than that, we had 20,000 pregnancy or immunization appointments that we helped facilitate between the people and the local health services. A lot of things that people don't really realize is the translation—talking with your doctor—which has been used a lot. We thought of it as a fringe feature. "Hey, we should have that." But it turns out, on average we have at least 500 to 600 conversations every month. People talking to our AI translation tool, it talks back in Turkish. That helps them communicate with their doctors and everything.

But yeah, those are what we've been seeing impact in.

Yeah. And you were just recently at the AI for Good Summit in Geneva. We're recording this in July, so a couple of weeks ago you were there, and you reached the final of one of the competitions in terms of social impact. Can you tell us a little bit about that?

Yeah, Hera was a finalist in the AI for Impact awards. There were so many amazing organizations. First of all, the summit was great in the sense that we often talk about the risks and threats of AI, and being together with organizations that are obsessed with using it for good was amazing. Being in their presence... and the competition was between organizations that are using it to help vulnerable populations access services like healthcare and education. I got to meet amazing organizations, some using fetal movement to predict if there's going to be a risk to the child.

Humanitarian OpenStreetMap— they're an amazing organization that we work a lot with mapping services and such. But yeah, it was super interesting. Yeah.

Awesome. And before we move on to the next section... you've been doing this since 2017, you said, and now it's 2024. There must have been some big challenges, things that went wrong, things that you've really learned from. Do you want to share anything that you felt was a big thing that you got wrong, or that you had to kind of change course with or learn the hard way?

I mean, a lot. How much time do you have? But one thing is I did it part-time most of the time because I was also practicing. If I wasn't practicing, I was studying for my Master's and PhD. So that was the biggest difficulty I had. Another one, as I said before, was not having a technical co-founder.

If you are a field person or a health person, first find yourself a technical co-founder because you need that. That was the biggest

issue we had, and I'm glad to say that it taught us a lot. Right now it's much easier for us to build tools on the ground because we understand the context really well. Another one was obviously funding—that's always an issue. Innovation in high-income settings is something that's easy to fund because it's for a good profit or valuation. But innovating for humanitarian contexts is different, because not only will it not bring profit, but it could also fail because it's an innovation, so people are more risk-averse.

But yeah, those are, I would say, the biggest ones.

And I guess these settings as well... you mentioned at the beginning the context is always changing and it could change in such a catastrophic way that you've got no ability to go forward, I suppose. So that's always a risk as well.

Yeah. I mean, the traditional way of applying for grants involves writing a project that's five years long. If I could predict what was going to happen in five years, it wouldn't be where I'm working. I can't tell you what's going to happen in five years. I shouldn't be able to tell you, or you shouldn't believe me when I say, "Okay, in five years I'm going to be doing this." That's not how it works. Not only does the context change, but also, as we know now, technology changes a lot.

I shouldn't tell you that in five years I'll be using Llama... whatever. We don't know what's going to happen. So that's the difference and those are the changes.

Let's carry on this thread because what you've just talked about, especially in terms of challenges, left us with a good segue into the next topic, which was really around funding, the challenges of that, and becoming sustainable. This is a context and setting—refugee health and humanitarian settings—that don't lend themselves well to investor funding, and even donor funding can be hard. I know one of the ways we connected was post-USAID funding, and you've had the rug pulled from under you. I want to use your experience to go into the meta-concept that you've alluded to: what needs to change in terms of donor funding, financing humanitarian causes, and how do we think about it? But maybe let's start with your experience of having your funding cut and stopped.

Yeah. It was 1285 when we applied for the USAID grant. It took one and a half years of back and forth before we were approved. And these were not short back-and-forths. Every time they sent us questions we responded, and they responded. Honestly, it was a long process.

Not only that, we were the first ones to be accepted from Turkey for a USAID grant. So much so they said, "Hey, we don't know how to give you money in Turkey. Can we give it in the US?" And you guys deal with that. I was like, "As long as you give the money, I don't mind."

And you were in the US at the time, right?

Yes. So the team is in Turkey. We have the nonprofit in Turkey and a nonprofit in the US.

Yeah.

So it's not a huge problem for us.

Yeah. Okay. And the size of the grant is not amazingly huge, but we also know that having the USAID name is the bigger thing because they do all kinds of due diligence. You being able to go through their due diligence means you have a high chance with other funders because they're like, "Okay, they have checked everything they can, so these guys are probably trustworthy."

We know that investors do that as well. It's interesting to see that happens in the donor circles as well.

Yeah. So towards the end of last year, we got the news that things were not going to come through. We weren't sure back then what was going to go down—whether all of it would be taken out or just pieces of it, or if we were going to go under more scrutiny. In January, we received the note of a stop-work order, which I... I went onto LinkedIn and said, "I'm not stopping. You can choose not to fund me, but I'm just not stopping," obviously.

Mhm.

But the biggest thing that people may sometimes forget is how much work you did to get to that point, which is a lost opportunity of working with other funders. Because we were pretty sure we were going to get the money, we thought, "Okay, let's focus on this rather than going after different funders," because this was going to bring a lot of impact with the money we were getting. We had a randomized controlled trial we got ethical approval for and everything. So it was a difficult process. And one thing is, when USAID pulls out, a lot of other funders also pull out. Not us, because we were lucky that our funders were supportive of what we are doing and really tried to help us, but in many settings, that means the money is not only gone from USAID, but also other things as well.

That must have been hard. What did you do next?

I mean, it was hard. It still is hard. We barely were able to fill that gap, which meant that we had to go into survival mode rather than expansion. We had to let go of some of our people—the majority of our field team. And with the recent changes with the administration, other funders were also kind of scared about supporting the work.

And was that development funding, or was that philanthropic funding? What type of funders were the ones who were feeling anxious?

I think all of them. I don't have a specific example, but we can see funding pulling out of global health and a lot of work because everyone was unsure what to support or what to do.

Okay. So you observed it having a ripple effect on your ability to carry on and have the impact you were having. You had to scale back your work. How did you approach thinking about what you needed to do? How did you prioritize? "Okay, well this is how we need to adapt." How did you think about how to deal with that?

You were in survival mode and then you needed to move from survival mode to "How do I sustain here?" How did you think about that?

One kind of silver lining out of all of this was really focusing on the digital side of things—community engagement and making more people aware of our tools using social media, social networks, and everything. So that's what we've been focusing on. Another thing, now that we're mostly done with our fieldwork, was just diving into the statistics and the data that we're collecting on health impact, outreach, and everything. We spent a couple of months with the team just brainstorming and looking at the data, what we are doing, and everything, and it did help us a lot in understanding the impacts of doing this virtually or digitally. I wouldn't say that is the only way you should do it—you always have to be on the ground with the population—but there's a lot that can be done digitally, which was the silver lining.

Do you have any examples so people could picture it?

Yeah. We saw that, now that we had the energy, we tried different Facebook ads to see what resonates with people and different wordings. We saw that pregnancy-related ads or showing the features of our tools on pregnancy were more effective than those for immunizations. One thing we also saw was that while we were working on the ground, the majority of the people we were doing workshops with were women with children rather than pregnant women. And the reason is pregnant women usually stay at home instead of coming out. So we realized that an online way of reaching pregnant women was more effective, while for women with children of vaccine age, it was easier to reach them in the field.

So it was an interesting learning for us.

So you looked back at your data and thought, "What can we learn from this to refine and see where we need to change strategy? Where do we prioritize and hone down?" is what I'm hearing.

Exactly.

Very good. I think that's a really good lesson: sometimes we are trying to look externally and thinking, "Oh my god, what do we need to do?" Actually, sometimes it can be good to say, "Okay, well, have we really looked at what's—let's do an audit or really look at what's happening on the ground right now."

Yeah, it was great that you did that. So you then used this to see where you needed to prioritize. What happened then? How are you thinking —what's happened between then and now, and how are you navigating turning Hera into something sustainable in this backdrop of reduced development funding? Donor funding is also potentially drying up or being earmarked, and it's being hard to predict where the next vertical priority is going to be. How do you think about that?

How are you trying to navigate this as a founder and as an organization?

A lot of conversations with funders and other organizations are about sustainability. How can we be for impact but sustain with some sort of business model? Which is great, but there are risks associated with that. For me, especially in humanitarian aid, since we're never going to be asking refugees to pay for it, we are going to ask the Ministries of Health or UN organizations to pay for it, which is good. But that money also comes from funders. So either funders are giving me money to do that or giving the service provider money to buy services from me.

I have some reservations about how that is sustainable or how that changes the mathematics of it.

But we do have those conversations. One thing that I think is going to be super important is being open-sourced. My impact needs to be sustainable, not me. If my work is being done—I mean, if someone else is doing it, and someone else is doing it better than I am—I don't need to be sustainable. I can cease to exist. That's fine.

I think that's the difference that people often forget. It's not Hera that needs to be sustainable; it's my work that needs to be sustainable. And I don't mind it being used by someone else or someone changing the name. Honestly, I don't. I can go back to being a doctor. My mom still says, "Hey, when are you going to make money?" As a doctor, she thought we were going to be rich.

Mhm.

That is a thing that we need to discuss, but I don't have a clear answer, honestly, on where things are going to go from here. I know that the refugee crisis is not going to end. With the climate crisis, more people are going to be displaced, and our health systems are not designed for them. They're designed for people who are born and die in the same place. So we need to change the way we think about refugee healthcare. And I think what we're trying to do— something that moves with them rather than stays in one location— is our take on how we can provide care for refugees with Hera and open-source tools.

Absolutely. Some really interesting perspectives there. I really like what you said: "Hey, it doesn't have to be me or this organization that needs to survive; it needs to be the impact for people," which is a really interesting take. And the route to then make this open-source fits with that thinking. And also what you said around... with the way that the world is going, unfortunately, there will be consistently displaced people, whether it's due to war and conflict or due to climate change.

How do we make sure health systems are designed better for that, and also the digital infrastructure? I was at a conference called Health where there was a panel about refugee health, and one of the panelists talked about the fact that it's really key. We talk about access and the way the health system should be able to serve them. But in this world right now, having a digital identity is such an important enabler. And Alain Labrique from the WHO has said this as well: one of our big failings right now is that people who are vulnerable do not often have a digital identity. To me, it...

in public health we talk about the inverse care law, right? Those who need medical care the most are usually the ones who don't get that. And there's no better example there than vulnerable populations and displaced people. As we're building AI into everything and transforming digital health, this is a form of health data poverty that exacerbates the inverse care law. So I wanted to get your thoughts on this and how it's such a foundational thing. They talked about how you don't always need to think about getting an ROI from this; you just think about it as an investment in being able to give people high-quality care.

And yes, there may be things down the line. You've worked with refugees in the company and on the field. These are very resilient people who can contribute to society if they have a good start. That was one of the things that they discussed. What are your feelings around this? Do you have any thoughts around what's been mentioned there?

Yeah. First let me say that Alain is a hero of mine, and he used to be my PhD advisor before he...

You're at Johns Hopkins. He was there, right? Absolutely.

Yes, he was. Then he went to WHO. And this is right. Similar to healthcare, identity is also designed for people who are born and die in the same place. If that reality is changing, then we need to think about it as well. And ROI-wise, ROI is a tool to compare different interventions for the same outcome and see what is cheaper for the same outcome, or what costs the same but has a better impact.

It's not an absolute thing to look at in absolute numbers.

Whether you should go or no-go, or continue funding based on the ROI number.

In my case, it could be like, "Hey, sending reminders two weeks before the appointment or one day before the appointment is more effective and costs the same." That would be where I would use ROI. It's not, "Should you do it or not?" That's important. And also we have enough evidence from all around the world that—not just immigration, but refugees— having refugees in the long term has huge positive economic outcomes in that locality. We know this for sure. So ROI-wise, taking care of people is not just equitable; it's a human right. Those are not even up for discussion, but it's always a net positive.

That's for sure.

It's interesting because most political commentary in Europe and the US, particularly, does not talk about that. It's often framed as a big strain on resources and society. So it's well-documented what you've said, but that just doesn't filter down to journalism and political rhetoric. That's really poignant. I wanted to talk about what's giving you hope going forward. Things are pretty tough right now, and you've pointed out that you're still trying to navigate through this.

You've talked about going down the open-source route. What's giving you energy, motivation, and hope to carry on?

I often think about that myself as well. But I think events like the AI for Good Summit—where I get to meet people who are going through similar things and had their funding pulled but show up every day—give me hope. I'm part of the Fast Forward group and am an alumnus of their program. I get to meet with the teams quite regularly. Seeing them going through similar things—these are amazing people who have PhDs, computer scientists who could have been making a lot of money and had a much easier life... choosing this instead of focusing only on profit is what gives me hope.

And also, obviously, the communities that we work with— they don't get to give up, so I don't see giving up as something that we can just stop doing. So those are the things that give me hope, honestly.

That's a really good message. And if you are... I mean, you haven't asked me to say this, and this is just coming from me, but if you are an organization that cares about this, then give Aral a shout, honestly.

Yeah, definitely.

If you are funding this or you think this is important and aligns with your investment thesis or some priorities that you have, then hit up Aral. They could do with some help navigating this. Let's wrap up here. Maybe we could end with what... there are a lot of people who are maybe building in this space, trying to do something similar or adjacent to what you're doing, and are starting out on their journey. You mentioned one thing, which was: find a technical founder.

Maybe a technical founder is listening to this and thinking, "Well, I'm already technical."

Then find a domain expert. If doing healthcare, work with healthcare people. Yeah.

Yeah. Very good. Any other big takeaways or things that you want to share for people who are building or implementing in underserved communities around the world?

I would say, if you're listening to this podcast or this episode and you're in a low point—maybe you did not receive the funding you needed, you had a bad review from an advisor, or someone said "this doesn't work"— just keep showing up. It's not a direct path, and I'm not saying this as someone who succeeded or is finished. We're all in the process of it. I've been through enough lows to know that you go high after a low. So that's what I would say, because it can be a really lonely journey. Even if you're with a co-founder or have a couple of co-founders, it's really hard to share this or have people understand what you're doing and empathize with your work.

So just keep showing up. That's been the most important feedback I can give.

Keep showing up. I'm definitely going to be taking that away. It resonates with some of the things that I've been wrestling with lately as well. So that's a really good takeaway. Where can people get in touch with you and find out more about your work?

Check our website, heradigitalhealth.org, or do a quick Google search. You can also see some of our presentations and our work featured in different places. But yeah, get in touch with me. I'm happy to share my email and I'm always happy to talk and brainstorm about other tools, because this is a small group. We need to know each other and need to support each other. Yeah.

100%. That's a great offer. So if you're starting out on your journey... that sounds like a good offer to take up for sure. Aral, it's been so insightful to talk to you. Thank you for sharing your challenges, your journey, the things that you're trying to navigate, and for telling us this honest, authentic account of what you're going through.

Showing up for people who are displaced and who are refugees, listening to them, and building to improve their lives is a great inspiration. Thank you.

Thank you for having me and thank you for the insightful questions about things that people don't often think about.
episodes.pullQuote: The communities he is serving do not get to quit. Why should he.
episodes.title: Digital health innovation with refugees. A founder's story.
episodes.description: As underserved communities go, refugees are among the most vulnerable. Aral Surmeli is the founder of HERA Digital Health, which has built an AI-powered tool serving Syrian refugees in Turkey - initially targeted at mothers-to-be and mothers with young children missing antenatal and child development appointments. This is not a shiny rainbow story. It's about real struggle, USAID funding being cut, and what it means to keep going when the communities you serve don't get to quit.

episodes.bio: Nick Martin is the Founder and CEO of TechChange, a social enterprise that has become a leading provider of digital health training and convening solutions worldwide. Under his leadership, TechChange has trained thousands of Ministry of Health officials in more than 90 countries through flagship programs including Digital Health: Planning National Systems, developed in partnership with USAID, WHO, and Digital Square. He also leads the Global Digital Health Forum, the premier annual gathering for policymakers, donors, researchers, and implementers working at the intersection of technology and health.
episodes.guestRole: Founder and CEO, TechChange
episodes.transcript:
Nick Martin (00:00)
I've been a little disappointed by the public displays of funding that have emerged. What I have heard is that foundations are doing more in the shadows to support, but they do not want to draw the public attention of the administration. I hope that's true. I've also heard from a lot of organizations that they don't have as long as they would like to make the pivots - and that the work they're doing is mission critical for the people they serve and they don't have a way to deliver on that. Philanthropy as a whole, and there are many exceptions, has not moved publicly as fast and as decisively as I was hoping. Nobody wants to fight this administration. I understand those things. But I was hopeful there would be more stepping up, and there hasn't been.

Nick Martin (02:03)
I was a modern poetry major in college at Swarthmore and studied peace and conflict. My father was set on me becoming a CIA agent - we got in a big fight about it. I ended up teaching English literature and then found a program in Costa Rica doing education, peace and human rights with a United Nations flavour. I came back thinking: technology is disrupting education everywhere. Maybe there's an opportunity to connect those dots specifically for the humanitarian, global health, and global development population and bring new kinds of training to them using the power of tech. That was the origin instinct around TechChange. We were lucky to grow up at a time when distance learning was just becoming available, and we married that with a whole slew of experts willing to share knowledge in cohort-based learning settings. Founded in 2009.

Nick Martin (07:27)
If you'd asked me what wasn't great about the before times: I do think USAID had gotten quite large, and there was not a ton of coordination in certain parts. And as a sector, we did not do a great job of making the case to the American people for the importance and value of global aid. That got very easy to politicise without a strong lobbying infrastructure or voter base. People vote based on issues that affect their lives. Our very small niche just didn't have that populist support. That made us an easy target.

Nick Martin (10:52)
That Friday, everything fell apart. I was on a phone call with Catherine Rayfelsen who leads Society for International Development when the executive orders dropped. In the following week it got quite real. My first instinct was to get a website up - globalaidfreeze.com - to give people a way to share the stories of how they were being affected. The response was overwhelming. Journalists contacting me. Thousands of comments on posts. But what I want to remember from those early days is not the cruelty and the flippant nature of this decision - it's the way the community rallied. The resilience and the generosity were tremendous.

Nick Martin (15:09)
The project I know best: we ran Digital Health Planning National Systems - a longstanding partnership with USAID's Global Health Bureau, going into countries ministry by ministry to train senior officials in how to digitise and strengthen their health systems. We had a whole year planned. Destroyed overnight. We have a waitlist of over a thousand people who are hungry for this training. The Gates Foundation has come in to support some of it. But this is the slow, prudent, hard, challenging work that is required in strengthening health systems. The effects of losing it will carry forward for years.

Nick Martin (18:34)
Eight months out, I think of this as a period of reckoning and reimagination. Crisis forces creativity - that's a truism I live by as an entrepreneur. We're seeing organizations think creatively about mergers and partnerships with each other. We're seeing groups pivot to selling services directly to governments, thinking about their offerings as products. At TechChange we're launching an accelerator to help organizations with that transition. And then there's another camp that are going to have to wind down in a dignified way. For individuals: many amazing humans lost jobs and are now figuring out what a portfolio career or consulting looks like. It is a very complicated and challenging market.

Nick Martin (39:28)
We're entering a period of scarcity, and I think you have to be really honest with yourself and your colleagues about what the runway looks like. Can you pivot your business model? Does it make sense to merge? Is it better to gracefully wind down? For people earlier in their careers: be on the wavelength that learns AI skills. The blend of technical abilities plus sector sensibilities is a powerful combo. Constraints and chaos breed creativity. When we started TechChange in 2009, nobody had jobs. We were able to build something beautiful because talent was available and people had energy to put into something new.

And wherever you can - often and always - prioritise learning and community. We are in a state of constant reinvention as humans, not just in our sector. The more you shift your mindset to never stop learning, and scaffold that journey with incredible humans and community, the more powerful you will be for any of these shocks and challenges that arise. Build your virtual community and prioritise it in your trajectory. Sharing is caring.
episodes.pullQuote: Nobody wants to fight this administration. I understand that. But I was hopeful there would be more stepping up - and there hasn't been.

We talk about the USAID funding crisis: what happened, what it revealed, and what the sector needs to do differently. Plus: the Global Digital Health Forum, fail festivals, and how to navigate a career and an organisation in a world of scarcity.

topics: Program theory and logic models: connecting intervention to intermediate steps to outcomes - not just the final number
The inSCALE study: evaluating a digital decision support tool for CHWs treating malaria, diarrhoea, and pneumonia in children under five
The unexpected finding: facility staff, not community health workers, were the main driver of improved outcomes
Why understanding how it works is as important as knowing that it works - for adaptation and scale
Formative research and co-creation: how to generate hypotheses on what to measure
Iterating during implementation: network outages, older CHWs, changing app partners mid-study
The community health worker who started a solar phone-charging business with the trial equipment

episodes.bio: Dr Shay Soremekun is an epidemiologist and Co-deputy Director of the Centre for Evaluation at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Her research focuses on child and adolescent health in low and middle income settings, including trials of low-cost digital disease prevention programmes. She is a member of the UK Government Evaluation and Trial Advice Panel (ETAP) and sits on the steering committee for the John Snow Society. She lectures at postgraduate level on evaluation, epidemiology, and public health, and leads an MSc module in Study Design.
episodes.guestRole: Epidemiologist and Co-deputy Director, Centre for Evaluation, LSHTM
episodes.transcript:
Dr Shay Soremekun (04:25)
I work with the Malaria Consortium - a worldwide charitable organisation that looks at ways to prevent and control malaria in endemic settings. They approached us about evaluating a digital intervention to improve the care that children receive for suspected malaria, diarrhoea, or pneumonia. Together those three are the largest killers of children under five in sub-Saharan Africa. These are treatable conditions and many of the deaths are completely preventable. But historically health worker capacity has not been great, particularly in rural areas where community health workers are the last mile provider.

Community health worker programmes were introduced with fanfare two or three decades ago, but over the last ten years they have been chronically underfunded. CHWs have felt poorly supervised, poorly trained, disconnected from the wider health system. Drugs and diagnostic tests in their kits weren't replaced promptly. Our goal was to design a digital intervention that addressed these concerns - to co-create it with them and thereby lead to improved treatment of children.

Dr Shay Soremekun (07:43)
The intervention was a smartphone programme providing clinical decision support to community health workers in the diagnosis and treatment of children with suspected malaria, diarrhoea, or pneumonia. It also improved their reporting to facility supervisors, gave them automated and personalised feedback from their submitted data, and enabled free calls to other CHWs and facility staff. Because electricity is unstable in the areas in which they worked, we gave them a solar charger and multiple charging pins for different phone models.

We used what we call a program theory - an approach to design and evaluation. We proposed that improving treatment of children would be based on a series of mechanisms of change: the intervention would lead to improved CHW performance, motivation, and retention, which would ultimately result in improved coverage of children receiving appropriate care when sick. We created a logic model to show this whole process, and agreed a set of indicators right along the proposed pathway - not just the final outcome.

Dr Shay Soremekun (12:49)
We ran a randomised controlled trial across large areas in Mozambique and Uganda. Areas that received the digital intervention versus those that didn't were randomly assigned, so we can be quite certain about the causal pathway. We saw improvements in appropriate treatment of children of between 10 and 26% - really good for a pragmatic trial.

But our process evaluation revealed something unexpected. The community health workers in both groups - intervention and control - showed similar levels of motivation, connectedness to the wider health system, and performance. What we actually found was that facility-based health workers provided better care where they had access to the digital package. A major area for true focus was not community health worker care, but facility care.

And it made sense - our qualitative research showed facility staff had expressed a desire to have access to the smartphones too. There could have been tensions if it was perceived that the CHWs had received extra support and they hadn't. The lesson: we need to take a wider, systems-level lens. Supporting the final-mile workers is exemplary, but it is often not enough.

Dr Shay Soremekun (18:52)
We didn't identify what to measure by accident. Before the trial, we spent two to three years on formative research in both countries - speaking to families of sick children, community health workers, health facility staff, mobile phone network operators, local and national government ministers. We did a pile-sorting exercise where we looked at various possible interventions and whittled them down to what stakeholders thought would work in their area. We did a large literature review on digital interventions - how they work, in which contexts.

All of that is published in separate papers because it really is a big job. But that process is how we arrived at our program theory. And then I remember days of workshops in Mozambique and Uganda - making lists and lists of intermediate indicators that we were both counting. Working with people on the ground who knew the context. Some things you might want to measure aren't even feasible to measure in a given setting. That's only something the people on the ground can tell you.

Dr Shay Soremekun (23:21)
We found a community health worker who had started a side business: charging his community members' phones for a small nominal fee using the solar charger and pins we had provided as part of the trial. He showed us his account book. He was so happy - it had increased his standing in the community, helped him feel more confident when treating children, and provided a small income. We thought that was brilliant. He was resourceful, he was offering a service to his community at a reasonable price. And we liked that very much.

Dr Shay Soremekun (27:52)
Our biggest challenge was network coverage in sub-Saharan Africa. Particularly in Mozambique, we just couldn't predict the level of network outages. And we had some difficulty with adoption among older community health workers who were well respected by their communities but found the smartphone a bit difficult. So we had to constantly take information in and adapt iteratively.

The first change: store report information on the phone so they didn't have to be constantly connected. They only needed to upload when they had network coverage - no deadlines, no timelines. We also learned you probably do need IT staff physically in the country to fix phone problems. You can't do that remotely.

Dr Shay Soremekun (33:12)
At the Centre for Evaluation at LSHTM - a school with historical links to the colonial past - we wanted to move away from a model of evaluation where you identify a problem in someone else's setting and then solve it using methods developed in high-income westernised countries over centuries. That disconnect is one reason why interventions often don't scale or get adopted even when they show positive results.

We want to make evaluation more equitable, relevant to low and middle income settings, and decolonial in approach. That means: who decides what matters? How are the people most affected by an intervention involved in designing how it's evaluated? Co-production - making sure the right people are leading the design on the ground - has a massive impact not just on evaluation quality, but on the chances of seeing success and the chances of it being adopted.

We're about to publish a scoping review of papers characterising indigenous evaluation methods - whole ways of knowing the world that we don't consider because they come from people who historically haven't been empowered. We're also publishing a position piece. These methods, incorporated into how we do evaluations, can transform the chances of an intervention actually reaching and benefiting the communities it's meant to serve.

Dr Shay Soremekun (45:02)
How to measure what matters: co-create your evaluation design with people on the ground - those who will conduct the research, those exposed to the intervention, and those with the agency to scale it. Consider your evaluation not just around a hard impact endpoint, but around the context in which it's being delivered. And try to measure things in that context.

For digital health companies choosing clinical outcomes: do formative research. Talk to the people who are going to be affected. Once you've produced a program theory - how does your AI intervention achieve its impact? - create a logic model mapping every stage. Then agree on indicators all along that process, not just the final outcome.
episodes.pullQuote: To understand why it improved care, if it did, was as important, if not more important, than understanding that it did.
episodes.title: Evaluation level up: Measuring what matters
episodes.description: Everyone's talking about LLM evals and benchmarking. But ultimately people care about impact - and impact is rarely a neat linear path to a yes/no answer. Dr Shay Soremekun of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine shares what it took to evaluate a digital health tool for community health workers in Mozambique and Uganda: program theory, logic models, process evaluation, and an unexpected finding that changed everything.

topics: Digital identity for displaced people is broken - and how this creates very real barriers to care
Two stories: a friend who fled imprisonment with no identity documents, and a Ukrainian mother whose daughter's chronic illness nearly went untreated
Why statelessness blocks not just healthcare but the ability to attach any human rights to a person
The collision of law, politics, healthcare, and innovation: why this problem keeps not getting solved
Whose data is it? Moving from records about refugees to records owned by refugees
Data security risks unique to displaced people: governments as bad actors, data that could be used for persecution
The inverse care law and health data poverty: the people who need algorithmic decision-making most are least represented in the training data
The business case problem: a refugee's health shouldn't live or die by a VC return timeline
What founders building digital health tools should do right now - even if refugees aren't their primary user group
episodes.bio: Nadia Kadhim is co-founder of Naq, an automated compliance platform for healthcare and digital health companies. With a background in international humanitarian law, child rights, and privacy from Leiden University and years as a privacy officer, Nadia co-founded Naq to make regulatory compliance accessible and meaningful for health organisations. Her father was an Iraqi refugee, and her passion for human rights and digital identity for displaced people runs through everything she does.
episodes.guestRole: Co-founder, Naq
episodes.transcript:
Nadia Kadhim (00:00)
How do we ensure that these people can access that data - and just the people that they want to share it with can access that data - at the time that they need it, at the place that they need it? I think we need to stop thinking about records about people and about refugees, and start thinking about records owned by refugees and displaced people themselves.

Shubhanan Upadhyay (00:24)
There are 43 million people displaced through conflict and environmental disaster. Refugees, through no choice of their own. The likelihood of this is going up. The likelihood of you being directly affected by this is going up. And yet our health systems are not really set up to deal with people who have come from a different place accessing healthcare.

Imagine you've had to leave at very short notice your home with your family. You've barely scraped together some documents. People don't speak your language. You have acute healthcare needs - maybe someone is hurt, sick, or has suffered trauma. How do you tell people what chronic conditions you have when you don't know the language? Maybe you have a health record in your country, but there is no way for anyone to access that in the clinic where you are trying to get your insulin. If you don't get it, you will end up in a really bad situation.

Nadia Kadhim (02:58)
My early career started after I did my law degree at Leiden University and a master's in international humanitarian law, specialising in child rights and the legal aspects of child abuse. I really just wanted to help the most vulnerable people in society. After my master's I became a privacy officer at a child protection organisation - my first introduction to privacy. The problems I saw with tech and privacy compliance and cybersecurity led me to start Naq with my co-founder Chris.

My father is an Iraqi refugee. His travel to the Netherlands in the early 90s was traumatic, as it is for millions of people around the world. My personal interest in helping people, in human rights and refugees, comes from that lived experience. And my work today is grounded in data - because data is power. Data can enable innovation. But a lack of data can block innovation, block adoption, and block human rights. The right to access healthcare is enshrined in international law. But that right is massively impacted if there is no data - and no legal identity - to attach it to.

Nadia Kadhim (13:48)
At the heart of this problem: it's very difficult to have rights attached to data, or even the right to healthcare, when there is no legal identity. We're talking about statelessness. Some estimates say 250 million people have been displaced over the last 10 years. And if you factor in the climate crisis, this will only increase. All the very necessary innovation in healthcare is focused on people like you and I who can go on holiday, who even if they don't have their digital patient file ready, have the means to communicate. Imagine when that isn't possible - when there's a massive language barrier, a cultural barrier, a lack of money, and no documents.

Nadia Kadhim (15:21)
Two examples. A friend of mine fled a conflict situation after nine months of imprisonment. They came to the Netherlands after a long time on back roads and on foot. They were sent to a refugee camp. Once shelter and food were sorted, there was finally space to think: am I healthy? But they had lost their passport - it had been taken. They had no way of using healthcare provisions in local hospitals. The lack of identity was a direct blocker to care.

The second: I spoke to a group of healthcare professionals and mentioned the need for a digital identity owned by the displaced person themselves. A woman came up to me afterwards. She was a refugee from Ukraine, travelling with two daughters, one of whom had a chronic illness. She couldn't remember everything - vaccinations, allergies, medications. She didn't have the language. She was too traumatised to start explaining. She said: this is exactly what I would have needed. Unfortunately, she is not alone.

Nadia Kadhim (22:20)
Why hasn't this been solved? Because it cuts across law, policy, politics, healthcare, and innovation. One of the core issues is recognition - just as countries need to recognise territories, a person needs a recognised legal identity to have rights attached to it. What counts as identity in one country, one hospital, one emergency care tent, is different throughout the world. That requires legal change, multi-stakeholder collaboration, and a very uncomfortable question: who pays?

I often say a refugee's health shouldn't live or die by a VC return timeline. This immediate ROI logic can't be applied to a problem at the intersection of healthcare, law, politics, ethics, and basic human rights. We need to measure returns differently: prevention of public outbreaks, social integration, economic contribution, human dignity. If we can't provide basic infrastructure for the people who need it most, our definitions of value need to change.

Nadia Kadhim (38:22)
One thing we haven't discussed: data can be used for harm. Electronic patient files contain very sensitive information. In certain countries and contexts, data about someone's sexuality, beliefs, or political history can be used as a reason to persecute them. So we really need to think about data holistically: accessibility, interoperability, compliance - but also security from potentially bad actors, in a context where government itself can be a bad actor.

And ownership. Who owns the data? We need to move from records about refugees to records owned by refugees. How do we ensure they can access their own data, share it only with who they choose, at the time and place they need it?

Nadia Kadhim (45:37)
For digital health founders and builders: your tool might not be built for refugees - but could it be? Is it built with ethics in mind: transparency, interoperability, security? If so, you are already building something that could potentially be used by these very vulnerable groups of people - whether that is someone in a conflict situation now, or your neighbour in ten years who has to find another place to live because of rising water levels.

Don't think of ethics and compliance as a tick-box exercise. Think of it as putting humanity at the centre. When you do that, you are already part of the solution.
episodes.pullQuote: We need to stop thinking about records about people and about refugees - and start thinking about records owned by refugees and displaced people themselves.
episodes.title: Why displaced people need a digital identity
episodes.description: There are 43 million people displaced through conflict and environmental disaster. Their likelihood of accessing good healthcare is already poor - and as we race towards algorithmic decision-making, they are becoming invisible in the data underpinning it. Nadia Kadhim, co-founder of Naq and daughter of an Iraqi refugee, explores what digital identity and data ownership really mean for displaced people, why this is an everybody problem, and what builders, policymakers, and funders need to do differently.
