But it's also very similar in the sense that there is almost like a sort of wink of "Oh, we have to put it in somewhere," referencing, "We must increase the diversity of the AI workforce." And all it said in there was the fact that 22% of the AI workforce is women. Like, okay, yeah, that's not great, but that is also a product of the wider pipeline. Fewer women go into data science in general—that's largely because I think the way that math is taught in schools is deliberately unappealing to women, but that's a whole other thing.

But that is a tiny, tiny, tiny fraction—and I'm saying this as a woman—but it's a tiny fraction of the meaning of the word diversity. It's got nothing in there about the fact that you also want people with different varieties of lived experiences. That means you need to have diversity from the perspective of sexual orientation, but also gender expression, people of color, and people who have different neurodiversity experiences, because they're all of these different things. And then the points of intersectionality. If you want to design a diverse workforce, you don't design it so that you have 50% women and 50% men—that is not a diverse workforce.

You want to design a diverse AI workforce from the perspective that we are designing tools that affect every single aspect of every single person's life. Therefore, the fundamental point of diversity has to be making sure that we have diversity in terms of lived experience. I think that was really, really missing. Again, I think had this thing been written three years ago, maybe there would have been more of those conversations in there. Instead, everything has been whittled down to metrized conversations.

Because the other one we haven't mentioned yet, but we should because it's the elephant in the room and people will yell at me if I don't: the whole conversation is now about safety instead of ethics. People will say, "Oh no, they talk about making sure that the AI Safety Institute is beefed up." Yeah, great, but "safety" is a tick-box, metrized thing. It has got nothing to do with the wider conversations with regards to social implications. But it is easy to achieve and it's easy to put in your budget. What we've navigated so far in the conversation is to break it down into two manageable chunks.

One is the policy determinants of how you elevate good outcomes in terms of equity and the other ethical principles that you mentioned. The other kind of stakeholder that's key in the room is the vendors and the builders. You've mentioned big tech and some examples of that. What's your take on how we can get ethical principles from being a "nice-to-have" to a business priority for a vendor? What's your thought on this in terms of Jess Morley's "state of the industry"?

Just the state of the industry. So, I think there are a few different ways of talking about it. The first one is the reason why people—especially vendors and especially SMEs—are sometimes reticent. I know this because a few years ago we went out and surveyed people. We spoke to them and I did interviews, and I was basically like, "What is it that prevents you from doing these things?" The number one comment was: "It's expensive and it eats into the bottom line." To a certain extent, I have empathy for that.

I think with everything being about ROI, I do think there is this underlying fear that we are in the middle of an AI bubble that is at some point going to burst, and all of the investment is going to drop out. I think, therefore, people are keen to avoid that by turning around big and fairly rapid returns on investments. That return on investment tends to be interpreted as economic return, not a wider social definition of value. So I do understand that, and I'm not coming in and trying to bang people over their heads and be like, "Oh, you must do this and you can't operate like a normal business." That would not be good. I also should say that I don't believe in role-based ethical probity.

As much as I am a massive champion for the public sector and civil society, and have spent the vast majority of the last 12 years championing the NHS, I don't believe that public sector is automatically good and private sector is automatically bad. I think there are actual blurs between those two lines, and we shouldn't immediately be rapping people on the knuckles just because they want to make money for their investors. Where I think there are ways in which we can change the conversation is: first, I think we have to get away from this narrative that ethics is just an extra thing. You can build ethics into your everyday practices without it necessarily being seen as an extra thing. For example, there are lots of good practices that are just actual good software design.

Doing good, pragmatic software design is a way of supporting ethical principles. If we are talking about things like making sure you have representative datasets and making sure things perform equally for everyone, there is a way of seeing that as being really annoying and, "Gosh, this is extra expensive, I have to go and collect data." There is a different way of seeing it: "Well, this means I get to sell my product to more people." Yes, maybe that's annoying to have to jump through those extra hoops, but those are actually principles that just come from best practice in software design. All we are doing is now expanding them to say that we also want that to have a social element. What I often talk about is: how do you get to the MVEP—the minimum viable ethical product? Then we can level up, then we can jump through hoops.

But actually, what are the things that really just mean we don't treat things with AI exceptionalism? We don't just let them get away with it just because it's AI. So you build those concepts into your everyday business as usual, rather than seeing it as an extra category of thing that you need to do. The second thing is: yes, I do think policy has an enormous role to play in this space. This is the point I made at the end of my post on LinkedIn about the AI Opportunities Action Plan.

Obviously the proof is ultimately in the pudding. Most of the time, what's going to matter is: what does the government actually do? How does this translate into where money flows? Where do we see the development of standards or guidelines or procurement practices? All of these things are signals—or what you might more formally call "levers"—that enable ways of changing the behavior of people operating in the environment.

But it's not just about that. Rhetoric actually has an enormous influence. Sometimes people roll their eyes and say things like, "Oh Jess, you're sounding too much like an annoying social scientist." But rhetoric has an enormous amount of shaping power because that is how people go in and pitch. That is how people try and win contracts with the government. That is how you get grants as an academic researcher.

That is how you sell your product in terms of advertising spiel. All of that is rhetoric. I think we have lost good shaping rhetoric from the government with regards to saying that these things are what we want to see. I would like to see some of that coming back in, because even without the harder levers, that soft shaping is really important. The third one—if we want to be super skeptical—is that at the moment we've framed this entire conversation about it being a "nice thing." Like, "Go and have ethics and good principles to achieve better outcomes." That's a very positive way of framing it.

The more skeptical, cynical way of framing it is: this also stops you from having egg on your face. This comes back to my point about the difference between the rules of the game and winning. The clearest example of this I can give is the government's repeated mistakes, first of all with care.data and GPDPR. For those listening who don't know, very briefly: there was a project back in 2013 where the government wanted to pull everybody's electronic health records and make them accessible to innovators. There was massive public backlash; they paused the whole thing.

Then in 2021, they tried to do the exact same thing, and the exact same result occurred. Now we are seeing the exact same conversation coming up with the idea of creating a National Data Library. Now let's think about ethics versus the law. All of those projects were entirely legal. There was nothing in there that was illegal; they can 100% do all of that.

Where they failed is in what social scientists call the "social license." They failed to understand that actually there was a reticence from a social perspective. Understanding that social reticence is where ethical thinking and ethical foresight analysis can play a role. If you really just want to strip it back to the cynical context, it is also about making sure that companies and governments understand that if you do this type of thinking—these activities that I'm saying you build into your everyday practices and don't see as extra costs—you ultimately see them as risk mitigation. It's a risk-mitigating strategy to prevent you from getting egg on your face, avoiding chilling effects where people stop investing in you because they think your product is a failure and nobody wants to buy it. I really like that.

Actually, if I relate that to my own experience, the times when it really worked was when we used it in pre-mortems— like risk-storming sessions where clinicians were talking with designers and engineers about: "Hey, we're going to be deploying in this context. Applying ethics as a quality pillar, what could go wrong here? Therefore, what do we need to do?" I see a line towards being able to operationalize and justify that internally. As an AI engineer, you want to justify why we need to spend effort on this. Within the machinations of a company that's leaning into building good products through a QMS and through regulation, it makes sense, right?

I take that away—that the reason it's a business priority is we're trying to make sure that we create a great product that users and clinicians really like using, and the health system will actually say, "Hey, that was great, we want to keep you guys because you get it." So I reflect that, yeah, that's the way to make it a business priority. Thank you. So we've talked a lot about the UK context and the US context. If I'm a health minister or a chief digital officer in an LMIC country, and I'm observing what's going on in the US and what's in Jess's hot takes on the opportunity plan: how do I apply this to my context as a healthcare decision-maker or to my healthcare system? What principles do I need to take?

Can we go into like a 101, but applied to these types of contexts? You touched briefly on social acceptability. I interpret that as cultural understanding and cultural context. If you could weave that in, that'd be great. First of all, I should declare my positionality.

I come entirely from either the UK or US perspective, and I wouldn't want to talk on behalf of people from different countries with different experiences. But set aside, from my view on this, there are a couple of things. The first one is really just avoiding falling foul of any narrative that AI or digital health is the solution to improving equitable access, or that it is the solution to getting away from issues of clinician bias. Those are two things that come up particularly in LMIC contexts or rural areas. This idea that AI will solve the access problem and any discrimination because AI is going to be more "objective" than a human.

So 101 is: avoid that type of thing. This leads me to my bigger point: think critically. Boil this down to a basic set of questions: Why is AI the right solution to this particular problem? Could this be solved with a different tool? What resources do I need to actually make this work?

And paired with that: Would those resources be better spent elsewhere? The clearest example of that: there is no point in having a very fancy algorithm that does great diagnostics and predicts the best treatment for a person if those treatments are actually not available in the context within which you are deploying the system. In that scenario, you might actually be better off investing in just buying the drugs. The third question is: Who decided? Who decided that AI was the right solution for this?

That is where I'm getting into the cultural context point. Social acceptability is: Are people happy to hand over a specific task to an algorithm? That is going to be hugely culturally variable. People forget that definitions of illness, health, and aging are culturally specific. How we handle death and end-of-life care varies enormously.

There may be some cultures where they're happy for there to be a digital mediator. There will be other cultures where it would be completely inappropriate for those conversations to be had by anyone other than a religious figure or family. They would be really antagonistic to a digital mediator. So, where was the decision made? The next basic question is: Who does it work for?

Does it work in my context—both for my population and my system? The last one is: What is the long-term impact? Is this helping me achieve my wider strategic goals? I frame this as "form follows function." We often lose these conversations and assume we just want to adopt everything. Adoption is the best thing, rather than asking: "What is it I want to achieve with my healthcare system?" and then working backwards from there.

I think that's a big thing that's missing. I observe that AI becomes a goal in itself. Particularly in the LMIC context, it's often a big donor who decided we're going to fund LLMs in this context. What wasn't thought of was: "Hold on, what are we trying to do here? What are the health outcomes first?" Because of economic factors, FOMO, and vibes, it's suddenly "the biggest opportunity of a generation." It might be, but only if we do it right.

Exactly. And what are the knock-on effects of that type of reasoning? If you have huge investment in LMICs for predictive models trained on electronic health records, the first thing they realize is that there is no electronic health record. So you bring in a company from the UK or US. They build that record in a way that reflects their context, not the local context.

That has massive shaping effects, and it makes that country beholden to an external company. Whereas there are opportunities in these places to leapfrog. Maybe we don't need investment in electronic health records; maybe we'll see benefit from ambient AI running in the background on your own device. But to get that, the signaling has to come from the local context rather than being imposed by big foundations or donors who decide what worked in their place should work here. To me, that smacks of digital colonialism most of the time.

There are more sophisticated ways of thinking about it. You've touched on the "why" of this podcast. I want to have more conversations about examples developed and implemented locally. Sometimes we in the NHS or US should be learning from them. For example, US Secretaries of State visited Eswatini for the EMR for community health workers they built there and were like, "Wow, this is a game changer; we should learn from this." It relates to an earlier episode where a funder said, "We're funding you to go in and listen.

It's okay that you don't know what the intervention looks like yet." Co-design it. It might be AI, it might be something else, but you've listened. To me, that seems like a great way to think about this. One thing I want to touch on: you talk about adoption. People might push back and say in these places there's a critical shortage of healthcare workers.

AI can help bridge this gap, therefore AI is the solution. That ticks the box of, "We've seen the problem and here's the solution." What's your take on that argument? My most cynical response is: AI is not a hammer, and not every thing is a nail. Sometimes people perceive me as being very anti-AI. I'm not; I'm actually hugely enthusiastic about its potential.

But my main thought is: be skeptically optimistic. Go in with enthusiasm, but keep your eyes wide open about the limitations and have those awkward conversations up front. This comes up in the NHS too: what's better—having nothing or a low-performing algorithm? Should we only ever deploy algorithms that are 100% safe, or nothing at all? I cannot answer that because it depends on the specific context.

But make sure you've had that conversation up front. Be aware of the trade-offs you are making. When you deploy these systems, as we see in the UK with automatic triaging, you are creating a two-tiered system. People who need the system the least have access to a human, and those who need it most but have least access get treated by digital solutions and algorithms. Morally, because "something" may be better than nothing, we might be okay with that—I'm not sure we are—but it's about being honest and going in with your eyes open.

And again: Is this really the best solution? Could we take this money and do something else that might be better? If the answer is no, then by all means throw AI at it. You've covered a lot. Do you have a summary for vendors— product managers, designers, founders?

What can they take away and action in their everyday work? Actually, it's probably the same for everyone. My biggest takeaway is: don't fall foul of AI exceptionalism. Anything you would apply to any other form of technology, apply it to AI. No clinical safety officer would buy a blood pressure cuff without knowing it was calibrated and tested.

So why would I do that if I was buying an AI solution? The same applies to policy folk. If I have a stringent procurement framework for other technologies, I would do the same for AI. Do you see regulation as an enabler for making sure ethical principles get upheld? And on the procurement side, how do you make vendors who lean into quality and equity win contracts rather than the ones who cut corners?

Regulation at the moment has a really bad reputation. It's often "pro-innovation regulation" or "regulatory flexibility." This doesn't compute. We can think of regulation as an inherent good. We can design regulatory-friendly innovation rather than innovation-friendly regulation. Design it so it is an enabler, not a stifler.

The other thing is: it's just boring. We like to talk about AI ethics as if it is entirely novel. It's not. We know how to do this: it's contracting, procurement, and licensing. You don't want this product used for people it hasn't been tested on?

That's a licensing thing. Put it in the end-user license agreement. You want to make sure outcomes are what they said? That's in the contract. If performance starts to drift, I have the right to terminate the contract.

Procurement is about how you design the framework. If we want to elevate these principles, we put them in the framework and score people appropriately. Then you make contracts public, auditable, and FOI-able. It's phenomenally boring, but some of the greatest, most successful things come in the boring. All of these things sound like they could be great.

If we come full circle, you said we've gone backwards and everything is about economic growth. Do you think these things will actually happen in procurement? I worry about that too. But framing this as procurement, contracting, and licensing—as opposed to "ethics"—might help it happen. It makes it seem more in line with the current state of play.

This is my skeptically optimistic take. Perfect. I want to wrap up, but tell us about the Yale Digital Ethics Center. We look at GELSI—the governance, ethical, legal, and social implications of technologies at large. We look at how to design a better digital future.

Not just in health; we have pillars for content, reality, and regulation. I just happen to be the health nerd. A couple of months ago, you had a session in Venice with global experts. We hosted "Global Health in the Age of AI." We tried to break down silos. Often you get techies over here, ethicists over there, and lawyers in a different room.

We tried to make people talk to their neighbors. It was productive; we were on a private island off the coast of Venice. You should see the consensus paper coming out in the next couple of months. We'll keep an eye on that. How can people find you?

I exist in a lot of places. I'm no longer on the website formerly known as Twitter, but I am on Blue Sky and LinkedIn. My email is public: jessica.morley@yale.edu. You post articles regularly, and your "health data nerd" stuff is very informative. I've learned a lot from you over the years.

Quick takeaways: 1. We've gone backwards. Before, being pro-ethical was a strategic advantage; now, the focus is on economic growth. 2. Build ethics into your everyday product thinking.

It’s part of building a good product. 3. Think critically: Why AI? Who decided? What is the opportunity cost?

4. Be skeptically optimistic. Is that a good summary? Definitely. Thanks so much for the conversation, Jess.
episodes.pullQuote: Don't fall foul of AI exceptionalism.
episodes.title: Making ethics actionable in digital health
episodes.description: What does it actually mean to make ethics actionable - not just aspirational? Jess Morley shares hot takes on the UK's AI Action Plan, Ethics 101 for vendors and policy folk, how health system leaders can elevate ethical approaches in their ecosystems, and what builders at health tech companies can do when ethical imperatives meet business realities.

topics: How Rwanda balances top-down mandates with frontline adoption to foster trust
Tackling antimicrobial resistance with clinician decision support as a case study
Systems thinking to measure success in evolving interventions - Andrew's "contribution lines" approach
Rigveda's wishlist for the ecosystem: from WHO priority areas to better alignment on patient journeys
Infrastructure, policy, and trust as the key elements for making digital health innovations stick
episodes.bio: Rigveda Kadam is an experienced global health strategist with expertise in digital health, AI, and public health programmes, driving impactful innovations and policy alignment. Andrew Muhire is the Chief Digital Officer at the Rwanda Ministry of Health.
episodes.guestRole: Digital and AI Lead, FIND · Chief Digital Officer, Rwanda Ministry of Health
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to this episode of the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. This is the podcast that unpacks learnings from people implementing digital health and AI for underserved communities globally to help you break out of your bubble and give you fresh insights on meaningful impact at the last mile of healthcare. Really excited today. We're changing up the format a little bit; we've got two guests on the podcast. We've got Rigveda, who is from FIND, and also we've got Andrew Muhire.

He is the Chief Digital Officer of the Rwanda Ministry of Health. Having that political aspect covered in this discussion will be so valuable, and to me, it's a really good connector to the previous episode we've just done, talking to an innovator who was working supporting mental health with digital tools in Rwanda as well. So today's podcast is really about the layers around supporting that work, like what enablers do you need from a political and infrastructure perspective? For me, that's really exciting to be able to connect the dots on that. Let's get these insights.

Rigveda, Andrew, thank you so much for joining us on the podcast. It's a real pleasure to have you here. I think it's going to be a very rich discussion for anyone in the global digital health space. Let's start with intros. Let's start with you, Rigveda.

I would love to hear about the work that FIND does and your role there. Thanks, Shan, and thanks for the opportunity to participate in this podcast. It's also my first time on a podcast, so I'll try to do my best. I lead the digital health and AI portfolio at FIND, the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics. It is a nonprofit that was created more than 20 years ago now, and it's a WHO Collaborating Centre for diagnostic evaluation and lab strengthening.

The work that FIND does is essentially supporting product development and innovators, as well as evidence generation and product introduction for diagnostics and diagnostic services in the context of low- and middle-income countries. We are a nonprofit, and we are funded via grants and government aid. We work with, now I would say, 400-plus partners across multiple countries, our biggest country offices being in Switzerland and in India. More specifically to the topic of the podcast, the work that we do in digital health and AI is a cross-cutting unit, so we essentially work across a number of health areas and disease areas. For example, one of the things that we've done, especially in the context of the COVID pandemic, was supporting countries in looking at their diagnostic data and responding on the ground at a primary and community healthcare level, but also looking at it at a national level to identify potential hotspots and how to essentially tailor their response in the context of all that data.

The digital health and AI work is to identify what are the current and potential problems impeding diagnostic service delivery and then, of course, how digital health and AI, if it can and where it should fit in, can address those problems. And so, are you working in particular with health ministries? Where do you fit in terms of the layers of the ecosystem? We work with ministries of health, national lab programs, as well as in-country research partners. For example, for product introduction or around policy shaping, we would work with ministries of health to look at how and if diagnostic products and diagnostic policies need to be modified and how they are currently being implemented.

But then if it is, let's say, an earlier stage, a relatively new product that needs more evidence to be generated to understand if and where it has value, we would work with in-country research partners to develop context-specific evidence that can guide overall policy development. One big part of our collaboration is with diagnostic manufacturers and innovators themselves, who we want to make sure are supported adequately as they are working to address these important challenges. So you sit in this layer between government organizations, and then innovators, healthcare delivery, and infrastructure? Yeah, that's precisely right, and that's reflective of this category of organizations called Product Development Partnerships, of which FIND is also a type. Perfect.

Thank you for that comprehensive overview. Let's move over to you, Andrew. It's really a privilege to have representation from a health ministry, particularly from Rwanda. By the way, the podcast that was released just before this is interviewing an innovator in Rwanda around mental health solutions; they're called YLabs. I think this is so great to have the completing of the circle.

We've had an innovator in Rwanda working on the ground, and then we've got FIND, who is a layer between, and then we've got the government layer, the infrastructure layer, and the decisions that need to be made on what enables them. Please tell us about your role and what your focuses are at the moment. Thank you. Yeah, thank you, Shan. Actually, I'm Andrew Muhire.

I work for the government and Ministry of Health Rwanda. I'm the Chief Digital Officer in charge of digitalization at the Ministry of Health. My background: I started working with the Ministry of Health since 2011, and since then, I was really contributing to the digitalization process. At that time, there was a pressing area that the Ministry of Health was really establishing to be able to have a Health Management Information System. So from 2013, I was the head of the Health Management Information System until now.

Currently, I'm heading digitalization, as I said. What I could say is that I am an IT professional by background, but I also have epidemiology, so that makes me fit well in the Ministry of Health and also digitalization. What I could say about Rwanda or the Ministry of Health is that AI is part of our digital priorities. We have seven priorities; among seven priorities, we have AI. And the good thing with Rwanda is that we have already laid the environment to support AI.

That's why you can see we have different partners working with us to make sure that we explore how AI could really improve the processes at the health facilities, but also the treatment of patients. Perfect. I think one of the things I perceive from the outside is that Rwanda is seen, particularly in Africa, as one of the pioneers of how to invest and think about digital infrastructure in general, and creating these conditions to allow the right innovations to thrive. So it's really great to get your insights. Okay, I think we've got lots of areas that we could talk about, but maybe we'll start with you, Rigveda.

FIND works across many types of ecosystems and many types of low- and middle-income country settings. As you sit in this layer between innovators and infrastructure, and then enabling or helping ministries to make good decisions on implementation, you probably have quite a good insight on what drives good innovation, what challenges there are, and what the barriers are. What's your read on the situation globally, and maybe we can then get into some examples. Yeah, sure. The work that we do at FIND, I think what we try to use as our source of truth is essentially the insights that we try and collect from end users, ministries of health, and all the partners that I mentioned.

Because especially when you're working on innovation and the more emerging tech side of things, it's often easy to get lost in the shininess of all the tech that comes towards you. What we did at FIND a few years ago is that we mapped out, via some 60-plus stakeholder interviews across four countries, along with 500-plus patient surveys, we mapped out what were the pain points and challenges both at an individual user level, at a patient level, at a healthcare worker level, and also at a national health program manager level that were stopping people from accessing diagnostic services or diagnostic data as and when they would want to. Using this as a framing, we then have used that to guide our work on what technologies or approaches should be prioritized. The outcome from all of that was, in the context of AI, guiding our work across four pillars. The first pillar is around the pre-point of care at an individual level.

The biggest gap is that individuals want to have access to trusted and quality information in a timely manner. So how can AI and digital try to address that in the diagnostic but also in the broader sense? The second category of our work is at a point-of-care level, around supporting healthcare workers and clinicians in understanding what is the context-specific, up-to-date set of guidelines around screening, testing, treatment, and monitoring that they should be using across different disease areas. Because a person coming to see a community health worker does not come in a TB workflow or a malaria workflow; they just come with a problem. The third category is around health program support: how do we make sure that tech innovations are supporting health program managers to manage supply chains better and conduct surveillance more effectively?

And then finally, it is more of an ecosystem kind of area where, especially in the case of AI, there is a lot of work that still needs to be done around regulatory and evidence generation support. So that, in a nutshell, is how we are structuring our work. I really like that because it starts with the on-the-ground challenges, particularly starting with access. I like the way that then mushrooms out from there. It starts with the beginning of the person's journey before they even seek care: information as a determinant of health, right?

Access to high-quality information. And then, yeah, how do you enable, once someone has gotten to the right care at the right time, how do you enable that care to be as good as it can be? And then how does that fit into disease areas that might be a priority at that time at a public health level? And then, the broadest ecosystem that supports that. So I think you've highlighted really well the different layers, centering it around how this affects and connects what's going on at the patient level and the overall health system level.

That's a great outline. Is there anything else in terms of the challenges that you've seen? Maybe to make it more concrete, let's use an example. Even while we start with this broader structure to help us figure out which problems we should be focusing on and prioritizing, I think there are still some non-AI-specific and also some AI-specific things that need to be done. For example, let's take radiology as an example.

If you look at the approvals that the FDA has done for software as a medical device that include AI, depending on the date that you look at, 70% to 85% of the total set of approvals are around radiology. If you look at the demand or the user side, the Lancet Commission on Diagnostics has flagged that there is a clear gap when it comes to access to imaging in low- and middle-income countries. In a multi-country survey, only 2 out of 22 countries had imaging technologies available at a primary healthcare level. And this is despite the fact that, if you were to rank the global burden of diseases by DALYs (disability-adjusted life years), 7 out of the top of these diseases have imaging as a tool that can help address that disease. All that to say, on the innovation side, there is innovation, if we were to take the FDA approvals as a proxy.

On the need side, clearly there is a need. But then why is it that we are not moving as fast as we can? X-rays and ultrasounds have been around for a while, and now we of course have AI. As I was saying earlier, there is a non-AI component to it that we cannot ignore just because AI has arrived on the scene, around infrastructure and investing in non-digital infrastructure but also digital public infrastructure. But then with AI, there is an opportunity to address some of the challenges around access to trained personnel.

That's the part where first making sure that you are designing with the user becomes critically important. Because what we are looking at, apart from the infrastructure part, is getting people to adopt something that's new and that has so many different perceptions out there. Will it take away my job? Is it something that people are going to hold me accountable for if it makes a mistake? These are some of the challenges that we do need to address even when it comes to AI.

I wanted to bring your perspective, Andrew, in here. Do you have any examples from the Rwandan perspective to improve some of the challenges of implementation? Yeah, thank you. Actually, we're working together on different AI tools that we are really implementing in Rwanda, including the radiology one. For our side, actually, I liked the idea of the patient journey.

Most of the platforms that we are implementing—I mean digital platforms—we are much more centered on the patient. Looking at the Rwanda context, you can see that the patient starts at the community, then at the primary, which is the health facility, then at the tertiary on top. In the whole flow, we are looking at the use cases that can really make it easier for the patient to have the better experience while they are moving through the flow. The first one was looking at the community health workers, to see what could we do to make AI really help community health workers to interpret some of the samples or exams that they perform, and make it easier for them to take decisions. We have one AI for community health workers that interprets RDT tests.

Then from that interpretation, it makes it easier for the community workers to be able to know what to do at the end of the day. It's like interpreting the guidelines and standards and making sure that at least the system is able to interpret the image from the RDT. They just take an RDT, then you take a picture of the output, then the system will say, "Do A, B, C, D; this is what happens." Another one is reducing the overuse of antibiotics. That one also, we have really implemented this, and we have a proof of concept. now we are looking at how we can inject it into our overall electronic medical record.

So maybe those are the two, including the radiology that also we are looking at. But again, what I could say here is that using AI in the patient flow and making it add value for the clinician and the patient reduces those challenges and resistance that we were talking about. 100%. And if we use the mapping out that Rigveda had mentioned at the beginning, of those four layers of the ecosystem, I think the examples that we've mentioned here are really at the point of care, right? How do we enable and create value at the point of care?

That's really great, like creating standardization of interpretation of rapid diagnostic tests. It's so important. And also, absolutely, a WHO global priority to reduce antibiotic overuse. To me, as a clinician as well, I wanted to get into this thing around how that is perceived on the ground by healthcare workers. So, either community health workers or even physicians or nurses on the ground where, of course, at a health system level, the decision to say, "Okay, we need to standardize and make sure that there's reduced antibiotic prescribing," is important, and most clinicians would say, "Yes, absolutely, that needs to happen." But then implementing a tool that is, at one end of the spectrum, assisting that decision, but at another spectrum of interpretation, it's like it's making that decision for me.

How does that land on healthcare workers in Rwanda? Do you see challenges there? How is that being adopted and accepted as part of a new way of delivering care? Yeah, that's a good question. Actually, first of all, everything starts at the policy level, where you have a policy that you have to reduce the overuse of antibiotics and also enforce the standards of treatment.

In Rwanda, we already have the standards for antibiotics and treatment that guide clinicians on how they have to prescribe these antibiotics. What we did was take the AI and use it to enforce the policy. Then what happens is that the clinicians continue the way they are doing their practices, but the system at the end of the day will suggest and say, "This is the medication you should give." It doesn't stop you from taking your decision, but at least at the end of the day, it shows: "These were antibiotics that were given that were not supposed to be given; this was the one that was given that was supposed to be given." At least that makes them, when they are discussing internally, see what the overuse of antibiotics was. They have statistics like, "20% of the antibiotics prescribed in this facility were not really based on evidence for prescribing it." At least for that situation, you can see that AI can go through all the decisions we're making, and it's able to tell us what we are doing that is not aligned with the standards. Coming back to clinicians, they see it as an added-value tool, because at least it's like another eye that tells them that even though you took this decision, you didn't consider A, B, C, D.

That's why we found that many of them were really happy to have that tool that can be able to guide them. But again, on the other side, some of them may feel as if we are forcing them not to do it the way they are supposed to do it. Maybe some of them will even say that that 20% was supposed—maybe the tool didn't... but again, the more you work with them, the more you bring them into the way the algorithms are being configured, they most of the time find that the tool is really adding value to what they do. That's really useful, because I think it relates to what Rigveda was saying earlier which is, you really have to involve the end users.

End users are not just patients; they are the clinicians who are delivering care, particularly when you have clinical decision support systems especially, right? If you want a decision to be supported, there are so many pillars to driving that trust—explainability and making sure that it makes sense in terms of the guidelines, and how clinicians are able to interpret those results. Ultimately, for any healthcare worker, they would think, "Okay, yeah, this technology is all well and good, but the clinical liability falls on me." And so it's great to have these things that help me think of certain things that I might not have thought of, but ultimately, the clinical decision comes down to me. Being able to see it and rethink how we make decisions and where it fits in that decision flow seems to me like an important enabler for healthcare workers to trust this. Do you also get feedback where clinicians feel threatened by this kind of clinical decision support?

Actually, this is a new area that we are trying to bring into the existing practice, and it's a change management issue. Some of them may feel that you're bringing another person to take decisions on their behalf, then they feel threatened that AI is taking over their role. But I think most of them think that it's really simplifying the way they are treating patients. Instead of taking much time to think and take decisions, there's another tool that immediately tells you, "Look at this, and this, and this, and this is the interpretation of what you entered." Since it is something that we are trying to bring into a process that existed long ago, that's why working with them and having them give input in the whole process makes it easier at the time we want them to use it. Resistance is there, but designing together and having them participating reduces most of this resistance from the side of clinicians.

And I think that comes full circle around the idea that if you involve people—communities and patients—they're more likely to trust it. The same goes for clinicians. Thinking about that as co-designing, co-developing, or implementing together for people, rather than forcing things on people, makes them much more likely to adopt those tools. Then you really do get the overall benefits because it's actually being used. Rigveda, do you have any other examples from other parts of the world of how this has either gone well or not so well?

Sure. While we are on the topic, I do also want to mention the Principles for Digital Development. These principles were put together by a number of stakeholders working in the digital health space and are shepherded by DIAL. In a sense, it's kind of like a handbook to ensure that digital innovations and work, including AI, follow a set of principles that have been put together based on years of successes, failures, and lessons learned. One of the key principles there is designing with the user, but then also how do we define relevant stakeholders and users?

To your point, it's not only the patients or individuals who are receiving care, but the people who will use the tools. In that context, in our work, we've seen a couple of models as to how country partners have chosen to engage with stakeholders. For example, both in India and in Kenya, partners have chosen to engage with these stakeholder groups—with physicians—to try and understand how they perceive the use of AI in ultrasound and what are some of the concerns that they have. For example, one of the concerns: even though task shifting is something that is possible with AI-enabled ultrasound, there are concerns around what it means to task-shift, and at a community health worker level, what would be the changes in policies, checks, and balances that would be needed. There is this model.

Then the Digital Transformation Office in Indonesia has taken another approach, which is looking more generally—without getting into product-specific use cases right away—at how we just engage with clinicians more broadly, educate them on broader applications of AI in health, and give them an opportunity to surface some of their concerns. We've seen both these working, but I think it's important to have that space. We've seen resistance to adopting AI-enabled ultrasound in some contexts because some of these concerns that have been voiced in other areas weren't actually socialized or consulted on in the specific geographies where it's happening. Absolutely. I think this is such an important takeaway.

Ultimately, whether you're building or whether you have a top-down policy that you need to impose, you need some kind of bottom-up buy-in; otherwise, it just doesn't happen. Aligning incentives, creating the conditions, and involving people... for example, the example that you've used, Andrew. The top-down policy and the mandate that needed to come from the government was, "We need to reduce the overuse of antibiotics." Working with the idea that we might have some opportunities with technology, but how do we work with you to do that? There might be some other layers around the technology as well that help drive reduction.

There might be other reasons that are not solved with technology. Rigveda, you mentioned the non-AI aspects and then there's the AI aspects. There might be a lot of other reasons and drivers for why antibiotics may be prescribed. For me, if you've got this kind of initiative or priority, AI or any digital tool is like one part of that, but actually, to solve the problem, we need to think about all of the factors that contribute to that. Otherwise, the other things are still happening.

Maybe there's increased pressure from the community, or people aren't educated about what antibiotics do, and so they are insisting to the healthcare worker who maybe just wants to say, "Okay, well, this person is insisting, I don't want to get in trouble, just take it." That's another driver which won't necessarily only be solved by AI. That was another reflection on thinking holistically about the problems that we're trying to solve with point of care and access to information to ultimately achieve the goals that we want. Any reflections on that from you, Andrew? Yeah, actually you are pointing to the reality. It's not only AI, looking at the antibiotic example.

You will see that there is this patient pressure. When we are discussing as patients—because I'm also a patient—you'll see a patient saying, "Ah, this is the better doctor because he gave me this batch of medication, but this one, when you go, he just says 'No, no, no, no, go and take water.'" So I think there's that pressure. But again, what we are talking about is: are we able to track the magnitude of the problem so that if we are enforcing the policy, at least we have a tool that can tell us, "Even though there is this pressure, the pressure has this weight." When you are talking about awareness and bringing in the patient side, at least when you have data, it makes it easier for you to plan for awareness and bringing different stakeholders to make sure that the problem is addressed from different corners. The problem we had at that time was that there was no data on the magnitude of overuse of antibiotics. Bringing in AI, at least, it is able to pick some cases from different corners; then at the end of the day, say it's at 20%, 10%, 5%.

That way, it makes it easier for the policymakers at the Ministry of Health to take decisions. That's very useful, and I think it's related to the podcast that I did with Richet and with Khushi Baby, talking about community health workers in India. That was that sometimes we rush to reach this outcome—we've got this ambitious goal, and let's do it and drive, and that's really important—but actually, first, we really need to work with people to actually get the real on-the-ground reality. I translate the similar type of problem that Richet was talking about with TB: needing to understand the ground reality of how bad the situation with TB was, rather than saying, "Okay, we need to get rid of it," so everyone's reporting that there is no TB. I feel like there are similarities or parallels here because it's important to reduce antibiotic overuse.

If you come in very heavy from the top, then people might not interact with it so well. But actually, if you involve people and say, "Okay, we need to do this together. Let's work with you to find out, through good data collection, what is the situation with antibiotics," you get a real sense of the reality and the shape of the problem: which antibiotics are being prescribed, where are the particular types of organ systems or types of illness where it's being over-prescribed? Then you might be able to have other types of campaigns, like patient education campaigns. Like you said, driving good government decision-making or health system decision-making by actually knowing what the shape of the problem is on the ground through good data.

I just wanted to press on that because I think that was really valuable and connected to previous podcasts. AI is a tool to help us get to the goals that we are hoping for in healthcare and in health overall. Really thinking about and attaching it to the use cases across the healthcare system through the four layers that you talked about, Rigveda. I think that's a really nice way to bring that all together. Okay, I wanted to move on.

One of the areas of work is evidence generation and clinical evaluation, and the overlap this has with layer four, which is around regulation and the overall ecosystem. Even in high-income settings, sometimes measuring the right things and evaluating the things that matter is difficult. How is this in LMIC settings? I would speak more narrowly to the work that we are doing, of course, driven by what we've understood from the needs of our partners. But to your point, I completely agree that in terms of identifying measurable outcomes for AI-driven interventions, I think there's a lot of work to be done still as to what you are looking for.

Are you looking at cost savings? Are you looking at improved quality of care? Are you looking at better clinician and individual interaction? That's one area that we are looking at via focus group discussions with healthcare workers in partner countries. The bulk of our work has been around supporting clinical evaluation of AI-driven diagnostic innovations.

The problem there that we're trying to solve is that if you look at the AI product life cycle and if you look at the generally non-AI evaluation life cycle, there is a huge mismatch. If you look at IVDs or any other health product and if you look at how much time it takes to generate evidence, it's measured in years. By which time, you will probably be on version six or seven of the AI product. So what we've been doing is working with partners and the WHO's Tuberculosis Program, and we've set up this Rapid Technological Evaluation Platform where partners can install AI software and where we then have been able to collect—again with our research partners—sets of data sets. Chest X-ray images, let's say, which have been collected from different WHO regions; they have been annotated and have metadata.

Then these software programs are rapidly evaluated on these data sets, and then each of the evaluation points is compared also with expert human interpretation. The entire process itself tries to rapidly look at how the AI software performs against the standard of care in this context, which is human beings reading chest X-rays. That's been something that we've been working on for two or three years now, and it's been really a pioneering effort. We are supporting the WHO to apply that for chest X-ray image analysis software developers for tuberculosis screening. That's been one really great learning experience for us as well.

I think that's particularly important because we live in a world where an AI algorithm is developed in one context, and sometimes people think that it's very easy to then just copy and paste it into another context. In some ways, some principles apply and are generalizable, but some things need to be adapted to the local context. It sounds like what you're doing is being this validation layer that helps people, prior to being implemented in a certain context, to have some independent or objective view on how your model or your product is faring. I guess that gives assurances to decision-makers like Andrew. It's fine that something is developed in another context, but I want some assurances that this actually works in my local context and is appropriate, and the outputs are appropriate and appreciate the nuances and the issues around the population.

The product itself is not only clinically adapted, but locally and culturally perhaps adapted as well. I think that's an important thing. The WHO has done a lot of work on this, like the focus group AI for Health, trying to do this in other modalities as well. This is an important piece of work. If you can give us a link to that platform and that work...

if anyone is in this TB space and wants to look at that, then they'll be able to access that. Yes, definitely. Incidentally, we call this platform the Validation Platform. It's around AI software validation. Rapid evaluation and getting these assurances is really important.

When we talk about outcomes and we talked about how things affect people who are delivering care and patients... you mentioned also the differences between hardware medical devices or medications, like drugs, and then the nuance of difference between software as a medical device. Part of the measurement of success is also: what impact does this have for people? And so, for me, there's also this qualitative aspect, which I think traditionally academia maybe scoffs at: "Oh, it is less good because we want hard numbers," right? But it seems to me in discussions that I've had, that it's actually very important to have, especially when we're thinking about adoption and trust.

Do you have any insights around measuring qualitatively the experience of healthcare professionals or patients in terms of their use and interaction with digital tools? Ultimately, that's going to be a marker of success. Definitely. I also want to say that if you look at the private sector—some of my friends are working in these big FMCG companies—for any product launch, focus group discussions and qualitative research are a key part of the product launch strategy. To understand contextual drivers of adoption and barriers to adoption, these tools are really a key part of making sure that the product being launched is actually fit for purpose.

For us, for example, for a digitized, community-level, integrated disease screening algorithm, we had conducted—with our partner in Kenya, Jomo Kenyatta University—focus group discussions with community health workers to understand how and if they would want an integrated, digitized approach to going into the communities and screening. There were some really great feedback points. One was being able to understand that there is... at least in that population group, they didn't have any resistance, aversion, or fear of having the tool come in and substituting what they are doing. But they did have very concrete feedback, which is that it needed to be very agile and they should be able to work with it very quickly.

Second—and this was more on the policy side—they felt that the current community-level guidelines did not cover the needs of the communities. Why are non-communicable diseases not included in the digitization? Really, I think that was a good way to not only uncover brand-new insights, but a way to document and share that this is what is needed. Sometimes we are just so focused on the optics and the success that we want to create that we miss opportunities to learn. Then it becomes a very black-and-white thing, like, "Was this a success or was this a failure?" whereas actually, it's a continuous learning process.

For me, this part that you've mentioned is an integral part of how you build those insights. How do you set yourself up as an organization, health system, or implementation partner to know that we need a mechanism to actively seek out these insights and plug them into the improvement cycle? I think that's really key. Another thing that you mentioned, Rigveda, was cost-effectiveness. Everyone talks about cost-effectiveness.

From a ministry perspective, Andrew, you're thinking about investing in the infrastructure or investing in this innovation. You as a ministry or government need to see that it's cost-effective and perhaps have some ROI that you can report back. How do you think about this? Sometimes it's not just the intervention itself that will give you ROI at the beginning. How do you guys think about this, especially with Rwanda being more forward-thinking, knowing that you have to invest in the conditions, and it can take some time before you see the big gains?

It would be great to get your reflections on this, Andrew. Thank you. This is a good question for researchers and academia, but at the Ministry of Health level, actually, the healthcare environment is complex. Improving the process there requires a systems-thinking approach. Many components are connected to contribute to what you want to achieve.

Maybe bringing in the AI perspective... the way we are handling AI, we're not handling AI as a tool to come and connect all components. When you bring in the systems-thinking approach, we bring AI into the area where we feel it can improve and contribute to the overall environment. For us, our way is embracing technology and AI, and then it leads to the quality care we are talking about. On our side, the reason why we invest is because we take a task; we don't take the overall care.

We just take a task and say, "When we look at the whole process, we can see that this task, if it can be taken by AI, it can be better performed than by a human, or it can contribute to the human." Our evaluation will just go into the small task where we really injected AI to see: how was it before, and how is it after? Then we can compare. As I always say, if it was taking longer to interpret the images—say, it took 1 hour to interpret an image—and we put in AI and find it taking 30 minutes, we just say the contribution of AI is 50%. If it's screening, and we knew that we didn't have people to go to each village and do screening, and we put in an AI machine and it's able to screen at the village level, we just say, "Before there was no screening at the village, but now we have screening at the village." That is how we are interpreting it and that's how we evaluate it. But I think it's not a question of AI only.

Even when you read scientifically, there's less evidence on how digitalization contributes. It's not easy to attribute the contribution of digitalization, including AI, to overall quality care. I think you've summed up in a nutshell the real challenge, right? You have this intervention that somehow everyone needs to say, "Did this thing work?" and therefore you need a baseline. But the paradox for me is that it's not just this thing in isolation; it changes so many things in the whole interaction and the whole way that we deliver care.

There's this old adage: "A rising tide lifts all boats." The way that might translate is, "Okay, we have this initiative, we're going to have AI, and therefore we're going to do all these other things to make sure that the AI works." I like the way you thought about attribution or contribution, recognizing that some of it will be directly due to the tool and the implementation of the tool, but some of it was just related to how people changed what they were doing around that as well. It's okay to think about it like that. Medicine and healthcare in general, and life, is just much more messy than putting it neatly into a box. I really like that this thinking embraces that. Even though it's complex, it still gives you some way to know how things are doing.

It relates to Stephen Gilbert's podcast, where he was thinking that in terms of regulation and evaluation, we should be thinking about systems overall and not just individual components of AI. I think that's a really great point. Moving on, this next area I wanted to discuss is a bit more zoomed out. Rigveda, you have the view on the global ecosystem, and Andrew, we've got your local context. There are lots of challenges in the global digital health space.

Let's start with Rigveda. Do you have a wish list or an area of priorities that you see for the ecosystem or this community as a whole? I would say, although we focused a lot on the challenges, I think it's also great that with the overall buzz and hype around AI, healthcare has not been left behind, which sometimes happens. I'm really glad that we are seeing so much investment as well as innovative interest. For me, the wish list would be all around making sure that in this phase, we can maximize the gains for the intended users and the communities.

The first point on my rather long but I'll keep it short wish list would be that it would be great to have a normative body like WHO pull together stakeholders and provide a priority R&D road map for where they think AI can add most value. This is something WHO has already done in other areas, like the priority R&D road map for Disease X or for primary healthcare. I would really want to have that mostly from an end-user perspective, but of course we can contribute from the FIND side as well. I think that will help so much in targeting the ongoing interest, investment, as well as innovator effort in areas that are in dire need. Point two would be more on the previous discussion of regulatory and evidence-generation support.

One key enabler for ensuring that innovators keep coming and working on these problems is how easy it is for them to get to the market, while also ensuring that the interests of the end users are protected. Taking the examples and successes of partners like Rwanda and showcasing them more globally—what is working well and what is not—and moving more rapidly on that would also be a great wish list item. Great. Thanks for sharing those. Andrew, from your context being part of the digital strategy in Rwanda, what do you want to say to the global community around what you want to see in this space?

Thank you. As I said, the healthcare environment is complex. I think that is the area where AI can play well, and it makes it easier for us to evaluate it. Another thing is that the government of Rwanda—not only the Ministry of Health—is really promoting the use of AI. From the Ministry of Health perspective, I don't see the future of medicine without AI.

That's why we are trying to bring together all academia, researchers, stakeholders, and private sectors to see how we could work together to have all this innovation well-coordinated and channeled into the patient flow. I always say the patient flow because we are patient-centered. Whatever contribution digitalization can make is around the patient. The last one I could echo is that we need to build—maybe learn from Rwanda—an environment that really promotes and incentivizes startups and innovations. As Rigveda said, if you have any innovation around this area, at least we have that infrastructure and environment that promotes and incentivizes these innovations.

For the Rwanda context, the priority is the use of AI in the complex setting of healthcare. Thank you for sharing those insights. One thing that you mentioned that I wanted to get your insights on: there's the global picture on regulation. Obviously, it's important to incentivize innovation, but regulation provides the checks and balances for quality and safety. Different countries have different risk appetites.

Europe is seen to take a very conservative approach, and at the moment, other places like the US are not as conservative. How do you take this in terms of your own government's approach to regulation? For the Rwanda context, we value solutions that bring value to what we are doing. We don't think as much about the "AI" or "digital" label as much as: "What can we do that can solve the problem we have currently and is cost-effective?" The reason we are talking about AI is making sure that we simplify the processes and services we are providing and simplify some complexity in the flow. Rwanda is embracing the use of AI to make sure that at least we improve the quality of service, the quality of care, and the quality of what we're doing currently.

Also, scientifically, we contribute to the process of treating patients. When we put the risks and the benefits together, we really balance them and try to mitigate the risks. We improve the quality and safety for the patient—that is the risk part—but we make sure that the benefits are the ones that we are promoting. We are really benefiting from the output of innovation around the flow of the patient or healthcare. We are promoting solutions to problems, and then we mitigate the risks.

Does Rwanda have its own medical-device regulatory framework that innovators would have to go through? What certifications exist? Currently, we have a Ministry of ICT AI policy that really defines the implementation of AI in different areas and how we can collaborate. This policy has attracted the private sector and different stakeholders to work with us. Also, having it in our strategy that these are the priorities—if we have seven priorities and AI is part of them—it makes it easy for innovators to check and say, "I fit here." Motivation comes from policies, strategies, and making sure the environment promotes the use of AI.

That makes a lot of sense. I wanted to bring things together as we wrap up. The main things I take away from your insights: first, if we look at that continuum of the patient journey—pre-point of care, adding value at the point of care, health program or public health level, and then the whole infrastructure and ecosystem—regulatory, evidence generation, and data infrastructure. To achieve the changes and outcomes we want, we really need to narrow down on those first two steps: how do we improve things for patients in terms of how they experience care, and how do we enable healthcare workers to deliver that quality care? Everyone thinks AI is this shiny new tool and let's think about where we can shoehorn this in.

I think it is better to think about what the overall healthcare problems are on the ground that we need to solve. There are lots of ways you can be innovative, even in terms of processes or giving people good information, including non-AI things, as you mentioned, Rigveda. And then how do we augment this with technology? I also really like this concept of systems thinking: not thinking about the tool in isolation, but how it interacts with people and all those layers around it. There are lots of things that might contribute to the overall outcomes and the way that the tool is adopted.

Any final messages from either of you? Maybe one reiteration: involving intended users and beneficiaries in the design and consolidation is super important. Super important. Not thinking about end users just as passive receivers of technology, or healthcare workers as passive minions who have to use it, but involving them and saying, "Here are the big challenges we want your help in solving." Andrew, how about from your side? Patient-centered design.

Perfect. It's been so valuable to have this discussion with both of you. Thank you so much for your insights. I'm really looking forward to seeing how things evolve in the Rwanda ecosystem and reading more about the work FIND is doing. I hope your collaboration in Rwanda goes fruitfully as well.
episodes.pullQuote: From the Ministry of Health perspective, I don't see the future of medicine without AI.
episodes.title: Policy insights from the Rwanda Ministry of Health and FIND
episodes.description: Closing out the year with two fantastic guests: Rigveda Kadam from FIND and Andrew Muhire from Rwanda's Ministry of Health. Building on Episode 8, this discussion dives into the critical connection between product development partners and ministries of health - and what it takes to create the conditions for successful digital health implementation.

topics: What real, meaningful co-design looks like in practice
Engaging communities, young people, and carers to build solutions they actually use
The mindset shift: going in with no pre-conceived notion of what will be built
Getting procurement and policy to value and elevate equitable solutions
Lessons from partnering with UNICEF, USAID, the King's Fund, and Health Foundation
Co-developing Africa's first evidence-based digital mental health regulation with the Rwandan Ministry of Health
Innovative evaluation approaches: from cluster RCTs to cyclical evaluation for digital health
episodes.bio: Dr Jana Alagarajah (MD MPH) is a digital mental health specialist, UK-trained public health doctor, and psychiatrist co-designing equitable and impactful digital health innovation in Africa with young people as Technical Lead at YLabs. Partnering with UNICEF, USAID, and the Gates Foundation, he leverages digital tools to strengthen health systems.
episodes.guestRole: Technical Lead, YLabs; Digital Mental Health Specialist
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. We are joined today by Dr. Janna Algara. He is a psychiatrist, a public health doctor, and also the technical lead for a digital health solution that is helping young people in East Africa with mental and sexual health. He's also involved in policy, so we're really going to get the full gamut of his wide perspective to really understand some unique challenges in the mental health space interacting with digital health, and also what it takes to really procure well and understand the value of these solutions over the long term.

So, very much looking forward to the insights that Janna is going to give us. So let's get into the episode. Janna, welcome to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. You're joining us from Rwanda, and so the first thing to say is, hopefully listeners and watchers just forgive us a bit if there's any delay or Janna drops off due to potentially unreliable internet. When we were just speaking and preparing before we started, we had a couple of drop-offs, so we'll do our best and hope the internet gods are in our favor.

Can you start by telling us a bit about yourself, your background, and how you got into where you are right now? Thanks. Yeah, firstly, thank you very much for inviting me on. It's a real privilege to be here, and yeah, thanks for giving me the platform to speak a little bit about my work. So, my name is Janna.

I'm from London. By background, I'm a psychiatrist. I trained in South London and then converted into Public Health medicine. So, I'm a Public Health registrar in the London training scheme. I had been working in London doing public health work, getting increasingly interested in the tech space.

I did a fellowship called the Bytelabs Fellowship, which quite a few people may have heard of. I've heard good things about it. Yeah, no, it's great. I mean, it's a great taster into the world of health tech for clinicians, and so that gave me good insight into the world of digital. Lots of mental health conditions go undiagnosed and untreated. There's a lack of access to quality care, and there are under-resourced health systems. The other thing about Rwanda, as I mentioned, you do have this history behind it as well. So I think there's a specific additional need here. There's also a lack of health workers. That's a great question. I think before I jump into that, I just want to really quickly make the case for digital. In terms of the work at YLabs, some of our interventions are analog. The reason why we chose to go down the digital route to address this specific problem is that there's rapid internet growth in sub-Saharan Africa.

I think sub-Saharan Africa has some of the highest internet growth in the world, and youth are leading this massive leap in connectivity. 35% of internet users in least developed countries are between 15 and 24, so it's very much youth-driven. This creates the perfect potential for digital solutions to address these mental health inequalities at scale, given the issues that I've highlighted in terms of lack of physical mental health infrastructure. I think that was the reasoning behind going down the digital route. Regarding how we approached it: we have an intervention called Tuzeheye, which is "Prep for a Better Tomorrow." This is a youth-driven, holistic digital learning and peer support program, and it aims to increase mental health literacy and psychosocial support for Rwandan youth between 10 and 1530 years old.

This was part of a seed funding grant that we got from Grand Challenges Canada to basically try and solve this problem. We are a youth-driven co-design organization, so when we got this proposal, we didn't know what the end product would look like. We didn't know what it was going to look like. Also, from my perspective, coming from the UK, I had no clue how Rwandans thought about mental health.

So, actually, from a humble perspective, I think this was great for me personally, because I really wanted to learn and understand how these people think about mental health and what's important to them. We had this two-year grant period. We researched, co-designed, and prototyped this intervention with 1530 young people across two urban youth centers in Rwanda. This was just after COVID. We were in these youth centers on the outskirts of Kigali working with groups of young people.

We held 24 workshops with over 600 youth. We also involved peer educators as part of this. Through these co-design sessions, we created a rough prototype and then created a final product, all in conjunction with young people and with peer educators as well. That was the process. It was a really interesting, immersive process of trying to understand what they wanted, what they didn't want, what was meaningful to them, and what the problem was in their eyes.
