Lots of challenges. This is a very challenging environment to work in for any kind of health work, but digital health work for sure. I'd put challenges into three major buckets. One is socio-cultural challenges. Most digital health interventions are designed in high-income countries, and if they are used in low-income countries, they're mostly "borrowed," copied and pasted, so they're not culturally adapted.

There was also a great NHS Race and Health Observatory report showing that even in high-income countries, people of color with different cultural and linguistic needs are not accessing bespoke interventions. The same thing happens in the Global North as is happening in the Global South. The challenge there was really to create a culturally adapted, culturally appropriate, linguistically appropriate product, and that's no mean feat. This is the first of its kind; this is the first digital mental health tool that addresses stigma and mental health literacy. Let me just give you a quick run-through of the intervention.

Tuzeheye, which means "Prep for a Better Tomorrow," we created and piloted it in 2021. It has two components: one is called Ibeko, which is an online learning platform—it means "prepare yourself" in Kinyarwanda—and the second part is called Turi Kumwe, which means "we are together" in Kinyarwanda. This is an offline peer support program. Both components were implemented with the help of trained peer advisers that we called Wellness Warriors. This is the way that we approached the intervention.

It's the first youth-centered digital self-care platform in Rwanda, and one of very few such interventions across any low-to-middle income country context. It's youth-centered and culturally appropriate. Regarding challenges: the first challenge was that there was nothing like this before. This is the first of its type, so we're starting from scratch. There are also very few culturally adapted mental health interventions in Rwanda, full stop.

We were working without previous interventions or targeted mental health interventions for this population in Rwanda. The second challenge is a technical challenge. As I said, in sub-Saharan Africa, internet connectivity is growing massively, especially powered by youth, but we still have massive connectivity gaps. 94% of those who are unconnected to the internet live in low-to-middle income countries, and of those unconnected people, you have certain groups that have disproportionately poorer connections: rural residents, and people from lower socioeconomic groups. There's very limited access for a lot of people in Rwanda.

Another part of the technical challenge was the lack of previous research data. Even finding prevalence data on anxiety and depression in young people in Rwanda—it's really hard to find data on PTSD, psychosis, etc. The data and the metrics don't exist or, if they do exist, they're very basic. Finding the ground truth and baseline is a common issue. I was just talking to Khushi Baby recently, who are in India, and they were talking about a similar challenge.

Even in high-income countries, there are certain areas where we have really crappy data. Exactly. I think there are some similarities, but across the board here, there's not like a dashboard you can go to. There's not granular or even fairly high-level prevalence data; it just doesn't exist. That's tricky, especially for a technical lead.

And the third thing is workforce capacity challenges. The important thing to remember is that the app doesn't sit in a vacuum. We want it to interface with the mental health infrastructure, the healthcare infrastructure, the school system, etc. We need to think about who the people on the ground are that can support young people with this. Africa has 100 times fewer psychiatrists than Europe, and 30 times fewer mental health nurses.

There's a massive shortage in mental healthcare professionals, and healthcare professionals also have very poor digital literacy. For example, a study based on Ethiopian healthcare workers found that nearly half, 48.2%, had poor digital literacy levels. I couldn't find anything on Rwanda, but in sub-Saharan Africa, healthcare worker digital literacy is an issue. Trying to engage healthcare workers as part of this digital intervention was very tricky. We were working with those challenges, and the ways that we solve them are threefold.

Firstly, co-design. Co-design for me is the best way to tackle cultural challenges. We don't want to bring our assumptions and our ways of doing things. We want the community to tell us how they think about mental health, what the barriers are, and what the important things are. We learned a lot.

I'll give you a quote to flush that out. But I'd also say that co-design—and this touches on my work with the King's Fund—is how you build trust. Asking people what they care about and what is meaningful for them is a really great way of engaging them and building trust with communities, especially given the power dynamics involved from a global health perspective. Why would they trust us? We're just from high-income countries; they don't know us.

We need to create that relationship and I think co-design helps facilitate that process. Did you have to do any ground preparation, like building relationships with community leaders, to even get those people in the room with you guys? Exactly. One of the cool things about YLabs is that we're based in the States, but we also have an office here. The office here is staffed predominantly by young people—I'm obviously not—and most people here are Rwandan.

For example, one of the lead designers already had relationships with these youth centers. We had people who knew the context really well and were able to link up with key stakeholders to facilitate that process, to get us in the door in the first place. Shout out goes out to my Rwandan colleagues. From an ethics perspective, this is also Rwanda-led on the YLabs side. I'll give you a quote to illustrate what we were learning from the co-design.

The quote is— I'll contract it a little bit—this is from one of the young people: "It's not our culture to talk about mental health." He went on to say, "I am very strong, I can do this." They are not aware of the signs, symptoms, and when to seek care for mental health. This points to this idea that, post-genocide, the optimal thing in Rwandan society is to appear strong, especially to those outside of you. Also, the idea that if symptoms aren't externalized, they don't exist. If you're feeling sad inside but you're able to just hold it together, that's seen as a positive in society here. That gave us a really unique window into how differently mental health is conceptualized here.

This was really integral to us trying to create this culturally adapted tool. The second key learning is to use diverse delivery channels. As I mentioned, the internet is patchy. People have smartphones, but a lot of people have feature phones that are very basic. We want to make sure that we can increase access and engagement by using analog and digital alternatives.

As I mentioned, we had the digital intervention, but we had trained peer workers who ran workshops where they were engaging with young people and sharing their own stories. That's a huge thing around stigma—if a peer is saying, "Hey, look, I felt sad, I felt depressed, I had mental health concerns," that also helps break down those barriers of stigma. Using familiar technologies like mobile phones and designing for different levels of tech is really important, but also making sure that we have in-person, analog alternatives for those people who don't have access, and also to create those relationships that help break down stigma. I think that's a fundamental pillar. If you're designing something digital, think about the touchpoints to the real world—not only for people who don't have access, but also because, in healthcare, ultimately at some point in the patient journey or pathway, there's going to be something happening in the real world.

We must be very intentional about the alternative if someone doesn't have a "happy path" on this journey and needs to step out or can't even start on it. What's the alternative so we're not exacerbating certain problems? I think that's an important takeaway in general for everyone. I 100% agree with you. I also think that the peer support element...

you can do that online, but I think that doing it in person, having events or having workshops in person, is really powerful for creating that environment where people can speak about their experiences and be vulnerable. Really, what we're also trying to do is create culture change in the way that mental health is perceived. And lastly, the last key learning was designing for low levels of digital and mental health literacy. In terms of how we created content, we wanted to make sure that all content was designed to be used with potentially low levels of mental health knowledge. We also knew that this intervention would be used by, or interacted with by healthcare staff, and they also would have low levels of mental health knowledge.

So we wanted to make it as basic as possible—use plain language, minimal text, clear layouts, lots of images, and multimodal content delivery: audio, video, text. Just to make it engaging for a youth audience. The Kinyarwanda was written by local speakers, but it was very vernacular as well to make it more youth-friendly and accessible. That's a really good summary, colored with some really great examples. Let's move on to impact and effectiveness.

Do you have a quick overview of the key headline impacts that this intervention has had? Basically, what we did is we created an endline study over five months with 220 randomly selected young people from the two youth centers. It was a pre-post study; we looked at a range of different validated mental health scales to assess impact. We looked at stigma, well-being, depression, anxiety, and substance use. We essentially found that there were improvements across the board in all five of these different areas.

The most profound impact was around stigma, which was good because that was one of our key focal areas. Among those with severe stigma at baseline, 73% of those exposed showed improvement, compared to 57% of those unexposed. There was a significant improvement in stigma scales as part of this intervention. This is a pilot, so really this is showing proof of concept. The endline study meant we could go back to the funders, Grand Challenges Canada, and say there are some positive signs.

Stigma could be seen as an enabler of other types of outcomes, and it could be defined as a primary endpoint and a goal in itself. How did that land on the funders and people who had an interest in this, since it's not a traditional health outcome like reducing a clinical outcome? I actually think that the funders... the core was really highlighting the need for stigma reduction and mental health literacy. Actually, the other aspects were fairly additional.

This is one of the key differences between high-income and low-income countries. In Rwanda, there are such huge barriers around stigma and mental literacy. Let's say you launch an internet-based CBT tool; no one's going to use it because of these barriers. The first priority is to reduce the levels of mental health stigma and improve mental health literacy to a point where you can actually start having those conversations with people and creating points of intersection where you can actually try and use some of those clinical tools. It's like a non-negotiable initial milestone that you need to reach before you can even dream about any of the other things that you're gunning for.

100%. Like I said, there's very little mental health infrastructure. For example, in Tanzania, where we also work, there were no mental health guidelines for the country itself. We were using WHO MH Gap guidelines. You're really working from a place where there's very little.

What we do know is that these barriers stop people even talking. They won't even go to see anyone in the first place for multiple reasons. Trying to address these is the primary target. Clinical outcomes are great, but as a priority, trying to address these is really important in a country like Rwanda—and probably in lots of other countries. In the UK, of course, mental health stigma and literacy are still issues, but they aren't barriers for people to seek care in the same way.

Anything else on the impact side? Importantly, what this did was it allowed us to present these findings back to the funders. They were impressed. Again, this is a pilot, so all we were trying to do was show proof of concept. What happened is we got funding based on this to scale this nationally.

We are now integrating this into our flagship sexual health platform, CyberRwanda. Now we're going to scale this intervention into this sexual health platform, so it will have a mental health and sexual health component aiming to reach 140,000 young people in Rwanda between the ages of 12 and 19 from 1530 to 2027. So, really, the impact of this is going to be massive. If you're talking about reducing stigma, those are like two big high-yield areas to put together. Two sides of the same coin, and they're highly related as well.

I think that's going to be massive from an impact perspective. Amazing. I'd love to follow that and see what kind of impact that has when you scale it up. We've touched on some of the challenges in measuring the right things. How did you measure things given the digital infrastructure that you had?

One of the tricky things is starting from a point where the mental health literacy was so low. Trying to get young people even just to think about mental health was difficult. Having reported outcomes was tricky because a lot of them had never actually sat down and thought about their mental health, or things like anxiety and depression. A lot of it hadn't been externalized, and if you don't externalize it, it's hard to have the vocabulary to articulate that to yourself. I think the starting point was a huge barrier because of the pre-existing landscape around stigma and mental health literacy.

The way that we evaluated this, because it was a pilot, was fairly crude—pre-post using validated mental health scales. Again, another challenge is that a lot of those validated scales aren't culturally adapted. You were using PHQ-9, which is well-used in Western contexts. How did that land in a different context? This is where the local staff came in.

You would have these questions, but they would have to do a lot of background work to contextualize these for the Rwandan youth. Even if you translated it, a lot of mental health vocab in sub-Saharan Africa is actually quite physical—maybe body pain, heart pain, or chest pain—where people are actually talking about what would be considered depression or anxiety in the West. The staff were the crucial bridge in giving extra cultural nuance and context to these validated scales. And I guess if you're using it for pre-and-post rather than a comparison across two different geographies, then as long as you're using the same questioning pre-and-post, you're measuring the difference. Amazing.

I want to zoom out now to the forest level—the 10,000-foot level— working on policy, procurement, and funding. With the Health Foundation, the work you've done with UNICEF, etc., do you have any insights to share from that cross-section of work both in the UK and with a more global focus? The digital mental health ecosystem is complicated. You have different actors with different priorities who are not harmonized. From an end-user perspective—as a clinician I care primarily about the end user and their health outcome— this lack of harmonization is a huge barrier to maximizing benefits for the end user.

This is the problem across the board. This is my major focus from the policy side, and I think this ultimately affects every element of the work: data, equity, effectiveness, sustainability, scaling, whatever it is. This is the problem that I'm trying to solve in collaboration with these organizations. Within the context of the NHS, what has been interesting: I've spoken to regulators, consultants, and clinicians. I've spoken to a lot of different stakeholders in shaping my thinking.

Essentially, from an equity perspective— we want to make sure these digital tools improve health outcomes specifically for those who need it most, who tend to be marginalized communities in the UK and globally—there's an essential tension between private companies and developers who are prioritizing ROI, which completely makes sense because they're commercial entities. But there's a point of tension between their priorities and public health or NHS patient priorities. I'm thinking about the levers that can be used to try and harmonize those goals and align those incentives. So far, from the conversations I've had, I found that procurement could be a really interesting avenue to go down. If you're an ICB and you want to buy a piece of technology, there are already things like the DTAC process out there.

A couple of acronyms there: ICB, Integrated Care Board, organizations in the UK, right? And DTAC as well. Yeah, so in the UK, there have been lots of changes in the way the healthcare system is organized. ICBs are a specific regional unit of the healthcare system. DTAC is the Digital Technology Assessment Criteria.

It was cooked up by the NHS and it basically gives NHS organizations a set of criteria to assess the kinds of health technologies that they procure for their patient population. At the moment, the DTAC doesn't really have much on equity at all, and I think there's a huge gap there. It's quite broad, but there's definitely a gap from the equity perspective. I also feel like there's a gap at the clinician level. Clinicians recommend digital technologies that aren't procured by their board.

You might have a GP who waves their phone at you and says, "Hey, you could use Headspace or Calm," which is great, but there's that gap in making sure they're evidence-based and approved. Just like you would from a drug level; your GP wouldn't just say, "Hey, I've got this drug that I found." It would need to go through the BNF and be licensed and approved at the ICB level. I think procurement is a very fruitful avenue to try and encourage developers to bake in equity in terms of how they create their products. Basically, if they don't, they can't sell to the NHS, which is a huge incentive for them. They want to access this market.

Trying to incentivize... that's one of the incentives that could be used. There could also be high-level government tax breaks for companies that promote equity. I think the procurement level is really interesting. My thinking is still developing in partnership with these organizations.

This is something that next year I want to get deeper into, but at the moment, this is my initial thinking. This resonates a lot and is one of the things we've connected on before. Procurement is a decision-making process on which vendor to use. How do you make sure you elevate the inherent value of various other things that are not just focused on dollars or pounds? A good example of this in the US is the Quintuple Aim.

You've got cost effectiveness—the financial argument— but then you've got clinician well-being, patient outcomes, equity, and population health. These are inherently valuable. If you're otherwise only evaluating something based on ROI, you're missing these other aspects which are equally important. What happens is you've created a process of natural selection; the vendors who survive are the ones who are able to be as lean as possible. Therefore, you've optimized for cost savings, but you've missed out on all these other things, including equity.

How do you elevate the commercial organizations who actually care about this stuff? Maybe that makes it a bit of a bigger investment to work with them, but long-term you're addressing these other problems like clinician well-being and equity. In the work I've done, I've seen more and more RFPs that include this as a category, at least in the US context. I guess there's a lot of work to do globally around elevating these other important things, equity in particular. 100% agree with you.

There needs to be explicit thinking about, to use your phrase, "elevating" some of these principles. If you let the market decide, it's not going to happen. You're going to get interventions that are made for quite affluent people who don't actually have the biggest mental health need. From a data perspective, we know that there are certain communities that have much poorer health outcomes, and those are the ones that we need to engage. We also know that a lot of those people have access to smartphones and devices.

There is a digital divide in the UK, but a lot of people do have smartphones. This is a great opportunity. We're seeing the same opportunity in sub-Saharan Africa as in the UK. Because of the health system that we have, we can incentivize developers to think about these populations. A lot of developers do want to do that, but from a business perspective, the business case isn't there.

I guess things like that would make it a business priority. Exactly. So much insight that you've shared at various levels. I want to extract one more thing from you before we wrap up. What is Janna's key takeaway for people building in this space for underserved populations globally— whether it's a software developer, clinician, researcher, or engineer?

My key takeaway is: build with people, not for people. From an ethical perspective, from an effective product perspective, and from an engagement and sustainability perspective, this is really key. This is also a great way of building trust and engagement with those users as well. That's my mantra that I could pass on to people: build with people, not for people. I like it.

Janna, how can people reach out to you? LinkedIn is probably the easiest way. I'm really open to connecting with anyone who's interested in what I'm interested in. Please look me up. Janna, it's been an absolute pleasure talking to you.

Thank you for sharing your work and the work of YLabs. Really useful stuff for anyone who's in this space at whatever level. Thank you for taking the time to speak to me and being on the episode. Thanks, Joss, for giving me the opportunity and for indulging me with all your questions. It's been really fun.

Cheers. Thank you. My key takeaways from this episode: we really need mechanisms that promote true co-design with communities. That means genuinely listening to their problems, to patients on their lived experience, and clinicians on what gets in the way of good care. There were such powerful examples of the cultural context— on how mental health is stigmatized and how people experience it.

We sometimes need to revisit what success is for this context. You couldn't dream of improving health outcomes without the groundwork of trust and challenging cultural stigma on mental health. There are so many insights that we can learn from, especially in our multicultural societies. A really great set of insights. In the next episode, we'll be talking to FIND and the Rwanda Ministry of Health, so it'll really connect well to this episode.
episodes.pullQuote: Build with people, not for people.
episodes.title: Co-designing mental health solutions with young people in Rwanda
episodes.description: What does real, meaningful co-design look like? Dr Jana Alagarajah shares what he learned implementing a digital mental health tool with young people in Rwanda - how to listen before building, how to engage communities and carers, and how to get procurement and policy to genuinely value equitable solutions.

topics: The role of ASHAs (Accredited Social Health Activists) in India's healthcare system
Challenges of integrating technology to support community health workers
India's digital public health ecosystem explained
When "too much digital" gets in the way of good care
Pitfalls in funding and investment approaches for health tech
The 3 I's that drive implementation success
Leveraging data for health system strengthening
Aligning incentives with ground realities to improve health outcomes
episodes.bio: Ruchit Nagar is the CEO and Co-Founder of Khushi Baby. For his efforts to deliver scalable public health impact, Ruchit has been recognised as a Forbes 30 Under 30 leader in Healthcare, a World Innovation Summit in Health Young Innovator, and a Distinguished Young Alumnus by the Yale School of Public Health.
episodes.guestRole: CEO and Co-Founder, Khushi Baby
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to the latest episode of the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. I'm your host, Shabs Saadi, a physician working in digital health. So far, we've had perspectives from Brazil, South Africa, and ESI, and now we can travel across the Indian Ocean and get the perspective from the context of India. I recently moderated a panel around Universal Health Coverage, comparing and contrasting implementation impact from the NHS and India, and so I'm particularly interested in diving much deeper into this. I'm going to be talking to Rishit, who is the founder of Khushi Baby.

They've been working for the last 10 years implementing technology that supports community health workers and their impact on the last mile of health in villages in rural India. There's a lot to learn for anyone building in this space, and we're also going to be getting some of the challenges that they faced as well that are going to be helpful for us to unpack and learn from. So if you're building, researching, or investing in this context, or in a similar context, you'll find this one really valuable. Rishit, welcome to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. It's an absolute pleasure to have you on the show and to get the first insights we have from the Indian context.

Thanks for taking the time to join me. Thanks for having me, Shabs, really appreciate it. Okay, so why don't we go into learning a bit about yourself, Rishit, and how Khushi Baby was born? Yeah, so Khushi Baby this year is turning 10, and it's a big year for us. But we were born a decade ago in a class project.

I was an undergraduate student at Yale, and the class was set up as a design course. The first day of class, they gave us a challenge statement: a million and a half children under the age of five are dying from vaccine-preventable diseases, and it was our job to come up with a solution and business plan to take that solution out of the classroom and into the field. Then we went through a whole course of understanding design thinking frameworks, human-centered design, and the whole iterative approach towards studying a landscape, identifying opportunity spaces, coming up with rapid prototypes, and speaking to users on the ground. Ultimately, we ended up focusing on data and accountability and working towards building a digital health tool to better track vaccine records in low-resource settings, especially in offline settings. The initial concept that came out was a mobile application for the community health worker and a portable, wearable, NFC-based digital health record for the person receiving the vaccines—the family.

That was connected with an NGO that was working in Rajasthan, India, that was already giving services to areas that the government couldn't reach, but it was tracking everything on paper and they were open to experiments. In fact, it's the same NGO, Seva Mandir, that had done the work with Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee that they talk about in their book *Poor Economics*, where they studied whether or not giving lentils as an incentive could help improve immunization rates in that same area. So they had a precedent for doing research, they had a real need to better track the services they were providing, and then we were coming up with a solution. It was interesting that our team actually had no developers or computer scientists on our randomly assorted initial team. We were using open-source tools like MIT App Inventor to code up a demo application.

We ended up eventually applying for some funding on campus, getting that initial investment, and then setting up as a nonprofit organization. I sent 40 cold emails to local professors in Rajasthan to see if somebody could help guide us. One professor replied with their doctoral student at the time who was interested in mobile health, and that person, Mohammed Shahnawaz, has been with us as the co-founder ever since and is now the Chief Operating Officer. So I would say it was a stroke of luck at the start, and it took us to India. The thing that I take away is that it can really start from anywhere.

In this case, it started from a class project, a collaboration of students who are interested in public health and design getting together and trying to solve a problem. You have to have a little bit of reckless abandon; you have to be a little bit naive to start to even approach such complex problems, and then the maturity comes over the next 10 years when you figure out how difficult those problems actually are. So that's kind of how it all really started. Okay, can we just go into the problem that you've touched on in terms of immunization and the problems that community health workers have? Can you just paint a picture of the on-the-ground problem that was faced, both on the community health worker and healthcare delivery side, but also for villagers and families who were receiving this healthcare, or in some cases not?

Yes. When it comes to what it actually looks like for people in these rural communities to receive access to healthcare, India has a decentralized healthcare delivery system. Every village has a locally elected community health worker. Every month, a nurse comes to each village, and she's responsible for four or five villages. She conducts, with the help of that community health worker known as an Asha, a maternal and child health and nutrition camp in which she will screen pregnant mothers for common conditions, and she will give infants and toddlers their vaccines and track their growth and development.

Now, whenever any mother, pregnant woman, or child is sick, they are referred from that screening camp to the Primary Health Center, where a doctor may be available, and then they may be further referred to the District Hospital. Ever since 2005, when this National Rural Health Mission started, India has had a very structured approach to ensuring that services have a way to reach people—at least a structure through which services can flow. However, the challenges still remain that you need to have the right people. Even in the hardest-to-reach areas, you may not have nurses that want to deploy, for example. You need to have the right facilities and supplies, the right training for the personnel, and you need to have the right data systems to understand what's going on.

That's all just on the supply side. On the demand side, you're dealing with low levels of literacy. Before we even get to health literacy, we have low levels of literacy in general. Then there's health literacy, high levels of multidimensional poverty, and families that have migrant laborers. The families themselves are not living together as a unit, you have multiple kids in the household, and the distance to the nearest facility takes a long time.

You have awareness and sociocultural factors that are also at play. Both demand-side and supply-side factors make completing the full recommended health journey difficult, even if the services are all free. What it takes to deliver a vaccine to a child—a vaccine carrier has to wake up early in the morning, go to the vaccine stock supply, bring the vaccine carrier to a more rural outpost that the nurse can then pick up. Meanwhile, in the village, the community health worker is going door-to-door and trying to make people aware that today there is a health camp, and you need to bring the pregnant women and the young infants to the camp. Then the health worker finally comes, the beneficiaries finally come, and the health worker is carrying—we still see this today—1739 different registers for different programs that they're responsible for, flipping through, trying to identify the patient, trying to update the records on paper, and then trying to make sure that they're giving the right medicine or the right vaccine to that beneficiary.

That process is incredibly taxing and time-consuming, and that process still continues today. The thing that has changed over the last 5 years, I would say, is that in addition to those 1739 registers, you now have 10 apps on your phone. While before it wasn't really imagined that Asha workers would be using smartphones, digital literacy has improved—there has been a sea change in that—but the work burden has only increased. We surveyed Ashas in Rajasthan, for example, and the majority are saying that they spend 45 to 50 hours a month on data reporting-related tasks. That's compiling the initial data, tabulating it into summary statistics, getting the required photocopies, traveling to the Primary Health Center, and sitting with the data entry operator.

In some cases, they need to give a cut of their incentive to the data entry operator or the supervisor. Ultimately, that whole convoluted series of steps takes 50 hours of their time that they could be spending with their family, visiting a high-risk pregnant woman or a newborn child, or giving other services within their community. There are over a million Ashas across India, so the world's largest decentralized community health workforce is spending—we're estimating here—up to 50 million hours or more on all these low-yield reporting-based tasks that could easily be automated with the tools they're already using if we're just able to intelligently design that system. Then the other question is: what are we really incentivizing? Do they feel intrinsically motivated by the data they're reporting—that if I'm going to report this data of sick people in my community, something is going to come back to me so I can better take care of them and better prevent the same problems from happening again and again?

That's the intrinsic value of the data you would imagine from a reporting activity, but that doesn't seem to have the same level of real-time connect or feedback that you would expect. And then the incentives—the incentives are showing that we need to be TB-free by 2025, we need to reduce infant mortality and maternal mortality. The incentives are not toward how we can best report the ground truth. How do we have the best quality maternal and child death investigations so we can actually understand the areas that need more support and get them more services? Because incentives aren't looking towards improving health outcomes through understanding the ground truth, and because there's a lack of supervision, and because these health workers are overburdened, all of the data they're reporting is severely affected in terms of its quality and its usefulness.

These are the kind of deeper-cutting problems we see today that have grown over time as we've tried to use technology to solve the problem. When I say "we," I mean the broader public health community. Without necessarily designing the system in a way that can be horizontally integrated, we're making things more challenging for the health workers. Man, you've traversed so many topics there. We will definitely bookmark the incentives piece and the goals.

I wanted to just touch on a couple of things you mentioned at the beginning. Just for those who are not aware, Ashas are the name for the community health workers in India. Can you just quickly mention what that stands for? Asha stands for Accredited Social Health Activists. They're considered to be the daughter-in-law of their village.

They have to be 18 and have moved into the village they've been married into, and they're a representative of their village. It's a democratic process to get elected. They then are responsible for health promotion, mobilization, taking pregnant women to the hospital to deliver, checking on newborn children, and screening for all the different programs. Their focus may have started with maternal and child health, but it has really expanded to 1739 activities across every single health program. Okay.

Next bit you mentioned: you said 50 hours are spent on data entry across multiple platforms. Is that per month? Per month. And then you said there were how many? Over a million in India?

Yeah. So you can extrapolate the potential cost of that time that could be used better in other means. Thank you for highlighting that problem. I think the other thing you touched on was all these different layers on the supply side in terms of healthcare delivery that are important to consider. They're so intertwined: the people, the facilities, the supply chain, the data systems, and then the technology that sits on top.

For those who might not be familiar, can you give us a whirlwind tour of the backbone system of digital health infrastructure in India? Yeah. The way digital health evolved in India, it started in a vertical approach. You had the reproductive child health bucket, which had its own portal that started at the state level and then was adopted by the Ministry of Health centrally. Later, you saw the national non-communicable disease bucket develop its own portal focusing on things like diabetes, hypertension, and oral, breast, and cervical cancer.

Then you had a third bucket looking at communicable disease—vector-borne illnesses—and a fourth bucket exclusively looking at tuberculosis. These four buckets built out their own solutions, initially web portals for data entry, then applications for nurses, and now applications for Ashas. They also have different portals that work at the facility level, like the District Hospital or the Primary and Community Health Centers. Now you're in this world where you have all these apps getting to the most decentralized health worker. But the problem remains: I could have a patient who both has a non-communicable disease issue like diabetes and is in my maternal health tracking system.

I need to keep track of them in both places and enter their data twice. People don't fall into just one bucket at a time. There has been a push now—and we're just talking about the government public systems, not even the private systems that have mostly been paper-based. Major hospitals have adopted electronic health registries, but it is a very fragmented ecosystem. So, what did India do?

Beginning in 2018, they came out with the National Digital Health Blueprint, which has moved towards creating an ecosystem in which all information systems can speak with a common language, which is FHIR. Using FHIR as a standard to communicate between different systems—public or private—to have a Universal Health ID and universal registries for both the facilities and for the providers. This way, information exchange can be more systematic, and you don't need all these custom APIs or channels to share data between System 1 and System 2. There's a common way to share that data, and whichever system needs it can pull it. They wanted it to be patient-consent driven, federated, and decentralized.

There are a lot of great properties around how it's designed. The interesting piece is that it still was envisioned for those living in tier 1 and tier 2 cities—the upper and upper-middle parts of the wealth pyramid who have access to smartphones, are digitally literate, and are health literate. Those tech-savvy people who use things like the Unified Payments Interface would also have a digital record of their health information. It wasn't initially conceived to figure out how we're going to work with people that may not have smartphones, may not be digitally literate, and are availing free services from the government. What does consent look like for them?

It wasn't designed from the bottom. Now they're working top-down thinking it will get to the bottom eventually, but they're starting to realize we need to rethink working bottom-up. Instead of having 40 different applications and portals, let's work on making a connector application that can link their apps, or an integrated application that replaces all the redundancy. That's ultimately what we're trying to do with our solution, which is called CHIP (Community Health Integrated Platform). It takes the 800 public health indicators these health workers—the Ashas and ANMs—are responsible for, simplifies it, gets rid of about 150 redundant indicators, and streamlines it.

It's a one-stop solution for the health worker that covers all her work-related requirements. She has an integrated work plan she can click on to see which houses she needs to visit today, broken down by program. For every patient she goes to, there's custom decision support based on national guidelines so she can figure out how to refer, and the next person in the referral chain can also see the relevant information. This is what we think would actually be helpful for someone responsible for covering so much primary healthcare. To draw a parallel, most healthcare is delivered by Ashas in India.

There's a real parallel with clinicians working in the West where you have this overburdening of the electronic health record. It's important to focus on clinician well-being. Most clinical care is delivered by community health workers, and we should make sure that the people out at the last mile are really benefiting and feeling fulfilled. You've called out an important thing there. While there are parallels, it's unique to this context.

Yeah. The Western example—being a resident doctor here—we spend two-thirds of our time in front of the computer instead of at the bedside. It's a cautionary tale, but I'm not sure that caution is being heeded. The same over-documentation is being applied to community health workers where you want them to be the least burdened so their counseling and mobilization can reduce infant mortality. It needs to be simple and user-friendly.

If I were to pick two indicators: how much time are we saving them, and would they recommend this to their peer? If not, we're not adding value. Even if the system is great, if it's the 14th app they have to use, unless you get rid of those other 13 or restructure them, you aren't solving the root problem. You're trying to find the real drivers of the outcome. Clearly, you've identified that a big lever is letting community health workers get out of their own way and just do the work.

Yeah. It's interesting because it runs counter to what the buzz is about—global health investment is going towards AI for health. We have to be careful. Funders will put in hundreds of millions of dollars towards these initiatives with expectations that capacity gets built, but the funding is not pushing us away from siloed systems. The funding goes toward a vertical solution for immunization or non-communicable diseases.

That makes the problem worse because then those large agencies have a vested interest in continuing that vertical pipeline of control to show their solution is successful. We need a radical rethinking and honest conversation about what collaboration looks like. Not everyone needs to be a digital health expert. The opportunity I see for digital health is first, make the system ink-free so they don't have to use paper. Second, make it integrated or interoperable so we don't need a million applications.

Third, make it properly incentivized so health workers feel their work is useful. These three "I"s—Ink-free, Interoperability, and Incentivization—are the three pillars we think are required for a successful digital health solution. Then the hope is it can help us get better data on the ground, better identify health inequities, and better allocate resources. Redoing all the plumbing is very messy and difficult once the plumbing has already been placed. Definitely.

If you're thinking only about vertical plumbing for the toilet or the radiator, you lose sight of why the house is not energy efficient. That's a nice parallel. So we have Rishit's three "I"s: Ink-free, Integrated, and Incentivized. Perfect. I want to backtrack a bit.

You talked about how you identified the problem. What was your approach to finding the levers and speaking to the right people to understand what was going on on the ground? Yeah. We did that human-centered design course, but the design didn't really start until we actually went to the field and walked alongside our community health worker partners. Those insights were tremendous.

We built it into our team structure to have a field monitoring team and a community engagement team that functions through a call center. On a daily basis, we are in touch with between 100 and 500 community health workers. That wealth of wisdom allowed us to understand and better design solutions. Critical to this is that the vast majority of software developed for community health workers is done by engineers who never meet the end users. It is so critical to understand what is actually helpful.

You have to see both the trees and the forest. You're building for a multi-stakeholder environment where the health worker is the end user, but public health officials need certain data and insights. Until national policies change, we have to satisfy certain requirements. Khushi Baby's interdisciplinary team composition is our special sauce. We have the field team and policy team sitting side-by-side with the design engineering team and an M&E team to see if we're actually making an impact and to be critical of our own approach.

You need all those components to have an end-to-end perspective. You mentioned that when you initially started, you had an NFC health record for the community. What have you got implemented now? This project started with tablets for nurses and this digital health necklace. Tying tradition with technology—the black thread was thought to ward off the evil eye.

It used voice calls in the local dialect for families and was focused on immunization. Then we moved from NGO to government and expanded to all maternal and child health. We did a two-year randomized control trial to see if the system would improve immunization outcomes. We were able to show we improved immunization by 12 percentage points in our treatment group. Have you got a link to that so we can share it in the notes?

Yeah, perfect. We took that evidence to the State Department of Health. They said we had five other projects to work on first to gain their trust and help figure out the mess of 40 portals. Then COVID came and they needed help screening the population. We ended up moving away from tablets and necklaces towards a scalable Android application that works on any smartphone.

That became a pivot in our approach—the digital health record added accountability because you had to scan it to update it, but you were losing off on the scalability lens needed during the pandemic. We went through COVID, helped do the screening, and because of the pandemic, a lot of red tape was removed. Not only did we screen for COVID, but we also screened for comorbidities that make COVID more risky—diabetes, TB, etc. Now you have a database of 14 million people and 60,000 health workers who have used the platform. We can go to vertical health programs and say we have this base, let's build on top of it.

We're starting to use the data to study what is working. For example, the TB department screens twice a year across the state. Because we've done this digital health census, we can pre-identify who is vulnerable. We can show that evidence to help move policy towards something more evidence-based. That's the bucket we're in now—using data for health system strengthening.

That's really interesting. You made the vulnerable populations visible in a granular way to help decision-making and target resources. We consider the community health worker to be the local researcher or journalist of their village. There's an old Sanskrit saying: "The taste of the water changes every few miles." We can literally map that because we have tens of thousands of workers sharing data on the social determinants of health. You can see the tapestry of poverty change.

This reinforces the concept that India is not a homogeneous place. Village to village, you're going to see differences. That data also has positive externalities—it can be used by other departments like education or public distribution. This is the new power of big public health data that can be unlocked if we enable community health workers. Nice takeaway.

I want to go to the people layer and incentives. What challenges have you faced and what have you learned from them? The solution is you have to be persistent and consistent. It takes a long time to rework the plumbing. Politics is at play, there are vested interests, and legacy platforms.

Once the central government rolls out a vertical solution nationally, you're going to have at least two solutions on the ground and you've broken the workflow. We're seeing that with immunizations right now. The success of India's CoWIN platform for COVID was a huge success story, but now it's being expanded to routine immunizations within a silo. How does that boil down to the person who has to juggle 10 balls at once? It should be easier to integrate across systems, but there is resistance and gaps in technical capacity.

If people are looking to invest, I would invest in supporting connections across platforms as opposed to developing new ones. Change is slow. We were very disruptive when we came in, and internal departments were skeptical. We are impatient as well, but for things to durably change, you have to get your gear within that machinery. Getting the right mandates at the policy level and collective buy-in is an ongoing problem.

We've worked in Rajasthan, but we're expanding to Maharashtra and Karnataka. Our criteria for entering is: is there a demand coming from the government? That is the single most important factor—what is the demand of those senior bureaucrats to move in this direction? How do you know it's worth focusing your efforts there? You reach out to senior health secretaries and pitch.

In Karnataka, they said they're going to have a competition between four players to make an integrated solution. They said they're not going to pay us, and they expect us to leave after two years so they have the internal capacity to move it forward. That's a very progressive approach. Let's visit the incentive thing now. Big goals often don't align with realities on the ground, which leads to a skewed picture.

This is the hardest question. Our goal is not to become the next tech giant or unicorn. Our endgame is to strengthen the public health department so they can own the system and use data effectively. Phase one is improving ground-truth reporting—indicators might look worse initially because of transparency. Phase two is seeing which interventions work.

Phase three is replicating effective interventions. We're still in phase one. That doesn't always look good to the donor. Exactly. Donors want you to build capacity and hand it over in a few years, but the reality is we need longer time frames.

The West's adoption of health registers was a 10 to 15-year journey. Now there's momentum towards AI for health. What capacity does the government have to regulate generative AI? We expect ethical review boards to magically have the capacity to adjudicate those things. We need to be very responsible.

If an AI tool screens for false positives, does that meaningfully improve referral rates if patients still don't have transportation to the facility? We need to go back to first principles. Our third bucket is research and innovation. We're excited about the potential, but we must do trials and qualitative research. Otherwise, we overstate the value.

If an AI chatbot tells a health worker to refer a patient to a dermatologist—which she already knew—what is the new value addition? You mentioned regulation. How do you see the regulatory picture in India? One of the biggest challenges is knowing what is the truth. National health surveys happen every four years, and estimates often vary significantly from what the official portal shows for the same indicator.

We need to first understand the ground reality. For example, "TB-free by 2025" is a goal used to motivate people, but it must be coupled with smart goals and supervision. The fastest way to become TB-free is to report that there is no TB. In Rajasthan, they identified 7,1739 target villages and gave 10 rupees for every screening. A health worker could easily say everyone was asymptomatic, get their village stamped TB-free, and receive the incentive.

That's not right. The truth is that health workers have a fear of reporting the truth. They worry about punitive feedback for finding a child died or highlighting a problem area. Now they've coined the term "supportive supervision." TB programs are moving in the right direction because they pay for identifying positive cases. The question is how to align incentives to avoid misrepresentation of data.

Asha workers have told me: "I get paid less than a daily wage laborer." They are responsible for huge drops in mortality but are getting paid about $2 a day. Why are they paying for their own data plans? India should increase health spending as a fraction of GDP. We also need better metrics to evaluate which workers need more support and allocate resources based on poverty or climate vulnerability indexes. In terms of regulation for health data privacy, India has a personal data protection policy, which is a good step.

But as you go more towards the community, regulation gets diluted. What does informed consent look like for someone with low literacy? India is unique—because of the gray area, you can innovate faster, but you have to be much more thoughtful when it comes to health. We can use AI to help prioritize house visits, but we need to be careful with prediction. The landscape is evolving with the ICMR and CDSCO.

There are new AI Centers of Excellence. It's emerging, and we need to build that infrastructure to test the future of public health technology. What's next for Khushi Baby? The first 10 years were about getting our foot in the door. The next 10 years are about making a big impact.

We've done the digital health census, but now we need to see how many people got referred and successfully treated. That requires deeper collaboration. Our goal is for the platform to be adopted as a digital public good by the Ministry of Health. How do you remain sustainable as an entity if you do it for free? As a software provider, you're not going to be satisfied functioning as a vendor; you'll be more fulfilled as a partner.

There are hundreds of millions of dollars being invested in this space. There is plenty of philanthropic support available, and if the government wants to engage in public-private partnerships, we are open to that. I don't think philanthropic capital is close to expiring. Some organizations in sub-Saharan Africa have budgets of $25 million a year for digital health at a smaller scale than what we're doing. I would argue we're 20 times more cost-efficient.

We want to switch from 70% working on the solution to 70% working on program delivery analytics. Generative AI has potential, and we are making a chatbot for Ashas. But how do you ensure it's safe? We have a large study using machine learning on images of the inner eyelid to predict maternal anemia. You take a photo—no blood drawn—and we estimate hemoglobin levels.

That will take time, regulation, and trials. We still have to ask: is that screening tool going to meaningfully change how many people get treatment? Let's wrap up. Do you have any other top takeaways for someone building impact for underserved communities? You have to visit the field.

That is the most important thing. You cannot build from the comfort of your home. The initial class was called "Culturally Appropriate Technology for the Developing World." Having cultural humility is very important. Think of this as a collaborative effort to co-create value, not thinking of ourselves as the problem solvers. That's a great takeaway for anyone building from the West and going out to implement technology elsewhere.

Learning happens both ways. Being able to have these honest conversations is a key piece to moving the agenda forward. We are a small community, but there's a lot of change we can make together. Rishit, I'm really grateful you've shared your experiences and impact. Thank you for your time.

Thank you so much. Before you go, a quick word. I started this podcast to expand our perspectives and learn from people solving complex issues for underserved populations. We can learn a lot about health equity, ethics, and implementation science from places where it's even more challenging. If you found this useful, please hit follow on your podcast channel.

Check out the website gpodh.org. We're also on YouTube and LinkedIn. If you have insights to share or know someone who would be great for this podcast, get in touch. If you're a donor or investor with startups that have insights to share, please reach out. These stories are incredible and a unique way of communicating impact.

episodes.title: Supporting rural healthcare in India with technology
episodes.description: A ground-level look at implementing technology to support India's community health workers - the ASHAs. Ruchit Nagar shares the challenges of integrating tech in rural healthcare, India's digital public health ecosystem, funding pitfalls, and the key learnings for anyone looking to implement at the last mile.
