episodes.bio:
Echo Vanderwal is a visionary leader in global health who has spearheaded innovative health and development solutions to serve isolated and underserved patients. Under her leadership, The Luke Commission (TLC) has delivered comprehensive healthcare services through more than 1.5 million patient visits in Eswatini since 2005. TLC's Miracle Campus, in the centre of Eswatini, includes a national referral hospital providing primary to tertiary care, Africa's largest PSA oxygen plant, a world-class snakebite treatment unit, and the globally recognised Training and Leadership Center of Excellence for deepening and extending a culture of compassionate care.

Echo's passionate advocacy for equitable healthcare access has led to TLC's international recognition for addressing systemic challenges throughout the HIV epidemic and the COVID-19 pandemic. Her commitment to aligning technology with community continues to shape public health, with plans to scale TLC's impact globally through strategic collaborations and scalable innovations.
episodes.guestRole: Executive Director, The Luke Commission
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to the latest episode of the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. Today we are going to be talking to Echo VanderWal, who is the Executive Director of The Luke Commission, who run healthcare services within Eswatini, a country in Southern Africa. We're going to be hearing about how they solve problems for people and enabled clinicians and community health workers to deliver higher quality care through a people-centered approach. I'm very, very excited to have their insights, and I'm sure we'll have a lot to learn. Let's get into it.

Echo, it's so nice to have you on the podcast. Thank you for taking the time to be with us here and share your insights. We had Dino from Alder on the podcast a couple of months ago, and after the podcast, he said, "Hey Shabs, if you want to get some real insights on implementation and really hear about some exciting work, then you've got to speak to Echo at The Luke Commission." So, after a few conversations that we've had together, I'm very, very happy that you've taken the time to come and speak to us and share your experience. Welcome to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. Thank you very much, Shabs.

Thanks for having me here. Why don't we start with the origins of The Luke Commission and maybe your story as well? It would be really good to hear about that and what got you into this. Okay. All right.

Well, actually, when I was eight years old, I felt called to work in healthcare in Africa. I had heard a story of someone who was working in Africa, and I just felt called to that. I know I was just a kid, but it stuck. And then my husband, similarly, when he was 17, felt a similar calling. Then we met when we were 19 and went to undergrad and graduate school.

He's an internal medicine and pediatrics doctor, and my background is a mid-level practitioner in surgery and pediatrics. So in 2004, someone invited us to Eswatini, and we had—maybe to back up just a little bit—when my husband was in residency, we had triplet boys. Then in 2004, we had number four, and when he was two months old, someone gave us contacts in Eswatini. So for the first time, we got a passport—I'd never traveled overseas before—and we flew to Eswatini. We didn't know exactly what we were dropping into, but we dropped into the middle of the HIV pandemic.

Someone took us immediately out to a rural area, and in literally every homestead we went to, we found people dying from HIV—young people. We started asking what were the barriers to people getting access to healthcare. There were two main barriers that everyone talked about. The first was lack of transport, transport being expensive for people who didn't have jobs. The second one that they talked about is that when they went to health facilities, they felt stigmatized.

So we started to realize very early on that compassion was going to be very critical if we wanted to work here. So we then moved here full-time, and this is our 20th year in Eswatini. We've raised six kids here— had two subsequently since we've been here—but we started first going to the rural areas. For the first eight years, my husband and I were the only medical professionals, and we worked with a team of about 20 local staff. We learned so much because we were literally getting the dust on our shoes of every single section in the country.

It's very true: when you walk with the people, you learn the challenges intimately. Then in 2013, up until that point, we just did mobile outreaches in rural communities. In fact, at the height of the HIV pandemic, we were testing 250 people a day positive for HIV, and at that time, we didn't have good access to antiretrovirals. So of those 250 people, we would have to choose only five that were allowed to go on antiretrovirals. That's how things were at the beginning of the HIV pandemic.

So it was very, very difficult but very fulfilling work; we really enjoyed it. Then in 2013, doors opened for us to be able to buy land in the center of the country. We bought 70 hectares and since then the team's grown a lot. We are a team of 700 now, and last year the team took care of 300,000 patients. So it's kind of very humble beginnings, but very important to get feet on the ground and understand intimately what the people were going through and then be able to...

We eventually established a fixed-site facility at the Miracle Campus—the site that I'm talking about now. It's been just really a joy to see things grow and the staff grow. It's been very fulfilling. So you bought this land in 2013, and as I understand, you used this to create a center for delivering healthcare, right? Can you tell us a little bit about that and how that enabled access?

Sure. Well, the land was a huge blessing because it actually borders our biggest river in Eswatini, and we were able to secure a kilometer of riverfront with the acquisition. It's also on one of the very main roads going north to south in the country. Having access to a main road and to the river has been very helpful to be able to establish a robust site for a centralized supply chain hub for all of the teams that go out to the country, as well as a referral center of excellence. We do a lot of specialty care and tertiary care here.

We are the largest provider of ICU care in the country and also we do a lot of specialty surgeries. The other thing that has happened here is that we've also developed all of our own support teams. We have engineering, biomed, fleet maintenance... we build all of our own buildings. They've built 1536 buildings and they've done an amazing job developing this place.

I just find when people build something themselves, they own it. You can just see an ownership from the team that is something that I don't see often, so it's a special team. I can say that. But now this site, as I mentioned, is the referral center for all of the outreach teams as well as from the other facilities in the country. Echo, you mentioned the barriers to care that people were having.

Can you paint a picture of what the problems were day-to-day for people in Eswatini? Sure. Well, I think that just understanding the underlying personality type of the country is also very important, because we're a shy, quiet, and non-confrontational country. So when you offend me, I will not tell you. What we heard very early on when we were moving in the chiefdoms is that people would say, "If I have to be treated like that, let me go home and die." Then you start to realize that this is a big deal.

It's not like Europe or the United States, where maybe somebody will file a complaint and go to administration, and then there will be some corrective action and things will change. People weren't reporting these things to a centralized place where it could enact change; they were going home and dying and they were leaving behind so many children. Of course, the devastation from that in our country—when at one stage 20% of our country was orphaned from HIV. So just understanding the socioeconomic impact when you don't work at the root level on some of these issues. I think sometimes, too, we bypass how important person-centered care is, how important compassion is in the engagement—the patient-health provider engagement—but it really for us has been the key.

When you are working side-by-side journeying with the patient, it's a much different outcome than when the healthcare provider is on top of the equation. So that was key for us: to realize how critical compassion is and then to learn how to develop a culture of compassion in our organization. Just because you identify it as a problem doesn't mean that your staff do that. We've been very intentional about that and started an onboarding process that's about 10 weeks long. During that 10-week process, there's a lot of things that happen.

We do leadership development and personal development, but we also inculcate a culture of compassion. What does it look like to take care of somebody like your own family member? That's really been key for us because that's something anywhere in the world can relate to: "How do you want your mom taken care of?" Okay, remember every person that sits in front of you is either your mother, father, brother, sister, or child. They are somehow related to you through the people that they're related to. So that helped us a lot as an organization.

This training was for people delivering care, right? Community health workers, clinicians? Actually, everyone. We learned that even if somebody's in a ward fixing a ventilator next to the bed of a patient, they need to have the same culture. So it's not just your people that are providing direct care.

At times we've had even construction projects happening next to where patients are admitted, and so you realize, "Oh no, it's your construction workers too; they need to understand compassion." So it's really helped us because the whole team is united around this culture of compassion. On the issue of transport, I wish I could tell you after 20 years that that challenge has dissipated, and it hasn't. For the most vulnerable, if you don't have any income at all, what are you going to choose? Whatever little resources you have, you're going to feed the kids who are crying at your feet for food. You are not going to board a bus and go to a hospital.

You will only board a bus and go to the hospital when you're at an advanced care stage. So that's one of the reasons we've prioritized so much going to the people. This is highly logistical. Our teams, depending on the sites they are at, can be anywhere from 5 to 50 or 1536 staff. Sometimes they see 500 patients a day in one community, and it's all really driven by the digital ecosystem which I'm sure you'll raise a little bit later, so I won't go into that right now.

But the coordination and logistics have been really important to going to the people. We also find who needs to be referred to more specialized care, so it allows us kind of a funnel to figure out who can be treated at the community level and who needs to be brought in. I'll tell you what: I wish I would have known this at the beginning—I don't know what it might have changed—but the thing that I've learned over the past 20 years is actually the biggest issue and the biggest barrier is lack of accountability and transparency in our supply chains. That one issue is actually disrupting access to care. I think probably not just in Eswatini, probably on our entire continent and I'm sure in many other places in the world.

So I do think that the introduction seven years ago of digital systems to provide accountability controls and transparency in our organization has just elevated the trust of this institution so much in our small country, because they know our supply chain is reliable. I think that's the thing that keeps people away from seeking healthcare early in disease, because they have learned that when they go, they're not going to get the medications that they were supposed to get when they went to the doctor. So then they say, "Well, if I don't get medications, what's the reason to go?" And then they only come when things are in an advanced stage. So I do believe, especially in our country, that this is something that we have to take very seriously because we're unnecessarily losing lives of people. It's, of course, evolving over time—figuring out what the barriers are—but I do think that definitely the last one is solvable.

Probably transport will always have to bridge the gap. I do think there's been some work done in just person-centered care that's more talked about now than it was when we first started here. But the part about the supply chain, I think, will be heavily impacted by an embracing of digital systems. That's a really nice segue. To connect some dots, you talked about the problems that were faced by people accessing care.

Sometimes we think about these as just what's locally affecting them in terms of what's going on in their life, but I think what you've highlighted are the systemic ecosystem problems that then contribute to their experience of care and the knock-on effects of them losing trust in the system. I think that's another great takeaway. So you set up this ability to deliver care, you set up the physical infrastructure around this, you enabled people to deliver care in a compassionate way, and you looked at logistics and supply chain. So, looking at infrastructure, people, and processes... the other part to this is how did you look at technology?

Sometimes we look at shiny new technology and say, "Hey, let's shoehorn this in." How did you think about it? You've alluded to this a little bit. How did you prioritize where it is going to be most impactful for us? How did you do this? Because there's lots of learning to take to health system leaders around the world to say, "Hey, we've created this infrastructure, we've created a way to deliver care, and now we have the opportunity to leverage technology to do this even more impactfully." You've had lots of learnings around how to do this so well.

Shabs, it wasn't like we said, "There's shiny technology over there; let's go use it." We had pain points. We were very dedicated to process, workflow, and to time and motion. We didn't want people waiting any longer than they needed to, and we had really high volumes at the sites that we worked at. But the challenge was we had pain points as we scaled, and the initial pain point that we identified is that scheduling is a real challenge in a spreadsheet. So how can we build a system to ensure that the right people are at the right place at the right time doing the right thing?

You get those four key components together and you've solved 80% of your challenges. That's what we found. Initially we built a scheduling system. It wasn't our intention to build this big huge ecosystem that it ended up being; we just started with scheduling. Then after that was working well, you're like, "Wow, this makes life so much easier.

What's our next biggest pain point?" And then we would just take the next biggest pain point and build a module for it, and then for the next biggest pain point we built a module. The thing that was really great about our developers is that they recognized from day one that user feedback is critical. So we've been able to be in kind of a leapfrog type of approach to development because they are so close to the users. During COVID, our developers would put on PPE and come on the ward with us. At the height of COVID, we had 138 people admitted and 91 in the ICU and 55 on ventilators.

It was very busy, and they would come in and watch our time and motion. They would go outside and they would write code, and 30 minutes later we would be using that code in the ward. That's a fast feedback loop. Totally. When they are so close and embedded with the team, it's amazing how fast the development process can work.

When the team feels like they can give feedback and their feedback is heard—it doesn't mean that 100% of what we say happens, it doesn't mean it all happens in 30 minutes—but there's a Dev queue. The development team is very intimate with our operations and they see things that are very critical and those things go right away. Once the team sees that their feedback matters, they just give you more and more good intel. Users know best, and I think what we've seen happen with other systems in our environment is that a lot of the developers are not in the country and they're not intimate with the challenges. It's very easy to become disconnected from the reality on the ground.

But because our developers were connected to the reality on the ground, it really changed our ability to scale and bring digital solutions to ground level. It's been really fun to watch the process. There were some key learnings that I think could be taken to other environments. One of them for me was—I'm not a tech person—but I understand how much tech impacts patient care and service delivery. In our case, it's patient care, but it's service delivery no matter where you're at.

Simplifying administration was so important for us, because once you simplify administration in the healthcare context, you're able to put a lot more effort into caring for people. Compassion becomes easier because the system is empowering compassion. These are the things that we've seen. It's really been fun—it's been hard and intense—but it's really been fun to watch the dynamics in the team. The unity that I see in the team drives the ability to do this rapid development.

The buy-in, because their voice is heard, brings more good ideas to the table. The developers don't have to go searching for good ideas; they're brought by the end users. The other thing that I probably need to say right from the beginning is that we prioritized this system being mobile-first. Why? Because we realized that the relationship between the patient and the provider is the most important part of the whole equation of our service delivery.

What we found in a lot of other countries is that in the first world, most of the time these systems are built for billing. They're built from that perspective. In our environment, systems are built for grant reporting. They're built from that office, and the patient is kind of a second thought. In this case, they developed this system from the bedside of the patient, and that has allowed there to be a different product at the end of this process.

And this was an EHR for the provider, for the community health workers, to deliver care and solve some of their administrative issues, is that right? Well, there are three main pillars: one is supply chain, one is HR, and one is service delivery, which in our case is the EHR. You've touched on so much that I wanted to get into. The first one is the importance of the fast feedback loop and having your design and development team really being as close to what's going on the ground as possible. The second is it's sometimes hard, at least in my experience, to get feedback that matters from end users.

The way to unlock that engagement is building that trust and having that fast feedback. "Actually, this is being heard. I know that if I engage with this, even though I have such a busy day, it will pay off because it's going to improve what I'm doing and my ability to deliver care." I think that's such a nice nugget and a nice takeaway. I just wanted to call out the frustration in the US, the EU, and the UK around EHRs and the problems with usability, and how they take people away from delivering care. You're just on your computer, not focusing on the person in front of you.

It's really interesting that everyone complains about EHRs in the US being built for billing, and so I really like this parallel that you called out. It's the same-same but different; it plays out in a different way where historically for you it's been geared towards grant reporting, right? The way you then solve that in a similar mindset but for a related problem really stands out. Thanks a lot. The other thing that I wanted to say is that we really have found that if it's right for the patient, it's right for grant reporting.

If it's right for the patient, it's right for billing. I just think sometimes when we have a problem, we forget the perspective from which we're supposed to solve that problem. We've had people come from all over the world. Right now we have three tours going on, just coming to look at the system in action. These people are from outside of the country.

Yesterday the same thing happened. It just is every day: people are coming from all over the world to look at the system. We didn't think we were developing anything special; we were just solving our little problems on the ground, we thought. When people come—people that really know what they're talking about—they say things that I can't believe. One political adviser from Washington DC who worked next to the president in Rwanda during their economic recovery after the genocide, he came here and did a tour.

We sat in a debrief, and the first thing he said was, "Do you know that this digital system that you built can change the GDP of countries?" I was like, "What?" Your perspective is just different when you're in your own little environment solving your own little problems. You don't realize that maybe you built something that can solve problems in other places. Recently we had a surgeon here from the United States who said, "I'm going to go back to my CEO at our hospital network and tell them that the EHR that I used here is better than Epic." Okay, maybe I shouldn't have said the name, but that's what he said. You start to realize—I didn't know that we were building something special—but you start to realize just by getting the perspective of other people from around the world who really are in places where they have exposure that, yeah, maybe it is special. What you just mentioned about this surgeon taking what you've done here back to the US is, to me in a nutshell, why we reach out to you to have these conversations.

You've just summed up the whole "why" of the podcast in that little sentence. Kudos to you and the team for focusing on that. There are books, seminars, and conferences that talk about "falling in love with the problem." It's really about the problem. There's lots of great academic theory about this, but it's really interesting that implementation still suffers from really getting that bit nailed down before you try to scale, right? This is really good learning.

You just worked with the people who are delivering care and solved their problems and made it work for them iteratively, with a very fast feedback loop. I think that's a great message for the sector as a whole in digital health of how you really just make it work on the ground. Great. Maybe before you shift gears, I wanted to go back to the part of getting user feedback. I wanted to share a little bit of what was maybe part of the secret sauce that could be shared and maybe help someone else.

From early on in the organizational structure, we tried to keep it flat. We wanted to hear from everyone, whether it's the gardener, the cleaner, or the security guards. I'll be honest with you: they've brought us some of the most valuable feedback that we've gotten from anyone. One key takeaway for us has been just to make sure that your leadership team—no matter how big they are, no matter how many qualifications they have—that they understand how important it is to also learn every day. In our core values, one of them is "teachability," which means that no matter who we are, we can learn from anyone in the organization.

Most importantly, we learn from our beneficiaries—in this case, our patients. I remember early on we were building the digital system. We actually have a plant manager here—he manages our plant equipment and he's been here probably 11 years—but he had probably been here about five years at the time, and he said to us, "You know, if I was a patient at the gate, I would not like ABC." He told us that there were things that he wouldn't like and the team took that information and completely changed the way that that process happened. I look at that today and say, "What if we would have never had that feedback? Would we still be making those same mistakes?" A key takeaway for us is just to hear from everyone; everyone's feedback is valuable.

It's not just the leaders, it's not just management, it's not just the technical people. Make sure we create these feedback loops from everyone, even patients. After every patient checks out, they get a text message that says, "Were you happy with your service today? If not, press two; if yes, press one." As soon as they push two, it creates a task in a task management system that one of our senior managers picks up immediately. Sometimes they haven't even walked out of the gate; sometimes we can correct our mistake before they even leave the site.

I call them "patient whisperers." They call with a really nice voice, and the patient tells them a lot of things maybe we needed to fix. That allows us to do real-time corrections and not wait till the end of a month for a report or until something has really escalated. Those feedback loops have been critical to us. The real-time correction thing is critical. Before we're 45 degrees out—when we're only one or two degrees out—we're able to easily correct.

I think that's so interesting that you've done that intrinsically and seen the value of it. One of the things that regulation is trying to do is make this kind of thing mandatory—I mean, not just trying, it does. To some degree, they call this "post-market surveillance." You deploy and then you monitor qualitatively and quantitatively. A lot of people say, "Hey, this is so onerous." I'm not calling anyone out in particular, but that can be the attitude. What you've done is said, "Well, we're going to invest in doing this because it actually helps us produce a better service and product," and you use this to actually actively look at how you can improve things.

For me, that's another great message around the value of taking this and not just paying lip service to it. It's actually a part of your continuous development and improvement. That sounds great. Have you had any challenges or things that didn't go so well that you've learned from? Every day.

Maybe I can say we've had a lot of challenges, but the second core value in our organization is "looks for solutions." These core values... we actually recite them every morning. In our divisions, we stand in a circle and we go over our mission, our vision, our core values, and our creed. It sounds kind of like elementary school, but to be honest with you, Shabs, it's made a difference. It somehow refocuses us.

No matter what happens, no matter what situation occurs, you refocus: "Okay, this is what we're about; this is why we're here." That number two—looks for solutions—has been key. In our induction program, we train that we know we're going to run across challenges every day, but we believe as a team that we can get together and find solutions for whatever challenge is in front of us. That has really changed the approach to challenges. We've had a lot of challenges that were difficult, but it's that core value that has been inculcated in the team: when they see challenges, they start talking about possible solutions rather than the challenge. It's very much a team approach to solving problems.

Sometimes when something good happens and somebody says, "Well, how did that happen?" I couldn't even tell you who was the originator, because probably 5% came from one person, 10% from another, and 15% from another. I think that really helps with team unity as well. It also helps people throw out more ideas because they don't have to come up with a 100% idea. One of our current challenges is that we really struggled ... we have really solved the supply chain thing internally.

I can tell you that we have a super strong end-to-end supply chain accountability system from procurement all the way to dispensing drugs to the patient. Really, nothing moves without it being visualized in the system. But we then started taking on more and more of the national healthcare system burden and did not plan well for how we were going to resource that. This happened during COVID when there were a lot of crises on the ground; we also had unprecedented civil unrest. So there was a lot of things happening, and one of our challenges we're still in the process of solving is how we balance the demand now.

When you have a high-quality service with a robust supply chain, then the demand just keeps getting bigger and bigger. So it's almost like some of the things that happened were too successful and we didn't maybe hedge the growth fast enough. It happened very fast: the number of patients we're taking care of has grown by 300% over the last five years. That would be hard in any context, let alone a low-resource environment. So that's one thing that we're still working on, and that's one of the reasons that we're starting to diversify.

We're really working on a totally different funding model. We're a nonprofit, and we have never charged for our services, partially because of where we started. We started in rural areas where no one had healthcare, and we knew that if we charged the poorest of the poor for healthcare, there's one thing that would happen: they would stay home and die. If any one of us doesn't acknowledge that, we've missed our social contract with the most vulnerable. It's important to understand that.

Now at our facility, we have people coming that could pay, but we don't know who those people are because our facility is seeing a thousand patients a day. How do you determine who they are? Those are some of the current challenges that we're working on solving: through an API, you can reference some vulnerability index so that you know whether or not people should pay or not pay. For us as an institution—and of course, it's different in other spaces—but if we charge the poorest of the poor, we've broken our social contract with our mandate, and it's just non-negotiable for us. We have to figure this out.

These are some of the things that we're currently working on, because we didn't realize that some of the efficiencies that we put into place were going to drive demand at such a level that it was a mismatch with resources. You talked about going to the people, and you've set up the ability to deliver telehealth in the most rural or hard-to-access areas. Can you tell us a little bit about that? Well, I think if we're honest with ourselves, telehealth is being used in first-world countries very well, and it's really efficient. If somebody doesn't have to leave work or home, it's just efficient for everyone.

It works a lot of the time, but what we realized is that in a context like the one we're working in, people are boarding buses again—going back to the transport issue—and they're spending those meager resources that they could be using to put their kids in school or buy their children food, and they're boarding buses to come to hospitals to get 10 paracetamol or 10 ibuprofen—things that you and I have in our homes. Not only that, they're coming for routine refills of antiretrovirals or routine refills of TB drugs—things that they don't really need to be seen in person for if there's not labs or other things. So we started thinking about four or five years ago, "What if we took telehealth to communities?" Some of this was driven during the civil unrest that we had because some of the facilities were closing, and we were trying to figure out, if you had to mobilize quickly in a crisis, how would you do that in a high-quality way? We started working several years ago on this "Health Hub" concept, for which we've just finished a prototype and are working on three more to roll out. We hope that this goes big; we really do, because we feel that it's special.

It's integrated with Luvlelo—the digital system that I've been talking about. Just a side note: "Luvlelo" in our language in Eswatini means "compassion," and we felt like it was a word that could easily be said around the world, so that's why we chose it. We have literally taken a 12-meter shipping container and fitted it with solar; they're completely off-grid. We use Starlink for connectivity and there are literally four bays. In the first bay, you go inside and self-register on a digital device.

In the second bay, we have a vital scanner that is integrated with Luvlelo, and you get your vitals. We really feel as clinicians that if we get a good set of vitals, we can pretty much know which direction we need to go in for the patient. In the third bay, you do a video consult with a doctor who's at our headquarters. As soon as the doctor orders the medication, it sends the patient a once-off PIN. Then they go to the screen and put in the once-off PIN, and out comes their medication out of a vending machine.

Behind the scenes, we've customized a vending machine for high-volume, high-SKU commodities. We want it to solve a lot of problems. For instance, if we take somebody's blood pressure, we can actually do blood pressure medication adjustments even at remote sites. We've been working on this for a very long time and have just recently started getting ready to take it out. In fact, we haven't launched it in our country yet, but we will soon.

You mentioned right care at the right place at the right time, and so this seems like an enabler of that. You're creating capacity by dealing with those people at the source who otherwise would be coming centrally for refills. That's great for them, great for you as a system, and great for your clinicians, who are freed up to see the people that they need to. It's a great example of solving across the spectrum. You said it's not live yet.

I was going to ask what the adoption was like. Have you done some trials? Yeah. We're trialing it inside of our network first, and then we are planning to... we're already in conversations with some potential customers for this solution.

It's really fun to finally have it at this stage. How do you solve the connectivity issue? You mentioned Starlink. How did you manage to get Starlink to agree to connect you guys up? Well, the Starlink process all went through the regulatory process in Eswatini, and it was approved.

So then it was easy for us to be able to connect via Starlink. We do know, for instance, our neighbors in South Africa haven't approved it yet, and some other countries haven't. But this is a game changer; we're the first to tell you that. We use about 1,1536 digital devices a day to do our work, and we have teams all over the country. Being able to use Starlink...

we just use Starlink with solar panels now at all of our remote sites. All those generators and the need for electricity—all that stuff is just gone. The connectivity is much better than even our local service provider for cellular service. It kind of harks back to something Bilal said from Digital Square in the podcast and something I've heard before where you can have all this tech and all these great services, but it needs the infrastructure. You can create the best train in the world, but if the rails are crap, then that's not going to be great.

Having the infrastructure as a way that enables you to do all of this... you need reliable connectivity to be able to deliver that service if it's going to work. I can see how that's, in your words, a game changer. Yeah, it's been a game changer. Now we're doing some installations for some of the other facilities, and so it's really exciting.

We are a bit of an innovation hub, an incubation hub, or a petri dish—whatever you want to call it. We're not really scared to try something and fail, or try something enough to go through several revisions. It's fun, then, once you've been able to find a solution for our network, to then be able to take that to other places and see the way that it transforms their operations, too. That's really what we want to do moving forward: we'd like our technical teams to be able to take some of these innovations to other places and other countries, not just in Eswatini. Hopefully that will help us to solve some of our challenges as we look for other revenue generators to continue doing our core work.

Amazing. Speaking of not being afraid of innovation, can you tell us about drones? Well, I'm really excited to tell this story, because you know how sometimes there's artificial barriers in some of the engagements that you have with different regulatory units. Sometimes it makes sense, but you just can't get it through the regulatory process. What I can tell you is that in Eswatini we've had the most amazing relationship and process with the Civil Aviation Authority, and I don't think most countries can say that.

I really want to champion their willingness to do something they've never done before, because we are the first approved drone network in the country. They didn't even have the regulations in place. But what I loved is that they knew what our goals were: it was to get high-value commodities—vaccines, drugs, snakebite antivenom, blood units—and reverse logistics for lab samples. They knew that that was important, especially in rural communities, and they just focused on solutions. Our team and their team worked side-by-side, and literally every single regulatory component that had to be in place, they worked together to do it.

It's just been the most amazing relationship. I've said even in the launch that if all relationships were like this, we would achieve so much. Again, the focus was on the end goal, and everyone in between said, "How do we solve these problems? Because it's good for our people." I was really, really thrilled just to see this come to fruition and get through all the regulatory process. Beyond getting drones in the sky, how were we able to do this so quickly in Eswatini?

It's a case study that needs to be looked at. That sounds really, really interesting. We've had several podcasts talking about the regulation and the problems from both angles, in terms of the ability to have regulation as a facilitator and enabler rather than just being perceived as being there to block stuff. Also, the attitude of developers and people who are building technology to say, "Hey, we don't necessarily need to skirt around it," but actually leaning in to talk to a regulator to say, "Hey, here's the impact that we want to have. How do we do this in a way that feels good for everyone?" How do you have the right level of safeguards and guardrails?

I think this is a really good model for how we're thinking about AI and LLMs, etc. You've leaned into it; they've leaned into it, with the goal of delivering this for people. So definitely, I think that should be a case study. So relevant. It's been really fun.

They all came to the launch and they were as excited as we were. It was just really such a joint achievement. I think no matter if it's internally and you're working together as a team, or you're working with external stakeholders, when you achieve something big, there's some euphoria that comes from a really tight collaborative process. The facilities are so excited. It's also, of course, driven by the fact that we have a strong supply chain supplying those drones.

Literally within an hour of them making their orders, those drones are landing. In fact, I think they've done half of their targets for the whole year in two months. I wanted to touch on two things. You started with a problem. There are certain types of medications that might be controlled or that you need to dispatch very, very quickly.

You mentioned antivenom and certain types of controlled drugs that will be impactful in the right places, but which might need a level of protection where you need to keep them centrally and then get them out to people. And then there's the time criticality—if you have been bitten by a snake and you need to get that person that antivenom very quickly. We already mentioned the transport issues. Do you have anything more to say around how you identified those? It seems like a no-brainer looking at it retrospectively, but any more comments on that?

Well, we do a lot of snakebite work in the country. In fact, we're the main referral hospital for all the snakebites. This year we've admitted over 400 snakebites alone. We have not had one snakebite death, really driven by really strong treatment algorithms and the time-in-motion is critical. How do we make sure that we don't over-inject antivenom?

It's very expensive and has its own side effects. How do you make sure that you don't miss early signs of severe envenomation or progressing symptomatology that needs a response? We've had really strong treatment algorithms and a team that really wanted to solve this problem. We have black mambas in our area. We were just sick and tired of seeing people die from these neurotoxic snakes.

One of our friends, who's a "snake whisperer"—she loves snakes and she loves people—she's worked really hard to bring awareness to the country. She told me five or six years ago, "Echo, if you have ventilators and you put neurotoxic snakebites on ventilators—if for some reason there's no antivenom or for some reason they come too late and they're severely decompensated—you'll save them." I was like, "Well, if that's what it takes, we're getting ventilators." So we did. That's why we started our ICU; it was because of snakebites. I'm telling you, we haven't lost a neurotoxic bite in the last three years because if people are severely decompensated, we ventilate them. Guess what?

After that venom neutralizes three or four days later, they come off the vent and it's as if they were never bitten. But before, they would die, and that's what the whole country thought: if you get bitten by a black mamba, it's a death sentence. The doctors used to tell people, "Just say your goodbyes," especially because they bite kids a lot. To say that to the parents is just devastating. We got sick and tired of that, and we just decided we're going to try to do something different, even if everyone says that there's no way to avoid this.

Over the past five years, we've gone from not only no deaths in our own facility... for the first time in recorded history, this year we have not had a snakebite death in our country. I do think rapid access to antivenom played a major role in us wanting to get drones in the sky because two years ago we had 1536 people dying en route. Last year we had nine people dying en route. We're like, "This is just not necessary." The problem is when you send this very expensive commodity out to 1536 facilities, it leaks.

It's expensive and valuable outside of the hospital. Additionally to that, it's oxytocin and other things that save lives, but again, if they're not in the right place at the right time, they're not going to save anybody's life. They're just part of our supply chain challenges that we struggle with day-to-day. So that's why we felt that hubbing high-value commodities at one place where there's a very robust supply chain, strong controls, and accountability, would work. Boy, is it exciting to now have this happening!

You get a call and literally an hour-and-a-half trip turns into 13 minutes. These drones fly at night and the payload is 4kg. We hope to diversify our fleet over time, but our initial plan is to run this drone fleet this year and see, of course, how we make it as efficient as possible. It's been exciting to close the last mile and see the change—it is really exciting. So amazing to hear the impact of that.

Some detractors might say, "Hey, drones are great technology, but you need the maintenance and the infrastructure." How about maintaining them? You need pilots; they need to be trained; they need to maintain their license. Eswatini is a small country; how do you tackle this? Like everything else: local capacity. That was a non-negotiable when we were talking to the drone manufacturers, because many of them send in their own pilots, technicians, maintenance teams, and ground operators, and it's a service provider type of engagement.

We just said if we're going to do this, it's non-negotiable that we're going to develop local capacity and have our own pilots. The companies that didn't want to do that, we just couldn't consider them. What we did—what we've done in a lot of circumstances—is that when there's an opportunity, we look at the people who have been faithful in the past and then start talking to staff who have shown great potential and say, "We're starting this new program; would you be interested in becoming one of the trained pilots?" It's not people that we bring in to perform a skill; we bring in someone who's already shown that they are sold out to the mission and vision, because that person will—it doesn't matter where you put them—they will do well. Why? They're bought into the big goal; they're not bought into their own personal space.

So we chose five people and sent them to South African flight schools. It's pretty interesting because it was a lot more than I thought it was going to be—I think they took about 1536 tests—and they all scored in the top 1% in those flight schools. I was very shocked to see how well they did. Then they came back and they own that program. So it's not just getting the qualification; it's also getting the heart behind what you're trying to accomplish.

That's why I say that what has worked with the drones is what has worked in every other circumstance: get people who are sold out to what you're trying to accomplish, and if they don't have the training, upskill them. Get them the training and the qualification, and they're the ones that will then make that next big idea a success. Great takeaway. Before we wrap up, I wanted to go into some bigger meta-challenges. One of the big things that enables you to carry out your work is funding, and part of getting funding is making sure that you're regularly communicating a very clear vision and your impact effectively.

Do you have any learnings on challenges or successes for people who might be trying to do the same? Well, if I could tell you we've solved the funding equation, we haven't, partially because of the scale at which things have grown. I'll be honest with you: we are better innovators than we are salespeople. So it's something we are working very hard to solve. In fact, we've brought on a business development team and marketers this year—we've never had that before—but the thing got so big that there's no way we're going to be able to do this without getting these teams right.

We're in the process of doing that, but if I was starting over again, I would have done this much earlier. We're working really hard to bring up social enterprise lines so that we can continue doing what we feel called to and doing it in a way that is properly resourced. Sorry I can't bring a solution to that one. I hope someone listening to this has a solution for me! Great.

You also have this really clear vision and set of values. Do you have any advice on how to help people create their own for the impact that they intend to have? Well, maybe if I could tell you: don't look at everyone else's. Sit down in consultation with your team and say, "Okay, it looks like we created something special here. Why is it special?" Start to figure out what that looks like for you.

I think our core values initially... I was like, "These are a little bit weird." They weren't weird at all; they were just not normal. The first one is "teachability," around humility and how you approach the learning process, making sure even your senior leaders are learners first. The second one is "looks for solutions." The third one is "commitment to unity." I did not realize how critical that was, but you can look back now and see. Number four is "dedicated to every last one." We don't leave any patient in line, because people board buses and come long distances, and then if we say, "Oh sorry, we're done for the day," it breaks the trust of the patient.

So that's really linked to trust. Our number five is "servanthood"—making sure we understand that the patient is number one in the equation; we're not number one as a staff. Number six is an attitude of gratefulness, because we learned that if we are grateful for what we do have, even while we're working on the things where we have challenges, it brings a positivity to the environment that actually catalyzes innovation and good ideas, and catalyzes people to share things that they might not otherwise be able to share in a more negative environment. I would say those... I've not seen those core values organized like that before, but they've been super transformational to us.

Listen to everybody on every level in your team. What do they see as important to the institution? That ended up being very helpful to us—swallowing my preconceived notions of what a set of core values should look like and saying it's okay if they're different. Obviously, it's not something you change often; if it's a flop, then you start over. Do you have any final words of wisdom, experience, or insight?

Maybe just two. One I wish I would have learned a lot earlier is: if you get to 80%, just jump off the cliff and work on the 20% while you're in motion. I am a perfectionist, so it's a little bit hard sometimes to do that, but I've realized how critical it is, because if I don't jump off the cliff with the 80%, I have 0%. The second thing is to dream beyond what you can see, because that's where we found the really big things happen that you don't expect. Obviously, we're a faith-based institution, so we do see God as part of the equation and we believe that we need to live beyond what we can see, because there's a lot that could happen beyond what we can visualize.

We've tried to dream big and then work together to accomplish those dreams. We've seen a lot of those dreams come true. I just encourage others to not put yourself in a box. I remember—I trained in medicine—about 1536 years ago, I told our CFO that I wished I would have gone into business and got an MBA. He was like, "No, Echo.

If you would have done that, you'd still be sitting in your office worried about making a mistake." I think sometimes we should ensure that we look at the sweet spots of our staff and position them accordingly, because sometimes what they were trained in is not what they're best at or what they're naturally gifted at. Those are some of the things that have been really key for us in our organizational growth. I really appreciate the opportunity to be able to talk today, Shabs. That "dream big and beyond what you can see" is a really nice takeaway. Echo, how can people get in touch with you?

Thanks a lot, and thanks for listening. Shabs, thanks a lot for having us. If you want to reach out to us, you can reach out at info@luvlelo.org or at info@lukecommission.org. We're also on the web under those same URLs. We'd love to connect to anyone who thinks they would like to be part of what we're doing.

We're really excited for the opportunity to be on today. Thanks a lot, Echo, for sharing such a rich set of insights and learnings. There's so much to take away regarding people, processes, quality delivery of care, technology perspectives, and leadership values. There's so much to take in, whatever part of digital health or impact you want to create. I'm really grateful for that, and I'm hoping that people get as much out of it as I have today.
episodes.pullQuote: When you walk with the people, you learn the challenges intimately.
episodes.title: Impactful digital health transformation through a clear vision and values: insights from Eswatini
episodes.description: What can a tiny country enveloped by South Africa teach the world about digital health done right? Echo Vanderwal shares how The Luke Commission built healthcare for those who needed it most - from telehealth hubs in shipping containers and drone delivery of antivenom, to a bespoke clinician-centred EHR - all anchored in clear values and a vision of what great care actually looks like.

topics: Flexibility in digital health regulation: adapting to a rapidly changing landscape
Integrating feedback from clinicians and patients into the regulatory process
Evaluating digital health technologies holistically, not as isolated tools
Suites and groupings of digital devices: regulatory approaches that acknowledge flexibility
Lessons from DiGA (Germany), PECAN (France), and what's coming in the UK
The stark differences between FDA and EU regulatory approaches - and the deeper reasons behind them
Regulation's role in promoting interoperability across digital health systems
Long-term thinking, clear goals, and continuous feedback loops for effective digital transformation
Why digital transformation in healthcare requires investment and time before yielding dividends
episodes.bio: Stephen Gilbert is a Professor at the Faculty of Medicine, Dresden University of Technology (Else Kröner Fresenius Center for Digital Health), leading a multidisciplinary team specialising in regulatory science for medical devices and in vitro diagnostic devices. With over 15 years of expertise in clinical research, computational biology, and regulatory science, he is committed to advancing digital health innovation and governance.
episodes.guestRole: Professor of Medical Device Regulatory Science, Dresden University of Technology
episodes.transcript:
You are tuned into the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. My name is Shabs Upad, a physician working in digital health. I'm keen to learn more about the issues, challenges, and successes where digital health can have a real impact for underserved communities around the world. If you're a founder, investor, donor, researcher, or are developing and implementing digital health anywhere in the world and you're keen to break out of your bubble, join me as I speak to experts and innovators and get a truly global perspective on digital health. Stephen, it is so great to have you on the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast.

Can you start maybe by telling the audience a little bit about yourself and your work? Sure. It's great to be here. Shabs and I, we are friends, former colleagues; we worked together at Ada Health. And lots of conversations there.

When I moved on from Ada Health, I moved to be a professor of medical device regulatory science. I would kind of see this role as regulatory and implementation science. I don't really see a separation between the modern view of what regulation is and the digital health space on the question of implementation. So my work focus spanned across implementation. Before I worked with you at Ada Health, I worked at a med tech company called Biotronik in Berlin.

That's in the area of internal defibrillators, cardiac implantable monitors, pacemakers, etc. And I worked in clinical regulatory for the implantable closed-loop variety of digital devices. Before that, I was in academia, and way way back, I'm a veterinary researcher by training. So I think there's two main areas I'd love to get into in our conversation today. One is the bigger kind of regulatory picture; maybe we can touch on that briefly at the beginning.

And then maybe we can get into the health tech assessment, clinical outcomes, economic evaluation, and the challenges. Because, as I understand, you've done some work with health systems and with governments on how they can get this right. I think that's a particular area of interest here, where we're focused on low-resource settings as well. So it would be really, really good to hone in on your insights into what you've learned from those types of conversations that could be applied in these other contexts as well. So on that, Stephen: Regulation, the global picture—where are we at?

It's a very interesting time to work in AI and medical device regulation. I sometimes have a slide that I show in quite a lot of my slide decks, which is that I think people think regulation is quite boring and they kind of groan. Many other professors jokingly, or not very jokingly, say to me, "Well, I'm glad you're working on that; I'm glad I'm not." Sometimes they're professors of clinical AI or professors of physics of AI, mathematics of AI, or other aspects of technology development. That's kind of seen as the sexy area of technology, and anybody who's intersecting with regulation, that's the kind of boring aspect. It's all paperwork; it's kind of paper pushing.

And I like to show this kind of carousel or mosaic of slides— actually, images I've taken from leading newspapers, mostly the Financial Times. It just has a title: "We're living in interesting regulatory times." And it shows a lot of discussion over large language models, over OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google, and some of the figures within those countries. All of these articles are about regulation of AI, and particularly regulation of AI in healthcare. We're really living through a period of a year and a half where the AI aspect of digital regulation is front-page news. So it's an interesting time to work in the space.

I was in a slightly odd position within the regulatory discussion because I'm an academic professor, and you tend to get a very polarized argument sometimes coming from the regulatory community, which is kind of, "Well, everything already exists, and everything already exists in a perfect form." You know, nothing is new under the sun. It's a question of taking a new technology and applying the rules. A little bit like the obvious analogy that I always use for this is Moses has carried down the regulatory rules from Mount Sinai and presented them as tablets of stone, and we only need to read them. You know, read the works of scripture and the tablets of stone, and we have the answers to every possible question of the future. And then on the opposite extreme, you kind of have the perspective that nothing is there— literally that nothing is there.

So you'd repeatedly read in the newspapers, in blogs, LinkedIn, and numerous sources that there is no regulation of health and how should we regulate this space, and we need to start from the absolute beginning because nothing is there. And, of course, neither of these things is true. Of course, we don't have perfect systems to regulate futures which we did not anticipate, and often we're extending principles from very far in the past from very different types of devices to the current. It's also true that we don't have nothing and that we have no foundations. You could say that's the boring middle ground; for me, it's the most exciting middle ground.

Because within how you actually get bringing in future perspectives, future approaches, adapting regulatory frameworks to what's needed for the future, and taking in the best of what's currently developed and adapting that, there are really very, very interesting thought processes and development of thought and interaction in the space. So your message is: "Regulation is sexy." Do you have a slide saying "I am passionate about regulation"? Maybe you'd be the only person in those communities. I definitely wouldn't be the only person to be passionate about regulation. People can get very, very engrossed in the topic within the regulatory community, but sometimes those very same people can be highly, highly conservative.

And there can unfortunately be sometimes a line of kind of patronizing, like telling the rest of the world that they're wrong. Now, some of that is inevitable because within the world of regulation, there is an aspect of a policing role; it is a checkpoint. So of course, an aspect of this thinking can come in, and it's inevitable; it's impossible to completely avoid that. But at the same time, you know me; I'm probably the humblest individual you've ever encountered, Shabs. The humblest ever, yeah.

Yeah, so there is room for listening and learning, particularly within the area of how regulation is developed for the future, and to stand back and actually ask the higher-level question: "Is it actually right and fit for purpose?" not making an argument into the future that it must. There's another major problem with regulation which is very much talked about also in the media, which is a kind of bottleneck effect of regulation. There can be a kind of attitude from the community which is, "And so it should be. We're there to slow down progress in the manner that we should only be allowing through the bottleneck"— they wouldn't use the word "bottleneck," but through the approval process—"those technologies which are safe for market." So inevitably, there's a huge crowd of technologies wanting to come through, and the responsible valve controlling what's flowing through and letting— as a very responsible function— making sure what gets through is safe. I think one's perspective on that way of functioning of the regulatory system slightly has to be looked at from the perspective of what's the need.

So for COVID, it became a very, very controversial point over COVID vaccination. Clearly, we faced a situation where there was an absolutely enormous world need on the side of vaccination, but also in the terms of medical devices. And during COVID, we did see a relaxation of certain regulatory rules. There wasn't a complete relaxation saying regulation no longer applies; there was a considered analysis of the challenges of the situation and of responses from regulators and from legislators even in certain cases to re-evaluate what the right balance was in that situation. And there is an expectation for digital health and digital medicine.

I would actually take this maybe as a useful example: the OECD meeting. A major focus of that meeting, I think was in February this year—January? January? January—was on digital health aspects of participative healthcare. This was a meeting with the heads of the departments of health of numerous countries, occupying two massive rows along the front of the meeting, and the panelists on stage dominated by the ministers of health from many OECD countries, actually stating that on a policy level from countries, digital health solutions interacting with other aspects of workflows are actually being seen as a critical aspect of future health delivery both in prevention and in treatment of the disease.

Now that is a situation that requires an enormous step-up of what's being delivered within the space, and that requires a cooperative and proactive response from regulators to ensure that that can be delivered. So it's not a vain hope. We cannot afford healthcare in the developed countries, nor in lower-income countries, without that step-up. It's a core part of policy certainly for the OECD, one could say worldwide, and the World Health Organization is quite good at recognizing this. That's got a responsibility that goes with it.

And it's not the same as to say there may be a slightly better version of a drug against this chronic condition that may slightly improve a very small—make a very small delta in the overall healthcare delivery system. It's anticipated, hoped, and needed that you get a massive change in healthcare delivery associated with digital health; therefore, the systems developed need to acknowledge that in all of their aspects. Often when I say those kind of things, sometimes people can see me as one of the drinkers of the Kool-Aid—those that are naively thinking digital systems can transform care systems and have no idea about how care systems function. I'm not talking about that from that level; I'm not even saying it's my perspective— actually, it is my perspective—I'm saying it is the perspective of very many governments and an acknowledgment from organizations like the OECD that there is a need to get those systems to work. What are you saying is regulation's place in this? I'm saying that regulation needs to actually make itself functioning to the task that's in front of it. There's a task in front of healthcare and health policy, and regulation needs to be absolutely ready to step up to the plate to be fit for purpose for the size of the task. You talked earlier about a spectrum in terms of people's position. You mentioned the two extremes and the reality being in the middle.

Countries, regulatory bodies within those, or policymakers will have different places they are on this spectrum. What causes the variability of people's stances on this spectrum? I would argue that it's absolutely not the wrong term. Can you define flexibility in this context? I mean, in a very broad sense. If we're—maybe we'll get into it later in the call—going to talk about this with very specific examples, but I think at the moment I would keep it relatively broad. One could always impose more stringent requirements, a further list of checklists, very very strict observation of exactly one way in which it must be done, and no dialogue across a regulatory approval system.

If you're not approving things in certain parts of the regulatory approval system, you're probably, within your own role and your own job, feeling less exposed than if you are approving things. Now I would balance that—and we'll come back to maybe getting into some more detailed examples of this—to say that the challenge in regulatory science is actually getting both things to work together. Getting the incentives right in the system where people are not only concerned about "Will it come back to bite me if it turns out to be a problem?" but there is actual working together, acknowledging that the benefits are needed because the regulation is about benefits and risks. It is written into the regulations, but the focus can then be overly on the risks. Of course, the risks need to be monitored. I think across all regulatory systems and countries, the importance of measuring risks—and particularly observing risks in the wild, post-market surveillance, real-world performance monitoring, etc.—are a critical part of that.

Maybe I could give a very high-level example of flexibility in regulatory systems which is slightly different than maybe examples we'll get to later, which is the area of decision support. clinical decision support. I always give this example because it's a situation where it gives stark differences between different regulatory approaches, and none is absolutely right or wrong. The stances come from the US Congress. US Congress passed something called the 21st Century Cures Act, often abbreviated to the Cures Act.

That looked at modern information communication technology around hospitals and it looked at electronic health record systems as a foundational set of technologies amongst other things. It was, you know, kind of as in the title—"Century Cures Act"—it was looking at approaches that could come in medicine that were in the 21st century but not in centuries before. It made certain decisions about not regulating as medical devices certain sets of decision support technologies which assisted doctors making decisions around the electronic health record. It's a bit broader than that, but that's effectively the gist of the decision made by Congress. Congress is the body that should be making these decisions, and then it's up to the regulators to implement those decisions; that's how it works.

It's a very bold decision from Congress, and it sets out that a whole series of devices are not devices at all—a whole series of decision support systems are not devices at all. Now, it's not all. Sometimes people talk about US clinical decision support systems as if they're not highly regulated. Some are highly regulated and some are not, but the groups that are not are really very expansive, provided they fit certain criteria. The FDA has set out a series of criteria for this: they have to have approaches to avoid automation bias; they have to be not for emergency situations; they have to have a level of clinical evidence that supports their use and that can be interpreted; they have to provide the basis on which decisions are made; and they can't interpret images and signals.

That's effectively the list—I could be missing one when I'm trying to recount them in real time on this video call. Now, the effect of that is to create what I always describe as a hundredfold difference between the US regulation of this space and the European regulation of the space. All of those clinical decision support systems— they provide clinical decision support around these use cases. You'll see in the US FDA clinical decision support guidance, if you read it, it's around the area of diagnosis and therapy of disease, sometimes of prognosis, but these would all be classified as Class 2A devices in a European context and would have to go through an incredibly rigorous process of regulatory quality management system approval, the provision of clinical data, clinical evaluation, and post-market surveillance for clinical evidence. In the US, they don't.

Of course, you could get disparate opinions. In the end, the US decision is actually flexible in the sense of saying, "We monitor the degree to which the systems fall within or without this category." We can even monitor overall the effect that decision from Congress has on the entire market. Congress can step in and make a change. You can even have a situation— an executive order, for example—if there was a major problem. So it's not fixed for all time, but it is a highly, highly, highly flexible approach.

You don't get much more flexible than that, which allows massive experimentation and flexibility within that space in the US. You can say that's wrong—you shouldn't have a flexible space around things that are about supporting decisions of healthcare professionals. To be clear, healthcare professionals are always in the loop by definition. They're not direct-to-patient tools; they're with a qualified healthcare professional taking this information in and being in a situation where they can survey it and make decisions on it. That is actually saying, "Well, let's be highly flexible and observe how that works." Assuming that the FDA surveys this properly, if we were starting to see signs of a very major problem, I'm actually confident in the US system that they could step in and stop that.

But it's a question of looking. You can't, of course, do it without looking. Now you could say, "Well, the manufacturers aren't tasked with looking because they're not a medical device." They can do that if they choose to, but other organizations are tasked with looking, including healthcare professionals. A lot of my current work is on actually suggesting approaches that can be used. Even if you're not under formal post-market surveillance, if you take the other approach, which is the European approach, there is almost no room for experimentation and for developing out of that sector.

You could always take a conservative and safety-first argument: "We shouldn't be taking any chance with even a single patient. We should always make absolutely sure we've tested everything, we've risk-assessed it, we've got the clinical data." Then we make a cold and calculated decision based on the evidence, and we decide what can move forward. And then the manufacturer can submit a revision, and we make a cold, calculated, and time-taking decision over the next change. But none of the interactions of what I describe as a kind of living laboratory of the country can actually happen. If one looked upon it from an industry perspective, let's say we have Europe wanting to build out an industry of clinical decision support systems, and we have the US wanting to build—and actually Canada as well, in this case, because they pretty much adopt the US system and deliberately write into their guidelines that they're effectively adopting the US CDS guidelines— you compare those two ecosystems.

You have—I describe as a hundredfold difference, but it could be a thousandfold difference—you have the ability to create new things in one, whereas you are tied down and very limited on your cooperation to create new things in the other. Now, it's not to say that one is moving and the other's not. Both are moving; one is moving very, very, very slowly, and the other is moving a thousandfold faster. Super interesting, and I like how you frame this initially. What it all falls down to is kind of the benefit and risk.

I just wanted to call out again that's really interesting— that the way that the conversation goes sets certain people up to skew towards being very risk-averse, like "I don't want something coming back to my desk." True. And it does shift responsibility. But who does it shift the responsibility to?

In the end, it shifts the responsibility to the physician. You're a physician; I'm a veterinary physician. I've done lots of clinical work, but in a different nature. I don't compare the two natures; it's relevant to my work and my thinking, but it's not the same nature. How comfortable you are with being in a situation where you have to, in your work, ensure that you're not succumbing to automation bias. There's a whole complicated science and paradoxes of explainability in that, but also making choices based on information which is provided from AI systems. Support systems aren't solely AI systems, but in reality, increasingly these are AI systems. Earlier you talked about the convergence of regulation around drugs and medical devices. I almost feel there's this third gravity center coming in, which is medico-legal and the regulation of clinician decision-making, which is all kind of being welded into this equation as well.

So I think that's super interesting. You promised us your stance as well, and maybe you could put it in the context of, "Hey, I'm a health system decision-maker in a low-income setting. I'm looking at what's going on. I see these different natures of risk averseness and these different flavors. How might you advise them to approach it?" I think there's very much that's right with the current US approach, particularly if we take the FDA line on the US and the interpretation of the 21st Century Cures Act. But I do think that there should be more formal processes of monitoring the market from the regulator's side. What the regulator actually has to do should be set out—what they will do in terms of their side of checking the market. And I think it should also be more formally set out what the healthcare systems have to do to monitor within their own domain of the market. And also it should be compulsory to build into tools approaches for feedback.

I'm doing a huge amount of work on this, and it's very controversial, but it's not the same as post-market surveillance. Post-market surveillance means the manufacturer is given or has the responsibility from a regulatory setting to gather data. This is a bit different: I'm saying there should be approaches built into tools which allow feedback from clinicians—not only to the manufacturer, but also to the system, to the healthcare system, to the regulators. And I actually don't think that's challenging. I think it's such a statement of the obvious that I'm slightly surprised that when I tell people about it or submit papers on it, people are somewhat surprised by the suggestion.

It's just a statement of the obvious. So you're saying that clinicians—clinician end-users, patient end-users—should be very, very, very easily able to feed back any type of feedback to health system bodies and regulatory bodies. I mean, we have that in drugs, right, in the yellow card reporting? We're likely going to fill a full hour of the podcast on this one starting theme, and I'm very happy to do so. And also that for drugs—for non-digital drugs—it's actually quite hard. Maybe I'm asking a revealing question about how many times you filled out a yellow card? I think I got a card out to fill out and then I was distracted with my clinical work. And that's only one type of feedback, right? That's an incident or something bad, like an adverse effect. Whereas you're talking about the full spectrum, the real spectrum. With drugs— if we're not talking about the next generation of digitally supported drugs and we're just talking about traditional drugs— you have to tear out the page, find time to fill it out, find an envelope, find a stamp, write the letter, remember not to let it fall out of your pocket, and actually put it in the post box.

How often is it done? It's not done. You can't do anything about drugs. So people have created online portals which allow doctors to report information on the yellow card online, but they're not very used. You don't even know what the portal address is.

The advantage of digital technologies is it's there by default. We both worked in the area of consumer-based tools in the area of symptom checking, etc. There you have—whether the manufacturer likes it or not, whether the developer likes it or not—on the app stores, you can provide feedback as a user and you can provide a star rating. I'm actually all I'm suggesting is a star rating and a feedback rating fit for the mid-21st century for the digital technologies we're building out. That is in the public domain.

Is that so shocking? Would you get nonsense? Of course you'd get a degree of nonsense. Are there ways of filtering out nonsense? Yes, there are.

You've worked on this; you've worked on evaluating the effectiveness of Ada within a low-resource setting in Tanzania and South Africa. Can you just broadly outline where the biggest challenges are when we're thinking about evaluation and getting a return on investment? Okay. I'll maybe answer the question from a slightly different perspective than you asked it. Your question is about the biggest challenges where we're falling down.

I'll give an angle— Steven's angle—on challenges we should address. There's something which I've recently become interested in. It comes from the work of actually some other researchers in the US academic and law side of regulation, and some of the groups which are in collaboration with the FDA University Centers for Regulatory Science. It's not a completely new concept, but it is to explore with AI and with digital health the extent to which we're talking more about systems and interaction—holistically interacting units— rather than discrete devices. And just to explore what I mean by this a little bit and see where it goes to and what the implications are for regulation and for health technology assessment.

I've been interested in this for three or four years, but particularly I started working on a Horizon grant which is in the area of health technology assessment quite recently. I have a module which looks at: "What if the thing we're trying to measure is not like a drug?" Health technology assessment of medical devices has really dealt with them as if they're drugs. They're discrete things for treating a certain defined target population, which can be quite broad, usually for a very defined indication. They can quite easily be measured: "Did they work or did they not work? Were they better than alternatives?

Were they not better? Given the degree to which they're better than alternatives, was it worth the additional money with respect to those alternatives?" What if digital health technologies are not like drugs? That's the starting point for this conversation.
