It started with a really good new PhD student that I've had for about nine months, really exploring this space and looking into the extent to which digital medical devices are like drugs and the extent to which they're not. And if they're really not like drugs, we have to accept that they're really not like drugs in everything we do with them.

If we treat them like drugs when they're not, we make them like drugs. I'll get back into more detail on that. We started working on a series of papers on this. There are actually three in the series now, but there's more. Two of them are about to be published.

The first of these papers will be published on the 18th of June next week— We'll link that in, yeah. It may already be published when this goes live, so people can look it up. It's in Nature Portfolio journals, Digital Medicine, and it's about suites or groupings of digital devices. At the very same time as we were working on this paper, the FDA commissioner made a statement at a conference in Las Vegas to the tech world, actually describing suites of devices. To paraphrase him—and it's hard to paraphrase him—he basically says: "If we acknowledge that increasingly digital health tools include ranges of sensors and different devices which are grouped flexibly together, we need to develop regulatory approaches that acknowledge the fact that they are flexible groupings of devices." That's what the title of our paper is about.

It's a series of two: one looking more at the problem and one looking more at potential solutions, although we don't pretend to have solved all problems; it's more of a starting point. The FDA commissioner, Califf, just in terms of his background: the FDA commissioner is actually a political appointment to some extent, but he had served as FDA commissioner once before for a number of years, and then he left the role and he actually went and worked for Google Alphabet for five years within their health and suites of different sensor devices, interaction probably with Fitbit, Verily, and Google Health aspects. And then he left that role and he returned to the FDA for a second role as FDA commissioner. It kind of explains part of his thinking. You could say that's a very bad thing—he's been influenced by Google and now he's thinking like Google.

It depends on one's perspective. I would say that's probably quite a good thing, where you bring somebody back from one of the world's leading companies and you have them in a position where they're actually responsible for regulation. I'm more concerned about the other direction of the revolving door than the revolving door back to regulation. I just wanted to clarify what you're saying then. I'm going to frame this from a developer perspective.

I'm a founder or I'm working in a software development company. My intended use is on a small part of a patient journey or a clinical workflow, but within a suite of products, there are others as well within this suite and we're all contributing to enabling this journey and this workflow. Am I on point here so far? You are, and there's nothing within current regulatory regimes which would stop you doing this, but they would make it very, very hard for you to do. That's Robert Califf's point.

Under FDA regulations and under European regulations, there's such a thing as systems of medical devices. You could define an entire system, but you would be required under current regulations to really tie the system down, to be in control of many aspects of that system, and to have systems for the monitoring of that entire system and clinical data on that system. I see. There's a recent guidance from the Medical Device Coordination Group for the European level on how that will work. Let's say the parts of the system that you're interacting with are sensors within an Apple Watch or sensors within a worn activity sensor.

There are ways you can do it, but they're extremely restrictive. And so that would be the conservative side of regulation saying "We have it already." I'm kind of glad the FDA commissioner is asking the question: "Do we really have it already and already have it right such that it's functioning for the future world that we're seeing?" If we get back to the suites in terms of how the paper presents it, we set out in the paper a description of what groupings of devices look like. I'll take one that illustrates the point quite well: sets of devices for monitoring in the home. You can have sets of devices for monitoring in the home for the situation of chronic disease monitoring. Let's take as an example the patient with type 2 diabetes.

They could have a series of devices including continuous glucose measuring devices, automatic devices for medication delivery, or even things like pillboxes. They can include tele-monitoring approaches, digital scales, etc. But they're focused around care provision in a chronic care setting. And then if we take another set of devices—sometimes those are really not linked together though they should be, and sometimes they're linked together in kind of a care package which is put together as a system. Another example, which is a recently very well-known system, is the hospital-at-home, sometimes described as a virtual ward.

This is very well-known within the UK, US, Switzerland, and Australia. Let's say a patient with respiratory disease—it could be COVID, but it could also be some other form of acute exacerbation of a respiratory condition. The COVID example is quite fresh in people's minds and is quite useful, but it doesn't solely apply there. You have a situation where the patient is an inpatient in hospital; they've been under monitoring, but they are released early to home in a virtual ward in a situation where, without digital support, they would still be in the hospital. So it's an alternative for ongoing relatively acute care.

It's not intensive care, but it's relatively high-level care. Because that is delivered by a series of digital interacting technologies, which include telemedicine platforms, approaches for tele-consultation, remote monitoring technologies—technologies measuring breathing, oxygen saturation, etc.—and can include things like pillboxes monitoring the delivery of treatment. And it can include actual visits from doctors; there's a human in the loop. Those are two sets of different technologies. They actually have a different target population and an absolutely different clinical indication, and they are in different levels of risk.

But they have overlapping sets of individual technology in them. They're kind of a "super-suite." They're a suite made up of a super-intended purpose; each of those devices has a sub-intended purpose and they're being grouped together. Now, within current technologies—for example, British Telecom has a partnership with the NHS and various startups to deliver a hospital-at-home— those are pretty much a medical device system, not necessarily regulated exactly within that framework and certainly not during COVID. But they are pre-defined and they've got relatively narrow sets of devices. We're increasingly entering a world where that model just does not make sense.

Are you going to have a series of different watches, a series of different sensors that you wear? You're already under the diabetes program, you're already in chronic monitoring, you've got perfectly good sensors on your arm. Do you throw out one watch and put on another sensor watch, or do you increasingly build sets of technology around frameworks that use and re-use appropriate devices within those frameworks? One can always say, "Well, that's possible under current regulation." Actually, that's another way of saying it's not possible under current regulation. If we give you a series of requirements under regulation you could never meet, then it's not possible.

That goes back to this argument about the role of the regulator. The role of the regulator is not to say, "Well, yeah, you can do that, but you can't secretly." You have such a hard job doing it, it would never get there. It is actually to find means of facilitating that. I'm maybe going to roll on to another paper that I have under review at the moment. I mentioned the FDA moving relatively fast in this space and taking the responsibility to the space very seriously.

Something that's very impressive—how it will work is a different question—is the FDA, about two months after Robert Califf's statement, launched a Health at Home initiative on a hub where they actually set out to investigate exactly this scenario. It's the use of devices in the home, around the home, and actually exploring the home environment. It's interesting because it's on the FDA website. If you look at the document, it mentions the word "equity" nine times. In the title, "equity" is there, and right through the document "equity" is there.

That's slightly unusual from the FDA and from a regulator. You kind of say, "What's the regulator got to do with equity? The regulator should be ensuring safety; let other people concern themselves with equity." But it's actually a very bold vision. What they're saying is acknowledging we have a societal responsibility. Healthcare provision at the moment may not be perfect; it is not perfect.

It's clearly not equitable; there are very large problems— problems of affordability. Acknowledging that digital technologies have a huge ask of them. But also, in parts of their launch document, they acknowledge that they're failing to deliver these responsibilities to an extent and that this failing is of systemic-level planning. It's actually kind of saying, "We're going to come in as a regulator and try and get the system to function." Because current regulations don't promote that. The current line of individual device regulations doesn't actually get these things to work well together.

They actually are more likely to get individual islands, and the individual islands are actually restrictive to a future which would involve more holistic and rational healthcare. We started talking about evaluating effectiveness, right? We started talking about: How do you see that this has created a benefit? What I've taken away from what you've said is that the way we think about evaluation is in these islands. I've got a very narrow intended benefit area because that's in my sphere of control as a developer.

I'm therefore thinking about this metric and this specific outcome and how I might contribute to it. And then we extrapolate some other kind of benefits around that. And then you make a case for, on the benefit-risk ratio you talked about, the benefits I've created. They're usually quite small because you have to focus on your locus of control. What you're saying is actually we need to think about these tools in the context of the bigger system and how they interact, not as islands but as the bigger piece.

And then how is the whole piece contributing to the bigger outcomes that are...? Exactly. That's true. Within the regulatory system, your notified body wants you to have an ultra-simple device, and regulation goes partly towards asking for that. But the notified body is much more comfortable the simpler the picture they're given.

They're really quite awkward if you don't give them the simple picture. Within the DiGA framework— at least the pre-update DiGA framework— just to check, if people are not familiar, DiGA is the reimbursement framework or the health technology assessment framework in Germany for apps in medical care. There's a separate program for those in elderly care. But this is in the medical setting and it was specifically designed— and you can come across as being a bit over-critical—it was way ahead of its time in many ways of having a fast track which would allow apps to get reimbursed before there was very, very hard evidence. But what it did in order to get to that point was to actually start from the metric, to start from the simplicity in the metric.

Effectively, they said, "You must be simple and you must be measurable," and that's the only thing they'll accept. So really narrowly defined target population, really narrowly defined ICD-1894 codes that you address, setting out a framework of how you're going to demonstrate a positive care advantage within those narrow terms. Now, that's fine as a program as long as you accept the consequences of it. And I'm speaking entirely with hindsight; it's unfair— the 20/20 vision of hindsight. What you get is what you allow to be created.

What you get is what you regulated for; you kind of deserve what you get. Speaking with hindsight: What did Germany get with DiGA? You get a series of solutions. It was also a requirement that there was this idea in the first version of DiGA—there are updates to the system— that you had to have systems which actually had relatively minimal physicians in the loop. What you get with this—it's not to say that none of the solutions have value—but they are narrow, they're not well-integrated, and they are not holistic.

You kind of look at DiGAs and say, "You're entirely wrong because, look, here's an example of 57 different products and they're all nothing like the things you're talking about, Stephen." The reason they're nothing like the things I'm talking about is because they're artificially walled off and separate. They have to be that or else they couldn't get funded. The French have the advantage of developing their system after having looked at the German system. It's not massively different, but there are two important points that I would pull out of the PECAN system in France which give me hope that we don't purely develop solutions in an island and we think more about how they interact within the healthcare system. One is an acknowledgment of codesign within healthcare systems, and the other is an acknowledgment of embeddedness within systems—that you're embedded within care.

That's a greater acknowledgment of interaction with a physician in the loop, and a greater acknowledgment that it's not your system as an island; it's integrated. Within the German system, it's being revised; there's a new law which revises it and there are stepwise movements in that direction. Now, I can understand the point of view that it must be measurable, we must start from the metric. To some extent, I'm giving a radically different vision: what you actually want is not necessarily something which is easily measurable; you want something which is really given the size of the problem. Which is—I go back to the OECD description of what the ambition is for healthcare system delivery—it's actually to acknowledge that that's not a one-step process.

And to even acknowledge you're not going to do it from 50 or 500 different DiGAs, all operating in isolation to address one part of the healthcare system without the physician in the loop. To me, that just from first principles would not get you very far. Highly controversially, I'm also somewhat skeptical about the value of a digital therapeutic on its own. The purely digital approach to treatment that doesn't involve a drug, doesn't involve a sensor in most cases, and doesn't involve a physician in the loop. I think there are examples of where that will provide utility, but I can say hand on my heart that most of what we will get in utility in clinical systems will not come from purely an isolated digital therapeutic.

It will be much more from the combination of that with physiotherapy, with a physician—it can be to an extent an AI-assisted physiotherapist— and the combination with drugs. But these things aren't an island. As a physician, if you were dealing with a sports medicine case—I know you're not an expert in sports medicine—would you ever really approach it like that? Say, "Well, this patient needs an entirely digital solution; we're going to do none of the psychological aspects of this conversation with them, and we're absolutely not going to use any drugs." Why would you approach the patient that way? Surely you would say, "This is a patient and the patient is holistic." They have multimorbidity, other conditions, the situation they come from.

I have an array of treatment approaches in front of me and I'm going to have to get those to work together. And controversially or not, when you combine those approaches together, you don't actually have a randomized control trial to say if I took drug one and drug two, combined them with this suggestion of their diet and exercise, that that would all work together. So how can you do it without the randomized control trial to say that the combination works? Within digital systems and digital tooling working together, there may be a situation where we need to reimburse combinations and settings where we don't always have the evidence in advance and we don't have the specific evidence that that set and combination will provide a positive healthcare advantage together. It kind of reminds me—I'm jumping onto the next theme—the Christmas edition of the BMJ with the parachute example.

People jumping out with and without parachutes. There was no difference in the randomized control study because the plane hadn't left the ground. That's a nice example. The point is that within current medical practice, there is application of common sense quite a lot, and there's not very good data recording and monitoring. One thing you have in digital technologies is a future where you can actually gather quite a lot of data.

In many cases where the risk is low, we should be looking at gathering more data, including feedback data, and we should be more flexible in the use of technologies together. There's some acknowledgment of that within the developing PECAN program. The question was: "Should resource be put into that?" The argument is always given: "We need to be really, really careful. If we start putting money into digital solutions, we're already completely bankrupt. Like in Germany, there are already hospitals going bankrupt.

If we start diverting resource into these new digital ideas which might not really work, then we're going to be even worse." My argument would be this is a completely wrong-headed thought process. Instead, you need higher-level strategic thinking about where you want to get to. What is the destination? Within the UK, I actually see much more of this than in other countries. Interesting, though they don't have a fast track program.

You have a definition of where you want to get to. Can you give an example of what that statement looks like? "Where do we want to get to as...?" For example, looking at a current model of care provision, we set out—as a high-level policymaker or politician, with medical experts—to actually say: "How do we think we could deliver this service such that it's quality in the future? What would be the high-level OKRs or KPIs in terms of system delivery? How would we stepwise try and deliver this program of care?" And then you promote and pay for it, including through a reimbursement program or other ways you can do payment.

Investment is necessary to get the thing you want to get. There are different ways you can approach investment: You could invest in technologies that would be run by the healthcare system, so you don't have private operators. You probably would almost certainly have private operators building many of them. Or you could have an ecosystem where there are continued private operators within that space. You would set off saying, "What do we need to create?" and you would put money into your system to get there.

You would acknowledge that you need investment. You don't get something for nothing; you need to invest to get to that point. It makes sense to invest because the point you would get to has advantages in care delivery. Of course there are skeptics, but that doesn't really matter in terms of building out a policy for the future. You either say, "Well, there are skeptics, we're not doing it"—that's mostly what most countries are doing at the moment—or "There are skeptics, we accept their point of view, but in the end we've been elected as a government and this was set out as our manifesto vision and we are working with the transformation unit within our system to deliver to these goals." Those goals acknowledge that there are multiple interaction component parts, but they are not all completely independent.

Within that, you would have a reimbursement system, and that system would not be devoid of having metrics, but the metrics would be sensible to what the holistic system should be moving towards. As you develop that system, you wouldn't have a static goal. You would be horizon scanning for technologies, and you'd actually not even be only scanning for them, you would be "horizon building" for them. "Our next step needs to be looking to incorporate this technology. A new technology is coming along which we can incorporate, and we have a program for building that out." You're saying then that the way you evaluate effectiveness is not then making the developer prove a set of incremental gains, but connecting the dots between that tool being implemented into this connected system and showing that it's contributing to the overall metrics or outcomes that you're going for?

Is that what you're saying? It only has an isolated return of investment if it was an isolated and unique technology. I would make the argument that many of these things are not. That's part of this discussion of interaction of systems and of suites of technologies. The difficulty is if you try and make them that, you actually build this highly, highly inflexible system where you can't actually exchange components, where they aren't provided by many different providers.

There is a reason why I have an Android phone in my pocket that interacts with a pair of Apple headphones, and you probably have an Apple phone in your pocket and it interacts with some Samsung headphones. You could say that sounds highly inefficient. Why don't we have a single manufacturer? They would make all of the technology and that would be the optimum, most efficient world. Why don't we have that system within any of our technology fields?

The alternative of our current system—which is what is acknowledged in the FDA initiative and in Robert Califf's statement—is that you actually get quite restrictive, narrow individual use cases which are probably safe but highly non-flexible. That's one extreme, versus trying to imagine that you can pre-design absolutely everything. You kind of have to get this match between enabling aspects and advantages of market incentive to deliver solutions, and laying down high-level interoperability requirements. Current regulatory and reimbursement systems do not support that. That's the problem statement.

I'm very clear in the vision that they need to support that, because that's the only way you could actually get digital transformation in healthcare systems. So many caveats to those that think digital transformation of healthcare systems is a folly, that it will not happen. I'm speaking from the positivist, convinced side: the way that we can get it to work is to acknowledge complexity in systems. We cannot know everything in advance, but we can measure what we're introducing. We can find ways of measuring through feedback, analysis, and quality improvement approaches which don't look at individual technologies.

They're not run by an individual manufacturer whose sole job is to show their technology is functioning. They're run across the system to say, "What are we actually generating?" And it will require investment. It's quite high-level, it's policy-related, but I think it's stating things which can from first principles be shown to be the case. If we step back a little bit from the problem: Especially for those in policy or implementation, thinking about measuring effectiveness—particularly at a health system or government level, say in a low-resource setting—you're observing what's happening in the rest of the world. I hear: Number one, have a very, very clear idea of the transformation and outcomes you're trying to deliver over the long term, and then design the way you might be evaluating that to make sure they're all tracking to those outcomes.

And then create a system that allows for thinking about how a private vendor is interacting with the system as a whole. No device is an island, and the system is also not a passive entity in this. You're thinking about how the system overall is benefited toward that goal. Is that a good summary? It's a summary.

And I think it addresses this point that we've not really talked about low-resource settings; I've mostly talked about higher-resource settings. Low-resource settings bring many additional challenges, but sometimes they have the advantage where you could be starting to really completely look again at how you would deliver care without having such established systems built-in with resistance to change. You can start off and say, "How would we like our system to develop?" Digital technologies are not things on their own; they interact with other technologies and your entire care provision. Thinking of what should your healthcare system delivery look like—you may not be looking at all areas simultaneously. You may be taking certain areas where you say that is a focus of our digital care delivery interacting with our doctor care delivery.

My argument would be it doesn't make sense still to bring a single soul provider to deliver everything. You certainly want the architect of the healthcare system overall to be the country itself. Digital companies should deliver that alongside the doctor's care network. You need to set out acknowledging that investment is needed. The payback does not start from day one.

That's a really good message. There are things banded around about how "this thing didn't achieve three times ROI within a year." Really make sure you bake in the initial investment and ironing kinks out. I would argue that any effective intervention takes time. Caution "any" because it's 100%, but almost all effective interventions will initially cost more rather than less, because they will involve changing the nature of care. You're providing more care where you were previously providing less.

It will cost more money in terms of changing the nature of your interactions with humans and even buildings. They will initially cost more in almost all cases. I know that's not a common message from the digital health industry or the tech industry in general, but I would make the argument that most things will initially be more expensive before providing a dividend. Very good. Is there anything else that you want to make sure you've spoken about, either in terms of regulation or this system-wide thinking of evaluation?

Talking about the intersection between regulation, health technology assessment, and funding policy makes it sound extremely high-level—like it's OECD-type stuff. Normally mere mortals aren't allowed to talk about this because it can only be talked about by the very refined group. Who is he to be suggesting we could do things in a different way? Of course, some of it could be challenged. In every single aspect of what I've said, you could have somebody shouting at their screen saying, "This is nonsense." I would at least say that aspects of what I'm saying are part of current regulatory thinking.

Have a read of the papers and consider if there are any aspects of it which ring true to you. Acknowledging that we cannot have technology sets which are completely in islands. It's not purely interoperability in the sense of the role of SNOMED CT and FHIR. That is about communications. It's not about interactions to deliver an intended purpose for a medical device.

We're talking about the interoperability of achieving medical goals rather than interoperability of bytes. It's an implication of developing systems which would never actually be interoperable, even if they were theoretically using FHIR servers and HL7. They still wouldn't be interoperable because they wouldn't be allowed to be. One final question given the audience: You've worked in top-down policy, and you've also worked bottom-up with Ada, showing proof points on safety, quality, and performance. What's your advice to people developing digital health tools in LMICs?

How should they be approaching evidence and evaluation? It sounds quite glib and maybe slightly naive, but build proper feedback loops into your technology from the start anyway. Can you elaborate? You want a situation where you don't need to plan a clinical investigation for nine months and have it running for six months in order to get feedback on how your tool is performing on the market. Wherever possible, you should be within your own technologies building routes and partnerships where you're getting continuous feedback on the performance of your tools.

Every interaction—or a high proportion of representative interactions—should provide feedback. You said from clinicians sometimes, as well? It depends on the nature of the tool. Some tools like DiGAs don't have a physician in the loop, so feedback would come from patients. "What do patients know?" Well, there can be highly relevant feedback in certain scenarios.

You don't want to be in a situation where, because you may not get every relevant feedback point, you're not getting any. The very point of Patient-Reported Experience Measures—you could employ an external consultant to do usability evaluation, or you could be building approaches into your tools to actually get that feedback. Sometimes monitoring patient-reported outcomes—it may not be possible to fully separate outcomes not related to your device, but you should be looking at that data from the perspective: "Does it give any early signal of a problem with my device?" If you can have a consent-based partnership with patients and their healthcare provider—not building that as you need it, but on the assumption you will need it— build that into your solution as you roll out. And in your contracts with partnerships and health systems. Most companies are doing that to a small degree, but not systemically and not all the time.

Look at it the different way: you are always building that in. You'd be surprised how many digital tools do not have easy, functioning "always on" loops to feedback on their products. Feedback becomes particularly important with the interaction with different systems. You need to have a range—not purely looking at one scenario or one use case when you're actually being used in different use cases. All digital tools are changed, and sometimes they're not changed as much as they should be because there's no feedback to monitor the effects.

You should build that in as part of your planning for changes. I published a paper in the Mayo Clinic Proceedings Digital Health journal that discusses approaches toward things like AB testing within a framework where you're doing risk-assessed experiments. You're exploring different approaches to providing tools, but you have feedback to actually look at which was the better approach. That's a very responsible thing to do, provided you set a framework of risk assessment and a regulatory procedure for Change Control. If your notified body needs to be informed, so be it.

Correctly monitoring data—these things could be seen as not like a thing you'd be wanting to do with a regulatory device, but you need to do it. Using feedback to monitor how well you're doing. Not just the quantitative side, but digging into the qualitative aspects. Great questioning approaches which also have free-text feedback. Free-text feedback is time-consuming to interpret, but it can be very powerful.

Very good. Use feedback; build that in. A good message to developers. Stephen, we've covered so much. It's been useful to have your perspective in terms of regulation, how to approach evidence for effectiveness from a health system policy funder perspective, and how to prepare yourself as a developer to see these different spectrums around health systems and governments.

I think there are some really unique insights that you can take. Stephen, thank you so much for your time and insights. It's been a great discussion. Thank you; I've enjoyed it. Thank you.
episodes.pullQuote: I don't really see a separation between the modern view of what regulation is and the digital health space on the question of implementation.
episodes.title: What is the right approach for regulation and evaluation of digital health technologies?
episodes.description: A deep dive into digital health regulation with one of the field's leading experts - covering the DiGA fast track in Germany, PECAN in France, what's coming in the UK, stark differences between the FDA and EU approaches, and what health system leaders, policy makers, and developers should learn from all of it.

topics: Digital solutions for overcrowded healthcare facilities: how digital health can alleviate pressure on healthcare systems
The role of AI and language models in enhancing diagnostic and conversational capabilities
Building trust and reliability in large language models through rigorous data handling and prompt engineering
How strong local partnerships contribute to successful technology implementation
Regulatory backing as a necessity for the safety and efficacy of new technologies
episodes.bio: Dino is a recognized global health leader, published researcher, and ER physician with first-hand knowledge of how technology can both help and hinder clinical workflows. He has dedicated his career to the advancement of global health through research and innovation, holding leadership roles at organizations such as Centre for HIV and AIDS Prevention Studies (CHAPS) and The Aurum Institute. As CEO, Dino enthusiastically drives Audere's vision forward and implements its strategy. Born and raised South African, he is passionate about Audere's mission to find solutions to the challenges facing low- and middle-income countries.
episodes.guestRole: CEO Audere, CEO/Founder Audere Africa
episodes.transcript:
You are tuned in to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. My name is Shabs Upia, a physician working in digital health. I'm keen to learn more about the issues, challenges, and successes where digital health can have a real impact for underserved communities around the world. If you're a founder, investor, donor, researcher, or are developing and implementing digital health anywhere in the world and you're keen to break out of your bubble, join me as I speak to experts and innovators and get a truly global perspective on digital health. Dino, thank you so much for joining me.

You've been tagged by Digital Square as one of the real great examples of innovators creating impact for underserved communities. Can you tell us about your own journey and also what got you to working with Audere and what Audere does? Thanks very much for having me today; it's a great pleasure. My background is in emergency medicine and public health. I've worked as an implementer in the field, both in emergency departments and in government and public health facilities for the bulk of my career, and in both settings, I came across challenges that have stayed with me my whole career.

Some of those have included very busy, overcrowded hospitals and outpatient departments with patients coming and spending entire days waiting to get five minutes with the nurse or doctor. In other settings, I worked as the junior doctor in a facility where perhaps I had to deal with a polytrauma and didn't have the support of a specialist in very stressful circumstances. So, I think both these challenging problem areas have always guided me towards digital health solutions and thinking about the potential of digital health more broadly, and more recently AI, in solving some of the human resource stresses and needs and some of the patient access points. Three years ago, I got an opportunity to move to Audere, a company that focuses on these types of problems. It's a nonprofit co-headquartered out of Seattle and Johannesburg, and we build a suite of AI tools that really focus on solving some of the challenges I just flagged.

That sounds great. I've been looking and reading about your experience and work reaching underserved populations in particular. There are so many problems and needs, particularly in the context within which you are working as you've highlighted. How did you figure out that this was worth working on and impactful enough for you guys to solve? Yeah, sure, Shabs.

I think I'll mention two. The first relates to an important part of any healthcare journey: a diagnosis. A big part of diagnosing a patient is a test result. In the developed world, we've got extensive lab infrastructure and a lot of that happens through labs. In the developing world, less so, and a lot of focus is on what we call rapid diagnostic testing as initial diagnostic touch points.

A big chunk of what Audere focused on was this equity to care in this important part of our healthcare journey, which is the diagnostic step which guides a treatment outcome or a prevention outcome. I'll talk about a chunk of our work that's focused on making rapid diagnostic testing more accessible, easier to understand, and importantly, linking that result to a care outcome, which isn't always the case with the use of these tests. The second part relates to what I said earlier: a huge part of any healthcare journey is the initial conversation. Probably 80% of healthcare is a conversation. It's the history taking, it's the instructions around medication use once a diagnosis has been made, and it's the triage of a patient.

The more recent potential of large language models in general to supplement this conversation within a healthcare setting and produce both efficiencies and limit patient frustration is huge. We've delved into both these two key areas. We use computer vision AI and digital use instructions to bring rapid testing closer to patients and closer to communities. On the large language model front, we're building a number of innovative tools which harness and use different types of large and small language models for very specific use cases, often around conversation, information, and smoothing out a clinical workflow with additional access to advice. Yeah, absolutely.

I'd love to get into both of them, actually. I'd love to start with the first one. You mentioned the use case around using computer vision to facilitate the reliability of results and enabling people to do these tests in the comfort of their own home, right? Can you explain a little bit about before you guys arrived on the scene? What was the problem?

I think one of the earlier forms of self-testing related to HIV self-testing, which has been quite topical since about 2018, I think, when the first self-tests emerged. I think within the HIV space, there was a need to take testing, which was stigmatized, and put it into the household or give patients the agency to test when they felt comfortable and to disclose and understand their results at their own pace. Challenges related to self-testing included not knowing when a self-test was being used, not being sure if the patient acted on the outcome, whether patients were implementing the test correctly, and how these tests linked to either a prevention pathway for that patient or a treatment pathway, depending on the test results. If the test was negative, how could you tailor a prevention package which meant that they wouldn't need to be testing again anytime soon? Or if it was positive, how did you make sure they linked to care, which was a crucial step?

Just as one easy example, people that are at risk of acquiring HIV can take a tablet once a day called PrEP. This significantly lowers their risk of becoming HIV positive, even during high-risk encounters. Another example is PEP, which is post-exposure prophylaxis for unexpected high-risk encounters. To access those medications, a negative test is important because we want to be sure that you're negative and not positive before giving you a medication to which you could develop resistance. So, most programs require a negative test as an entry point to accessing PEP or PrEP.

That test is traditionally needed to be done with a healthcare worker to confirm it, and more recently we've used self-testing in a private location and a validated AI image as the entry point to be able to send that to a telehealth consult and receive PEP or PrEP medication remotely. The workflow would be: you acquire a self-test, you test in the comfort of your home, you capture the image and result, and that gets transferred to a telehealth service. The healthcare worker gets a high-quality picture which is enabled by AI; it gets an AI interpretation, and the human can look at the image themselves. They've got the AI-verified photo and the high-quality image, and they can make a call: "Yes, it's a negative test; let's dispense the PrEP." You can then collect your PrEP through a vending machine, an e-locker, a home delivery, or a community healthcare worker. So, that's one example of a workflow and access point that's been made more convenient where the AI plays a key verification role in that workflow.

If we think about the COVID pandemic, which I think a lot of us still have front of mind, self-testing in many countries with rapid tests was very prevalent. It wasn't in South Africa, and we should get back to that when we talk about regulation. The regulators took a very long time, and by the time they finally regulated the self-test product, the opportunity had passed. But that is a conversation for a different day. In countries where the regulators were more forward-thinking and you could self-test, a big question was: what were the results?

Were those results finding their way back to a system? By people taking a simple photo of that result, the AI could capture the image and automatically link that result back to public health reporting and surveillance, giving us real-time data of how the pandemic was progressing. Unfortunately, in most places that didn't exist, and we really had a bit of a blackout when it came to data coming from self-testing. Super interesting. You've touched on some really, really important points there.

I think a couple of the things that are really powerful about this, that I take away, are the thin end of the wedge of the opportunity that you saw. In terms of the problem that you wanted to address, it was "here's a group that's particularly vulnerable and we have an opportunity to improve access for them." You could have stopped there, right? But actually, you thought deeply about the propagation of benefits through the workflow and the system, and the benefits in terms of how we connect that to what treatment options they have and how we make sure that we're again targeting another value proposition for the system here, which is: we're targeting the use of medication that is at risk of resistance, so we need this reliable result. So again, there's a stacking up of benefits that's not just for the patient but for the system overall. There's an enabling of the community health worker being more confident in the decisions that they're making in the workflows that they have, so that they're targeted to the right counseling or the right benefits there.

And then I think I really like this third part that you said where you then connected it to the capturing of the data so at a population health level and a public health level, you're able to understand what's going on and decision-makers at that level are able to get insight. So for me, that's a really powerful example. You have a benefit to a patient, but you can clearly see the benefits to people who are delivering healthcare and the system overall. So, that's a really, really nice example. Just to mention, Shabs, it's not just about the self-care journey.

When it comes to rapid tests, a couple of quick other examples: when it's a provider test, we've taken rapid testing into communities through pharmacies, through private pharmacies as a new delivery channel. Global donors that want to see patients not having to go to a facility for their diagnostic journey can now access in a number of countries a local, small, informal pharmacy where providers had been providing some medications, but they can test for malaria or HIV. Those pharmacy providers are quality-controlled through the functionality of the computer vision, which also has a quality check embedded. There's an audit and verification of a unique test result. So, donors that are paying for the test and the medication can verify this person had a test linked to the medication, and suddenly we have a trusted channel in a private pharmacy—a trusted, verified channel which is a new diagnostic and treatment touchpoint for the patient which is opened up in communities that really need them.

Similarly with malaria and community healthcare workers, we can provide them with greater confidence in their testing abilities with digital instructions and a computer vision-verified test result. If there is an error or a problem with an interpretation, it flags it to the system to say this community health worker potentially needs some retraining or they've got deteriorating eyesight, and the whole system becomes more quality-controlled, safer, better for the patient, supportive supervision for the provider, and ultimately a healthier system in general. I would love to come back to your approach to this quality assurance and the ways you work with local partners, but just before I do that, you mentioned the more vulnerable communities—the communities that are underserved and hard to reach. Can you shed some light, maybe painting a picture, on who these people are in this context? Who were you reaching or trying to reach that you weren't able to reach before?

Sure. So, again coming back to my earlier example, you have a mom in a semi-peri-urban or even rural setting in Kenya or in West Africa, and they have a child with a fever. Fever management as a concept is quite important, but often one of the primary risks is malaria. That mom would like to get her kid tested quickly. Normally she would have to access a public health facility, she'd have to wait a very long time to get tested, she would have to then wait for the test result, and she'd then have to access a long pharmacy queue to access her medication.

That process would probably take her the whole day, and she would lose the income from the day; she'd have transport into the clinic, and there's lots of barriers to entry to that healthcare journey which, unfortunately, is still all too common. With the private pharmacy I just mentioned, she has a small informal pharmacy in her community. She's able to go there, probably without a queue, and get tested rapidly. That pharmacy is incentivized by global donors to still make it affordable, and that process suddenly becomes potentially a 40-minute process. She doesn't lose income, she's got her test result, and she's got her medication, all funded through an adjunct of the public health system using private infrastructure and delivering healthcare more effectively.

Talking about HIV, we have certain key population groups that are high priority in HIV programming. We want to make access to PrEP—that preventive medication—as easy and as simple as possible. Convenience is key to people's healthcare-seeking behaviors, and being able to conveniently test at home, even in an urban setting, link that test result to an outcome, and receive your medication without a difficult journey ensures that people stay on PrEP more reliably and stay on their medication more reliably. We could even talk about TB as another area where people have to be on meds for a long period of time, and that convenience means that those key programs, especially the treatment components, stay more consistent. Those impacts benefit the community as a whole.

So, these interventions aren't specific to very rural last-mile. Yes, they help, but they aren't specific to urban areas. They work across urban, peri-urban, and rural settings, servicing different community members for different reasons. Really, it becomes about ease, access, convenience, and cost-effectiveness, both in terms of personal time and other cost drivers. Very pertinent and a quite vivid example of the actual impact you can have on an individual's life, particularly around the convenience.

Maybe finally on this, I wondered if there is also a layer above convenience, or as an aside to convenience, particularly with some underserved communities or vulnerable communities, particularly with HIV. I'd love to get your take or perspective on what you've experienced. Are there particularly—I mean, I read one of the media articles that were associated with the HIV populations that you're trying to reach within South Africa, so transgender, queer, etc. Have you experienced that there was more uptake with this community because it was able to be accessed at home or closer to where they were? Yes.

So there's—not just with our intervention but with this notion of differentiated care—we're trying to tailor care journeys that are more appropriate to the individual's needs and convenience. There's various ways of doing this. I mentioned e-lockers earlier. For patients that are HIV positive and on treatment, being able to collect your medication from an Amazon-styled e-locker with a code that you get sent every month instead of waiting in a pharmacy queue has proved very successful. Similarly with PEP and PrEP, the ability to access those easily with a remote test result and an AI-verified image is also becoming more pertinent.

There's a growing body of research showing that convenience is key to health-seeking behavior and consistency. Super interesting. I really like that and the way you also understood what was happening on the ground to leverage local infrastructure and reach people through actually delivering the actual medication that they need through local physical infrastructure. Lovely. Let's get into the quality assurance side of things and maybe some of your experiences working with the local partners and community health workers.

You talked about the importance of making sure you had reliability and making sure that you trusted the AI and people trusted it. And when I say people, I mean you trusted the process as the developers, and the government, health system, or public health trusted that, and also the people using it trusted that. Can you talk about your approach to this and ensuring the AI that you were actually deploying for this use case was doing what it said on the tin? Yeah, sure. I think this is a great segue into our other work with large language models.

At the moment, we're tailoring certain large language models and small language models for targeted conversations. We're starting again with the HIV space, and a huge part of a conversation using AI is: will someone trust it? Will they trust this as a conversational tool? Will they trust the information it gives back to us? Can it engage them in a way that they are familiar with?

This all starts with the design process. We work with a lot of local partners to establish trust. It has to sound, feel like, and be consistent. There's different pillars to trust: you need to be able to explain something, you need to be able to reproduce it, you need to be able to have empathy, and you need to make sure there's no bias. These are key pillars of establishing trust.

In our design process related to how our AI leverages language model tools, we include users from the very beginning. It's not just about the users; it's also about how we build our datasets, which are built in-country and locally. How we augment those datasets—we can go into that—how we label products locally both for our computer vision and for our conversations. This localization project of the community needs the individuals we'll be talking to. Slang is a great example.

We've just built a massive slang dictionary for South Africa. I'm South African, and there's a lot of words I've never heard in there; that's how comprehensive it is. But the idea is —can you give some examples of healthcare ones that make sure— Sure. A common healthcare term for an STI in South Africa is called "the drop." If a patient comes in and says, "I've got the drop," it means urethral discharge, which is often linked to an STI. Another one—I didn't know this one but I saw it recently in the slang dictionary—"lamb chops." "Lamb chops" refers to a type of STI in South Africa.

So, there's various medical references that the LLM would have to understand that an off-the-shelf tool wouldn't normally have, like your ChatGPT-4 or whatever you're using, like Claude. When you have conversational things and the large language model is saying something like, "How's it, my chomy? You know, how was your day?" there's a couple of pieces of slang in there that may also confuse the large language model. We've seen some of them, which are trained in different languages, switch languages automatically even though it's not a language switch; it's English, but some of the slang comes from different language groups in South Africa. So, that confuses the language model into thinking, "Oh, I need to change to Afrikaans." We know it's an English speaker, but part of that language was an Afrikaans word, right?

Another language in South Africa. So, there's so much nuance in getting that context right, and it's so important when we come back to this trust factor that you spoke about. Yeah, let's get into that. I want to get into this one. You were talking about the work that you've done to make sure that there was reliability and quality assurance of the computer vision work and the way you work with local partners.

Just to complete the circle on the computer vision work and then let's get into the use case of the LLM work and the work you've done to make sure you label correctly, as you've alluded to. Sure. So, we learned a lot from computer vision which led us to our learnings about language models, which was quite interesting. With computer vision, we needed to be sure that we were able to read these test results using an image at a greater accuracy than an expert human. To do that, we use large image datasets that we generated initially in simulated lab sessions.

We augmented that with synthetic images, and we used local labelers to look at those images and give us guidance on what they showed. This was images of the RDT—the rapid diagnostic test. I guess different versions, like the control one line and the test line, etc., right? Sure. But the important part was we had to simulate local conditions where the tests were happening.

We couldn't just take thousands of tests; we had to simulate poor lighting conditions in facilities, blood splatter on the images, rainy scenarios, skew, and someone holding a cassette at different angles that the AI would need to read. Every adversarial condition that our local partners could teach us about, we trained the models on. And that's what made the models special: they were ready for adversarial conditions when they occurred. That's what gained trust in the users, saying, "Wow, I'm not being frustrated. It's a dark room and I'm still getting a result; there's blood splats across the screen, I'm still getting a result; there was a skewed photo, it doesn't have to be the exact distance for it to work, I can take a picture from here or up close and I'll still get an interpretation result." Those conditions, the trust in the user, and the convenience in not struggling with the tech was one of the success factors in that programming.

So you designed this in your approach and the process by which you did this. You proactively said, "Hey, we know through working with our local partners and actually knowing what's going on on the ground that we need to cover for this eventuality; this is a risk in terms of the quality of this and we're going to do this work to mitigate this risk." How did you think about that? How did you come up with these adversarial conditions? How did you know to think of that? The reason I ask that is to be able to extract and take away the learning: how would innovators who are trying to do something in their own modality or context approach this?

How do we think of all these eventualities? Yeah, so I think the complimentary skills within our team is a perfect blend. Half of our team has grown up and lived in LMIC conditions, and a lot of them have experience in facilities and in the field. Another part of our team is North American-based and are really deep AI experts and have a strong strong R&D component. When we combine these and when we pick and choose local partners to work with, you get this blend of knowing the right questions to ask and having the capabilities to solve them.

I think it's been part of our formula for success. From a personal point of view, I get very frustrated with tech and have my whole life. When you get excited about something, you pick it up, you start to use it, and it hits a small glitch and you aren't that tech-savvy to start with, and you're like, "Ah, this is frustrating; this is why tech doesn't work," and you put it down, right? I think a lot of people have had bad experiences with tech workflows. If my technology is not reading enough of those cassettes and it's not smooth for a user to work, that healthcare worker will put it down after one bad experience and be like, "Let me just go back to the status quo." Similarly with language models—if you've dealt with one recently—I was trying to deal with an airline language model giving me advice, and it looped back and forth and it wasn't particularly helpful, and I was like, "You know, this language model—I can't book through it." So, I think the trust the user has to have, the convenience of using it, and the smoothness when adversarial conditions pop up and the variations it has to account for make the tech experience pleasant and consistent and build that user trust.

Absolutely. Great examples. Let's get into these LLM use cases that you're working with. Yeah, so just as a disclaimer—as I mentioned, my background is in healthcare. I'm not the tech expert on our team; I'm, let's say, tech-adjacent.

So, some of the concepts I'll describe are from a high-level viewpoint and my understanding of them. But my tech team's done a good job of upskilling me and understanding some of these concepts and how they relate to our work. I think the two big parts of trust related to a large language model—and it's both donors trusting investments in it and people using it—the models have to get the "how" of what they respond to correct. So the accuracy—you could think about this as clinical accuracy, right? If I'm a healthcare worker and I'm using this tool to help guide my workflow, and I need to check in with it on a piece of advice because I remember part of the textbook but there was a step I forgot—"what should the dose be?"—I need to have trust that it's going to get the "what" right when I ask it a clinical question.

The second part of it that is a bit harder, and that our team works very deeply on, is the "how," or the viability and how messages are communicated. The "what" has to be right in terms of accuracy, and the "how" things are communicated in terms of context needs to be accurate. That comes back to the example we spoke about in terms of slang and language. If I'm building a tool for a South African end-user to extract information, and it can't both understand and communicate back in slang in a way that person is familiar with, it might have a lower level of trust. I need the human to trust the language model because, through my prompt engineering, I'm trying to guide the human towards, as an example, a better understanding of their own personal risk.

It could be related to HIV; it could be related to a non-communicable disease. But once they're trusting the tool, I can prompt engineer certain nudges that they trust, which is guiding them towards internalization of their health risk. Once we understand our health risk, we're more likely to reach out and seek advice, change behavior, or seek assistance. So, I think the crux of the engineering work is understanding that language models are tools; they aren't end products. We have to understand what these tools can do and what they do well, and where they have limitations and supplement them through smart, innovative engineering efforts to have productized, reliable products in the field that can gain and maintain user trust.

That makes a lot of sense. As part of the trust, you needed to build a local slang dictionary. So, were you using that to augment the model that was already being used, and then being able to give it the ability to access that source of information to then draw from in the interaction? Correct. So, both when it comes to the clinical accuracy and the "what" of something, we look at grounding this in datasets that are specific to the use case, using RAG as a methodology to fine-tune.

And with the "how" part and the local context, we again build specific datasets for the use context. We augment those additional datasets all the time. With AI, everything is about the data: the quality of data. Those datasets make that end product or tool turn that tool into an end product that's so much more refined and so much more accurate. I think when we come to challenges later, when we speak to donors out there and investors, this is one of the parts I battle with: you can build a so-called chatbot for $30,000, or even just at home by giving something a persona and doing some prompt engineering, or you can put $100 million into it.

The difference in that span is significant, and I'm not sure we have enough people that are understanding the differences in terms of what the outputs at the end will be and how things will function. The nuance in getting these tools into high-quality products comes within that spectrum of investment. So often we'll produce something and we'll get compared to something else: "Well, this chatbot cost $100,000; why did you need X amount?" We're trying to get people to understand some of these nuances and why building those datasets is important, the clinical grounding and other guidelines, and how you can use and pull in different language models in one funnel or workflow and use different ones for their strengths and weaknesses within a conversation to make that chatbot even better. Then, of course, in the work we do, we pull in computer vision as part of our workflow and we pull in—we don't do the predictive analytics ourselves, but we have key partners we pull in. So, within an experience, you've got the conversation, you've got the eyes.

We're looking at pulling in acoustics where you can listen to a cough, for example, through the speaker with partners that specialize in that. You've got the eyes, the ears, and then you've got the brain, which is analyzing that whole workflow and feeding back nudges that are specific and tailored to that user. I think that's the dream. That sounds so pertinent and so important. You mentioned this thing around nuance.

Just for the broad audience, you mentioned RAG, so this is Retrieval Augmented Generation, right? Essentially, what this does—and you might be able to describe it better than me—is instead of drawing from all of the information on the internet, it's being instructed to draw from specific sources of information that you might have previously vetted or pre-thought of as a reliable source of information. So, I think the idea, at least, is that you reduce the chances of contextual noise and things that are inappropriate for that context or hallucinations, etc. Would that be a good description? That's 100% spot on.

I think large language models that we work with do very well generally, but when you need them to get to 99% accuracy on a specific ask, you want to guide them to specific datasets first, and that's what you've spoken about. To me, there's a broader thing that plays out—we've touched on this in a previous episode with Professor Alex from Brazil—about the trade-off or the balance in thinking between if you invest, as you said, in making something super relevant for a specific context and a specific use case and a specific workflow, and then there's also a need from health systems and society in general to think about how these are generalizable to other contexts. So, do you have any experience or how do you think about making sure that, yes, absolutely, we need to be completely effective and perform well and be useful and create value for the specific context and use case that we're in, but then how do we take this technology and this LLM to be deployed in a different part of South Africa or a different part of Africa or Asia where the slang is different? What are your thoughts about this? That's a million-dollar question.

I think we're learning more about that all the time. I don't think it's an easy one to solve. I think there's components that are transferable, and you use those transferable components. But I think the quality of the fine-tuning and nuance of every specific context and use case—I'm not sure we can get away from that right now in terms of needing to do the hard yards on those. As part of our work with HIV, it's one of the areas we're exploring and trying to learn about for the global health community and translate those learnings into doing better.

But I think it's early days on that front. I wanted to complete another circle on what we mentioned: the rapid diagnostic test use case with the computer vision for HIV. You mentioned malaria as well. Do you have any numbers on the impact this has had? You talked about that type of individual story of, you know, the mother who instead of having a few hours to access care and get the result, it's now a 40-minute episode.

Do you have any bigger data or impact on a population level on the benefits that you're seeing from this implementation? Yeah. I think our big impact play is: we do have our own app platform that we use in certain research settings, but really what we've done is we've tried to build this toolkit of AI components and we've been really particular about how those would integrate. We have different integration options: API, SDK. And we go to front-end platforms that are already scaled in the field.

They could be community healthcare worker tools, they could be EMRs that are facility-facing, and we say to them, "Not everyone needs to go away and figure this out." Especially in the global health community, we're well-funded; we are trying to figure out the hard AI problems for your platforms, and we want to provide these for you at the lowest possible cost as a nonprofit to be able to scale them. So, you don't need to figure out your own language model journey; we're going to figure it out for you. We're going to give you those capabilities and we're going to scale through your platform in Ethiopia, Nigeria, Rwanda—wherever the scaled platform is—and that way augment the impact and amplify it. Same with our computer vision models. The Gates Foundation and other donors have funded our computer vision models, and recently a foundation model which can read almost every rapid diagnostic test cassette that's rectangular with a very high percentage.

We're not having to create new algorithms all the time. The idea is we want to maintain that dataset as an AI function and a global good, and give it to anyone who needs it to integrate it. So, we're not all recreating the same wheel over and over; we're offering a service function for LMICs and global good that can access computer vision, the large language models, the best-in-breed of predictive analytics, and the best-in-breed of acoustic AI, and say that the CHW app that used to basically be an EMR is now a multifunctional AI partner to the community healthcare worker. The scale is unlimited when you think about it that way. In terms of impact, are you able to share some outcomes that that's reached?

For example, how many people were you able to reach with this? Has it improved adherence to therapy? Has it reduced the amount of new infections, etc.? Any data around that? Yeah, for sure.

I think our biggest program has been in Kenya, where we've worked with a very large online pharmacy to access PEP and PrEP. We're presenting a bunch of this data at the IAS HIV conference this year, but we've reached thousands of people with this technology already. We've definitely seen improved PrEP cycles with more convenient PrEP access. We've seen people accessing PEP much more frequently and with far more ease. I think we've also seen, for the pharmacy provider itself, cost savings and economies that are provided with this remote model.

So, the early indicators are all really good. In South Africa, we ran a project with the Aurum Institute and KEOPS groups. That project's funding ended a little sooner than we would have liked, but we're looking at how to recreate it. Initial signs were really positive, and we have one rolling out in Eswatini soon with USAID and a local implementing partner where people can self-test and collect their meds through lockers. So, we're excited to see what the data from that specific access model looks like.

Awesome. Great to hear. I think this is also a good segue into the final bit before we go into your recommendations. You mentioned a couple of things: cost savings, etc. In high-income settings, you might have data on baseline costings of the standard of care, and you use those as assumptions for economic modeling to say, "Hey, we could have this impact," and then you can observe that.

In particular, the reason to do that is you need to prove the return on investment, particularly thinking about the cost savings that you're making. What's your experience on this? What have been your challenges to prove the ROI of the work you've been doing? I think this is the single biggest area where we face challenges for a variety of reasons. We have published and have a lot of research showing the quality of the AI, the accuracy of the AI, and user uptake feasibility.

But when it comes to cost-effectiveness studies and modeling data, we haven't been well-funded to do that yet. As you mentioned, there's certain key components within the system that are often missing, which makes modeling even difficult. I'll give you a very tangible example. With our computer vision models, when we think of how to supply these into the marketplace, there's an operating cost to running the computer vision service. There was a cost to develop the algorithms initially—the R&D—but we also want to make sure it's cost-effective.

When governments ask us, "Well, what is the operating cost of this model?" we need to give a figure that is cost-effective to the government. At the same time, we need to give a figure that eventually, at scale, is cost-recovery focused for sustainability reasons. Even as a nonprofit, you have expenses you need to cover, right? That balance—and then, what is scale? Do you start off—if you charge too much at the beginning, uptake will be slow.

If you charge too little, it takes you too long to get to scale. What does sustainability look like, and does your runway shorten? It's been a really difficult one when we superimpose organizational sustainability, the cost of a service like computer vision, the initial uptake as the use case takes hold, and needing to balance that value to the ecosystem. I'll give you one other good example related to this. We've been asked to build a tool related to supporting training.

There's a huge training cost in retraining healthcare workers every time a new test is introduced. With computer vision and a digital tool, you can run virtual training, virtual modules, and you can supervise the first 100 tests of a new test. Think about this even for climate change and pandemic preparedness: a new threat hits, you've got a rapid test, but you need all your healthcare workers to know how to use it. How many drops? How long do you wait?

Are you interpreting it correctly? You need to do that fast. You can't fly 10,1330 healthcare workers in a rapid period of time to one spot. It costs a lot of money and it takes a lot of time. Could you have a virtual model with AI—it could be computer vision or LLM—that supplements that?

The answer is yes, we can do it. The question is: is it cost-effective? So, what is the baseline cost of their training data? What is the cost of the technology? How do you compare them, and how do you make that case to governments?

It is very hard to do and very hard to get the data components to do it accurately. So, I don't have a good answer for you. I think a lot of tech companies are trying to figure that out. I think especially if you're a nonprofit, you're trying to stay true to that core mission and look at what cost recovery really means and offer this for free or as cheap as possible. But you also need to stay sustainable: maintain the AI models, make sure they're tuned, check that they're working.

There's operating tech costs that go along with running the service, as I mentioned, that need to be covered. You've covered so much there that resonates. From my perspective, when we think about ROI, we're focusing on the financial benefits. Then we look at the other types of value, I.e., clinical outcomes, patient experience, clinician experience, and sometimes we're trying very hard to model those with assumptions. At least from my perspective, I think there's room for valuing those things as well.

So, we're thinking about cost-effectiveness, but we're also seeing the other value and the other benefits that you're delivering, right? The million-dollar question is: how do we get governments, in both high-income and low-middle-income country settings, to recognize this inherent value and say, "Yes, and we still think—you might be cost-neutral, the cost-effectiveness still plays a part, but we're raising the profile of these other value points for patients, access, etc., which might not necessarily make something cheaper in the long-term run, but there is a benefit"? I see that's when philanthropic groups come in and they say, "We'll fund evidence generation and learning," and we need to gather that data in a very specific way, in a reliable way, that we can package and then present to governments and to other stakeholders to convince them of the value-add—let's call it health impact, right? I spoke about financial sustainability, but the ROI in terms of health impact could be an HIV infection averted. What is that worth to your system?

What does that extrapolate to in terms of five years' time? That's where we have really good modeling companies, but they still need support; they still need data. We still need the M&E frameworks as well as the research protocols that go with them to prove out some of those areas. Super valuable to get your take on that. Thank you.

Dino, I want to get into—we're coming towards the end and wrapping up. What are your top few recommendations to founders or people in this space who want to create impact for underserved populations in their context around the world and help those who need innovation the most? I always find it tough to do recommendations because I always feel like I'm learning all the time and changing my view and perspectives. I think when it comes to my experiences with tech and healthcare, founders and companies can be targeted in two key areas. I think, one, there's a need for specialization and a niche focus on a specific problem and specific use case, and we've chatted a little bit about that.

I think, two, there's also a space for a group in the middle, almost a function that helps to bring together the manufacturers or producers of tech, like AI, and the platforms that are using the tech. You need some service provision and some thinking in the middle which makes that transition easier. So, when you're thinking about your tech offering, for me it could fit in one of those three spaces: the front-end or direct-to-consumer, that middle component, and then the AI tool production. You need to balance that out. In healthcare, digital cycles take a long time; sales cycles are tough.

You need time. When you think about your runway, always anticipate needing an extra 50% of what you thought at the start. It's hard to convince people in health tech because the stakes are high. People's healthcare is important, and the stakes are a lot higher. In other forms of consumer tech, you can be more nimble, you can be quicker; but when it comes to healthcare, timelines are longer.

Keep that in mind—it's the one thing that I think my tech team, a lot of whom came from consumer tech, has been frustrated with. Having been in healthcare my whole life, I know how many RCTs you need before you can introduce a new healthcare product or tool. The same is applying to tech. It's going to be very interesting to see how the AI journey plays out. What is—I think Bilal touched on this—what is a medical device?

What is an information tool? Are there new regulatory standards that we need to consider? What is the spectrum of nuance in terms of where an activity and function starts and ends, and how do we have appropriate barriers that ensure safety and security, but not barriers to entry that are so high that innovation is stifled? My last recommendation is more for global stakeholders: donors, regulators. This is controversial: I feel like there's so much noise in the tech space.

It's very hard, if I'm a government decision-maker, to figure out what EMR I should use when there's a thousand pitching to me every week. What chatbot works when I don't understand the nuance of tech? How does this integrate with my system? At one of the conferences, I spoke about whether the global health community, donors, and stakeholders should be helping to pick a smaller group of winners when it comes to tech offerings and simplify decision-making for people who have to pick products which are hard to choose. It's hard to understand, especially with AI, what works and what doesn't, and how it's verified.

So, on one hand, innovation's great and having a lot of options to choose from is good; on the other hand, when it comes to the tech world, part of me thinks it's really hard for decision-makers. How do I assess technology quality when it's not really my job as a Minister of Health, for example, and how do we simplify that more as we go forward? Yeah, what do you feel is the vehicle? Because at least looking from the global perspective, there are a few potential vehicles for this to enable that decision-making: various initiatives in the WHO, various things in specific country settings as well. I know of one in the UK, for example, that helps create some kind of threshold.

Some people say regulation itself can be this vehicle. What are your thoughts on how to enable that? What can be the way to make that happen? You know, at a global level, I think the WHO plays an important role and, with the right investments and funding, could be a critical stakeholder. They are trusted; they're seen as—they do what they call product pre-qualification for a lot of the introduction of new tools, diagnostics, and medicines.

Could they fulfill that role for tech? I'm not sure they're set up to do it right now, but I think they're trying to figure it out.
