Country by country, though, regulators are trying to figure out that problem. How do we support those regulators? They've had to figure out a diagnostic and a medicine before; now we're asking them to look at technology.

Again, are they set up to do it? Probably not. I think it's an area where there's huge amounts of investment and support needed which doesn't currently exist, and it's not super "sexy" to fund TA to regulators. But I think it is important if we're going to set the right barrier to entry, have the right verifications, and want innovation but also don't want a free-for-all, at least in my viewpoint. Dino, it's been so valuable to hear your insights across your early journey, your experience as a clinician, and how you've welded that thinking into your approach to choosing the right problem, ensuring quality, and making sure that you're impacting the right parts of the ecosystem.

And also getting your recommendations and understanding the nuances of regulation, economics, and surviving as a company, particularly within this space, to create impact for people. It's been very, very valuable to get your thoughts on this. So thank you so much, and I'm looking forward to seeing how you guys progress. How can people get in touch with Audere and find out more about the work that you guys are doing? Yeah, sure.

So, first of all, thanks for having me; it's been a lot of fun. I've really enjoyed it. In terms of contacting us, our website is auderenow.org—so, a-u-d-e-r-e-n-o-w.org. We've got an info line there; they can write to us. A lot of those get directed to me to answer, and the rest of our leadership team.

The website is very comprehensive in terms of our journey, our products, our tools, and where we're headed. So, that's a great place to start. We're also on LinkedIn, which is a good place where we share a lot of innovation research. I think that's also just Audere. Those are probably the two best spots to interface with us.

Great. We'll definitely put those links in the show notes as well. To the audience, I hope you've managed to take away as much as I have from this session with Dino and finding out about their work. Thank you so much; it's been a pleasure. Thanks.
episodes.pullQuote: Probably 80% of healthcare is a conversation.
episodes.title: Creating impact with AI in isolated communities
episodes.description: How digital solutions and AI are revolutionising healthcare delivery in underserved and isolated communities - covering diagnostics, large language models, trust, and the critical role of local partnerships.

topics: Digital public goods: how digital solutions can be accessible public goods
Health data poverty and its effect on global health equity
The importance of strong data infrastructure
Regulatory challenges and the work that still needs to be done
AI and large language models to improve healthcare outcomes
episodes.bio: Dr Bilal Mateen is the Executive Director of Digital Square at PATH. A physician by training, he has an academic interest in health-related applications of data science and machine learning. He holds an honorary professorial appointment at University College London and a clinical data science fellowship at the Alan Turing Institute — the UK's national institute for data science and AI. He served as the clinical technology lead and senior manager for digital technology at the Wellcome Trust, where his team worked on funding digital public goods and the software infrastructure that underpins the science to address three key health challenges: mental health, the impacts of climate change on human health, and emerging and escalating infectious diseases.
episodes.guestRole: Executive Director, Digital Square at PATH (now Chief AI Officer at PATH)
episodes.transcript:
You are tuned in to the Global Perspectives on Digital Health podcast. My name is Shabs Ahadia, a physician working in digital health. I'm keen to learn more about the issues, challenges, and successes where digital health can have a real impact for underserved communities around the world. If you're a founder, investor, donor, researcher, or are developing and implementing digital health anywhere in the world and you're keen to break out of your bubble, join me as I speak to experts and innovators and get a truly global perspective on digital health. I'm really excited about this episode.

As a clinician, I'm always keen to get to know other clinicians in the digital health space. Today I'm thrilled to have Balal Martine, who's a clinician by background and he's Executive Director of Digital Square. You'll find out a little bit more about what Digital Square does later, but as my summary: if you want some real know-how on what it takes to bring together policy and actual impact on the ground for people, then Bal's insights are for you. We're going to go into how to create real impact for people in villages and rural areas, and really get into what the challenges are in bridging policy and ensuring that tracks to meaningful difference in an individual's health and life. So, I'm really looking forward to this one, and I hope you enjoy it.

Bal, I'm thrilled to have you as a guest on the podcast, and I'm sure our audience will have a lot to learn from your experience and insights. Could you start by telling us a little bit about yourself and the work of Digital Square? Absolutely, Shabs. It's a pleasure to be here. I'm super excited about the conversation.

We've spoken several times and gotten into it, so I'm sure we'll get into it again. For everyone listening, my name is Balal Martine. I'm the Executive Director of Digital Square. I am actually a medical doctor by training, but it was alongside medical school that I fell into the world of academia around informatics and machine learning for health. I spent a lot of time trying to expand my expertise around AI: the risks, the challenges, and the opportunities, especially in the healthcare space.

I had the pleasure of working at The Turing Institute and the Wellcome Trust—a philanthropy for national super-AI. I did some really interesting projects at a national level which taught me a lot about the difficulties of scaling these technologies. Then, more recently, I moved over to an initiative called Digital Square, which is hosted by PATH, a global NGO. Our job is really to expand and support the world to achieve health equity. That's by accelerating the development of medical products, increasing access to those products, and protecting vulnerable populations like women and children.

The work of Digital Square really is to strengthen health systems through digital and data transformation. That all really came about—I don't know if you remember, but from 2014 to 2016 there was the West African Ebola outbreak. We didn't do as well as we could have, and it was in the aftermath of that outbreak that all the donor, philanthropy, multilateral, and implementing partner communities came together and said, "What could we have done better?" The through-line from their reflections was that there was a fragmented digital ecosystem which hindered our response. It prevented the right data being brought together for the right people to help make action-oriented policy decisions so that we could address the outbreak and contain it, and we lost a lot more lives than we needed to as a consequence. So, it was really the US government—USAID—and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation that recognized that what we needed was this market-shaping entity to help support governments, strengthen their capacity for how to design these systems, and build out their digital health strategies and implementation plans for scaling national infrastructure in digital health.

We also aim to really coordinate the donors at the national level so that they weren't supporting a thousand wildflowers, but were rather directing their investment towards those strategies, and then doing interesting things like figuring out how we pay for this stuff at the global and the national level. That's really the work of Digital Square. I'd like to believe we've been pretty successful. Over the last seven years, we've mobilized just over $150 million in capital to support work across 36 countries globally. So, the mission continues.

We have a lot of work left to do, but step by step, I think we're getting there. It sounds really broad, the scope of what you guys do. One of the things I saw on your website talks about digital public goods. Can you just quickly explain what those are? Digital public goods are open-source software, content, or services that are available to support an SDG.

In our case, it's SDG 3, which is about supporting healthy lives. We actually talk about a subset of DPGs called "Global Goods for Health." There are so many digital public goods. You and I, in the next half an hour, if we wanted to, could write some code, say that it was to support SDG 3, and then submit it to the Digital Public Goods Alliance and get it registered. What we realize when working with governments is that they need mature digital public goods—things that have demonstrated the ability to be used in multiple contexts at a national scale, meet enterprise requirements, have thought about cybersecurity, are interoperable (complying with all the important standards that we care about), and have a healthy and robust community of practice committed to supporting their maintenance. We whittled them down through this competitive process, and we repeat it annually now.

It's actually an open process, so you can submit at any time. We whittled it down to 42 "Global Goods for Health" that are mature, scalable digital public goods. The idea is we're trying to address that information asymmetry that governments face. In a low-to-middle-income country, often when you're doing procurement, you don't know what the field of technologies looks like, and you end up just defaulting to the last one you were told about, assuming it meets enough of your requirements. We really wanted to help governments get out of that trap of defaulting to the last thing they heard about.

So we created the guidebook to say, "Here is your menu of options, here is what these tools often get used for, and how they could be used in your context." Very, very interesting. You mentioned information asymmetry as well. In the last episodes, we were talking about Health Data Poverty, which I think is another type of information asymmetry, right? I'd be interested to know—maybe this is the second part of the question—regarding creating, for example, one of the actions or recommendations was proactively trying to create inclusive and representative data sets. I can imagine that being a digital public good, or a data set that was existing that was doing that.

But do you have any thoughts, or do you have a perspective particularly with your work in Digital Square on Health Data Poverty and how it plays out in the context that you work in? Absolutely. I should mention that I think Xiao is incredible. I think the work she's done on the topic of Health Data Poverty, especially with the Standing Together initiative, is probably one of the most prolific things that more people should know about. Thanks so much for giving her a platform to talk about it.

In our context, Health Data Poverty, I think, has much more of an emphasis on the "poverty" aspect. We know there is a lack of representativeness in data sets globally. We know that leads to disenfranchisement of communities and individuals. The downstream consequence is that we widen the health inequality gap. I'm thinking about it daily.

In the context of all routine healthcare information systems, they end up falling victim to that issue. There is a lot we can do to strengthen them, to enfranchise communities to engage so that we have better quality information on them, and so that we can develop policies that support them and reflect their needs. But like I said, we anchor a lot on the "poverty" aspect because many of the communities we're trying to help, at what we call "The Last Mile" of healthcare, don't have consistent access to WASH infrastructure—Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene infrastructure. They don't have access to either electrical grid connectivity or internet connectivity. They don't have access to core infrastructure that you and I, I think, just take for granted.

What that means is we've got two layers of an issue. Even if we built the brilliant digital health information systems, how do we get them out to these rural, underserved communities in a way that we can consistently get the information we need? It introduces a whole bunch of challenges that we think through on the technical side, which is like, "How do you build the same information system so that it can function offline?" A community health worker can go out to the community with a phone and a power bank. The power bank is the critical bit, so they can do three days' worth of work collecting information, and then when they come back to the city or where there's internet access, upload all of that information so that the community is now represented. Huge, very similar problems, I think.

Probably a little bit more exacerbated in the countries that Digital Square works in, but principally really similar, just with the additional angles of what true poverty means for not just health data, but data, technology, and digital transformation at large. Yeah, and thanks for outlining that Health Data Poverty is kind of only one aspect or vertical of problems or issues that you deal with that are actually impacting people on the ground. I like this term that you use: "The Last Mile of Healthcare." It feels so important. We often work so hard to do all the bits around the deployment and the technical aspects, and kind of just reminding ourselves that it's actually this last-mile user or the last mile of healthcare that is the really important effect or end of this. It's so important that I think there's an organization called "Last Mile Health," right?

Just I think it solidifies the importance of this concept. Do you have anything more to say on this "Last Mile"—or maybe for our metric people, the last kilometers of healthcare? Maybe it's useful just for me to share with you what the actual definition is so that we can all anchor that. In International Development terms, reaching that "Last Mile" or a rural, isolated community involves reaching villages, communities, and individuals that would normally have access to things like paved roads, little access to communication, and overall poor infrastructure. Without services flowing in and out of these areas, people are disconnected from incredibly valuable products and technologies.

They're often left in a state of perpetual poverty. So, it's that higher-level issue of poverty of which health data is one critical access point. The difficulty in reaching them is that there are just constrained human and financial resources. To give you an example: the way the healthcare system operates across Africa is really different from how we do it in the UK, where you and I would call up our general practitioner to make an appointment with a primary healthcare physician. The frontline of healthcare, or the first line of frontline healthcare in Africa, are actually community health workers.

These aren't medically trained professionals; often, they have several days or a few weeks of training on how to use information systems and really basic knowledge of triage. But they have such a critical role because they're trusted members of the community, so everyone comes to them and, often, they're forced to work at a much higher level of competency. They're forced to make really critical decisions about whether someone should be going to hospital or not, because that journey to the hospital could be several months' wages. That's all to say that when we think about health inequalities, the reason reaching the "Last Mile" of healthcare and these last-mile communities is so important is... I don't know if everyone has the context—I think I've learned never to assume that they do—but when you go to a country like Kenya, Nairobi is remarkably similar to a lot of the high-income, developed nations' metropolitan cities that we visit.

It's very easy just to think of it as, "Oh, everyone has worse healthcare." There are some phenomenal hospitals in Nairobi. It's the inequality gap that often exists between those in Nairobi and those out in much poorer slum communities. So, I wouldn't tar with the same brush everyone in a low-or middle-income country. Really, if we're going to address the inequality gap, it requires us to get out into those underserved populations. 100%.

And I think Professor Alex, who was in Brazil, kind of mentioned a similar thing. We really need to think in a more nuanced way, even if we're thinking globally. You know, if we think about high-income countries, it's a well-trodden path where people have talked about how life expectancy changes across the Jubilee Line in London. You know that plays out. I was at the OECD high-level policy forum where the Secretary of State for Health from the US talked quite candidly about the tragedy that is in the US where some of the maternal health outcomes there, in some parts of the US, are comparable to some areas that you've been talking about in low-and middle-income countries.

So this plays out in many contexts. It's not as simple as saying, "Oh, in all low-and-middle-income contexts it's the same, and all high-income contexts it's the same." Really getting contextual there is really important. That plays out in terms of underserved communities being in any of those contexts. What are we doing to proactively reach out to them? Really, really great framing there.

You've kind of gone into a little bit around the challenges. You've defined what this "Last Mile of Healthcare" is and how important it is, and how the impact of a well-thought-out innovation can really impact people's lives in tangible ways on decision-making and also on community health workers who are this linchpin of the community and the way healthcare is delivered. The work that you've done has enabled health systems and enabled innovators in these contexts. Have you got some standout examples of how this plays out, or some positive impacts that you've seen? Absolutely.

I think I'll—otherwise we'd be here all day with me just listing out great groups—focus on the examples I've got in the AI space, and I'll throw in Large Language Models because it feels like no conversation about AI is complete without mentioning them. On the simpler machine learning side, folks have been doing great work on predicting the likelihood of people with HIV discontinuing care—not showing up to the clinic to get the next batch of anti-retrovirals that they need to suppress their disease and live a relatively normal and healthy life. What you can do is, if you can predict people who are at a high likelihood of discontinuation, you can give them a longer treatment course. You dispense them six months or a year's worth of drugs instead of one month's. That means that they're more likely to keep taking their medication because it's in the house.

It means they're more likely to keep their viral loads suppressed, and that prevents onward transmission. It also means that they have better health outcomes, and you can do that using the routinely collected information. We know that there are really key risk factors for discontinuation: living further away from the clinic or being of a certain demographic. I think that's a really key and easy way to get ahead of a problem that we know continues to fuel the AIDS epidemic globally. You have cutting-edge research on the Large Language Model side.

The Google Health team released a paper describing a trial they did of AMIE, which is their diagnostic dialogue system. It demonstrates that you can get superior performance in terms of collecting information from potential patients and more empathetic dialogue compared to primary care physicians from a Large Language Model, which is really interesting. Not to suggest—and I love Alan at Google Health, who's one of the senior authors on the paper—he was saying this to a group of people when they went, "Oh, but if it's better than the physician, let's just replace the physicians!" This is the case for autonomous diagnostic systems. He was like, "Let's calm down, hold our horses." It's as important for the physician to be wrong. It's that classic adage of, "If you hear hooves, think horses, not zebras." A lot of the stuff we're testing LLMs on are the really rare cases, and often it's that cycle of going through the common differentials that means we pick up the key stuff.

So I don't think we're there yet with autonomous systems, but it's really exciting to see that research show the prospect and the value of Large Language models. A slightly more realistically anchored example: I mentioned community health workers earlier. There's a company called Viamo, this Canadian NGO, that created a call center service that's backed by an LLM. What you see among the community health worker community is that they all love texting each other on WhatsApp to ask each other's advice. They basically leveraged this and said, "Wouldn't it be cool if they could text an LLM that could access a canonical data source, whether that's the internet or all of the primary healthcare guidelines that exist, and go, 'I've got this patient, I think I've got this problem, what do I do next?'" Then the LLM can give them some advice.

Lots of work still needs to be done on making sure this stuff is safe, but I think the early evidence around its effectiveness means that you can really support community health workers to do their job better and make sure that, again, people at the Last Mile of healthcare are getting world-class care that kind of exceeds what you could get from putting a physician in the field, which we know is far too expensive to practically do. But there's a world in which we could get there. I think the last one I'll give you, Shabs, if you'll allow me, is that there are great companies like Audere out there in the world as well that have been thinking about how we take generative AI to support self-testing workflows—to leverage computer vision to create a new foundation model for reading rapid diagnostic tests, which we know is a key bit of the clinical pathway you need to navigate if you're going to access anti-malarials for malaria. Do a malaria RDT (rapid diagnostic test), show that you're positive, and a pharmacy will dispense you anti-malarials. Malaria continues to kill many, many people globally, and it's about how we inject AI really usefully into the workflow without thinking about how we need to replace someone, but rather just make it easier for someone to read a test, because that red line can be pretty faint sometimes, so that the right person can get the right drug at the right time.

And that makes so much sense. We will definitely come back to LLMs, but I guess, if I go one level up, I think one of the things that I like about the approach or the way the way you talk about this is that you frame this as the task to be done. I guess it's taking in the nuance. There are many tasks that people have to do. You could think about that for a patient, or you could think about that for a community health worker or any type of healthcare professional, and then think about where the value ads are for a type of task, rather than maybe shoehorning technologies into workflows.

Thinking about the tasks that need to be done that could leverage automation, LLMs, or other types of technologies seems like a more valuable approach. Absolutely. I think it's the story of your career and mine, right? The technologist realized that just having a data set wasn't enough to create a product; you really need to understand the clinical workflow and where you could have a value add. It's partnering with health workers to go, "How do we make this bit of your job easier, more effective, or more efficient?" It not only reduces the barriers to adoption because we're the end-user in a lot of the cases, it also exposes those bits of the health system where there are opportunities for cost-saving, cost-effectiveness, and improvements in efficiency.

We talk so much about the billions we could save. I don't think that you're ever going to find that use case without speaking to one of us humble physicians. Absolutely. Let's get into cost savings a bit, because part of it... we've talked about impact.

There's an impact to make patient life easy at the Last Mile. There's an impact in terms of information enabling clinicians to make better decisions. That's a benefit and a value add. And then there's this separate, overarching thing around how do you create cost savings? Sometimes they are linked to those two; sometimes they are not.

That's also a balancing act that health systems and governments have to do. What are your thoughts about how we measure that impact in any context, but in particular in low-and-middle-income country settings? Oh, what a great question. It opens up a real can of worms for me because I've had a gripe for a long time with the fact that most of the research that comes out fixates in terms of impact on accuracy, right? "Oh, we've got superhuman accuracy, we're 99% effective on diagnosing X on an X-ray." There's a wonderful paper back from a group at Stanford—John Ioannidis's group.

If anyone wants to look it up, it's Siontis et al. from 2015, where they really clearly demonstrate there is no link between—when you're comparing diagnostic tests head-to-head in an RCT—how much better the diagnostic test is and the downstream benefit to a patient. So you can have a massive performance gain on a diagnostic test and no benefit. You can have a tiny gain in diagnostic accuracy and a huge benefit. It's intuitive, right?

The healthcare system is this complex ecosystem and diagnosis is a small bit of the clinical workflow. It's making sure the right patient shows up and asks the question that prompts that diagnostic test. It's about having the therapies needed to do something about it. We've for a long time struggled with whether we should be doing diagnostic tests for Huntington's disease, because it's a genetic disorder for which we have no treatments right now. Some people want the test because they want patient choice—great, let's enfranchise that right.

A lot of people don't because there's nothing we can do. In terms of impact and cost-effectiveness, there's just not enough studies. I know of one RCT that was funded by my colleagues at the Wellcome Trust. In terms of the world of funders, there's one RCT in Africa that I know of that actually looked at the cost-effectiveness of an AI tool that was published. Again, Dr.

MacPherson from the Malawi-Liverpool-Wellcome. It's a TB chest X-ray computer-aided diagnostic tool, and it's actually an opportunistic screening of people that are coming to an HIV clinic. By most cost-effectiveness thresholds, it is actually not cost-effective, which is a little bit of a disappointing result, but they use much lower thresholds than we would use in the UK. That's all to say that you get these wonderful high-level papers from the consultancies saying that we're going to save $100-plus billion from the introduction of AI into the healthcare system. Show me the proof.

Show me the individual use case where there's the proof. I'm still waiting for it. Do you think that we should be thinking beyond cost-effectiveness and other measures of value and impact? Because, just to touch on something you said: we're evolving from thinking only about performance to thinking about value. I guess my soapbox is that value isn't just cost-effectiveness and saving money.

There's other bits of value that we talked about. Sometimes one bit of value, which is saving money, is directly in conflict with another bit of value, which is giving someone a smooth experience or reaching the Last Mile of healthcare, for example. There might be actual direct conflict with each other. How do you balance that? How do you help governments think about that in Digital Square?

No, you're absolutely right. We spend a lot of our time trying to convince governments to think about improvements in human morbidity and mortality as the primary outcome they should care about. It's about making human lives healthier. The weird thing is that most of the efficiency gains that we get—what I have been referring to as "non-cash-releasing efficiency gains"—if you make a doctor more efficient, you don't pay them for fewer hours of work. They still work nine hours; they just see more patients.

So, we've helped to improve the lives of more people, but we haven't released any money from the system. The government hasn't gone, "Oh, I'm paying less to see the same number of people." I am seeing more people, which is great, but it's really hard for them to then document the win, which is where I completely take your point. We need to help them see the value in improving people's lives. It often comes back to money—maybe not money that they have in their pockets, but the money that they get from making that person's life better. I 100% agree with you.

It's not to say that we shouldn't be thinking about cost-effectiveness, it's just thinking broader. What are the second-and-third-order effects of that? What does that saved money enable? It enables better use of resources, continuity of care, or more healthcare workers. It enables time saved and enables connection to a person.

So it's thinking beyond cold, hard numbers and thinking about the actual real value that they enable. So, yeah, that's a good one to think about, and thanks for framing it particularly within this context. What opportunities do you think still could be explored? Where do we need to focus? Where does work need to be done so that people who are really trying to create impact in this area can really hone in on it?

I'll go one upstream and one downstream. The upstream is we need to focus on strengthening the data science ecosystems in the low-and-middle-income countries and in the communities that we're talking about. A lot of the products that are being developed are being developed by people in high-income Global North countries, or in technical powerhouses like India and China, and they're being exported. It's not to say that the products are bad, but we will never understand to the same extent as someone living in that community who is experiencing these problems how best to solve the problem—what the hurdles are they need to navigate. It's their lived experience that really needs to be captured, and there are two ways to capture that lived experience.

Either you can meaningfully involve them in the product development, which I think is the basic thing we should be doing, but ideally, if we strengthen the ecosystems in the countries that are experiencing the problems we're trying to address, they can become the agents of change themselves. That's a lot of what Digital Square focuses on doing. We call it our "Localization Agenda." We're increasingly hearing about localization from our donors as well, which we're super excited about. It's investment in local innovators and entrepreneurs so they can be leading the way on the next generation of AI-based technologies and digital health innovations that we're going to see. So, that's the upstream bit.

The downstream bit is: there is no point in us investing in all of this research if we're not going to invest in the enabling environment that gets that research and product to the bedside. There is this really unsexy thing that no one likes to talk about, and that is regulation. Regulation exists to safeguard the population and to put up the right guardrails to make sure the right technology is making it to the bedside. Given how disruptive these technologies are, there are huge questions around whether the current state of regulation is sufficient. That really ends up with two things happening.

Either you have regulators going, "It's probably not sufficient, we don't know what to do about it, so none of you get to do anything," and we're just going to put up this massive hurdle that says, "Nope, not until we figure this out." At the rate the bureaucratic process moves, it'll be years before we figure this out and you can do anything about it. Or, you get the Wild West, where regulators are kind of turning a blind eye, everyone's doing what they want, and we are definitely exposing people to things that aren't safe or effective. I'm not sure how comfortable I am with either. Yeah. Do you think there's a middle way?

Do I think there's a middle way? There must be, right? Otherwise I wouldn't get up in the morning and do my job. I think the middle way is helping create these safe environments for us to test the innovative thing with additional safeguards while we understand what the guardrails for everyone need to be. You hear this term "Sandbox" a lot.

My dream is: can we start supporting a series of AI-as-a-Medical-Device and Large-Language-Models-as-a-Medical-Device sandboxes? Not just in the UK, where the government announced an "Airlock" (which is their sandbox that they'll be running over the next couple of years), but across Africa, across Asia, across Latin America, and the Caribbean. Like I said, I think I'm a broken record at this point: if we're going to solve the issue of health equity globally, we can't be running these sandboxes just in the UK. I really like that. In particular, it comes to the "Why" of this podcast series as well.

Our gaze in digital health is often very focused—at least in my bubble—on the EU, the UK, and the US. I think this plays out in regulation as well. Our regulatory gaze is very FDA-focused. Even if you look at the members of the IMDRF (the International Medical Regulator Forum), it is very, very heavy on high-income countries. There are a few represented—you mentioned South Africa when we were talking before.

I think we need stronger voices and representation from other contexts. Earlier you mentioned localization in the context of the actual deployment. I think this plays out in regulation as well. How do you get it right between needing a body creating core international types of standards, while there is a need for local context, nuance, and needs? The regulatory needs, or the way it shapes out or plays out in a local context, might be very different.

I'll give you an example: some people think, "Well, actually, when we think about regulation, we're thinking about benefit versus risk, and do your benefits outweigh the risk?" That's like a central tenet of what it's trying to do. Sometimes when you're thinking about certain contexts, some people are proponents of saying, "Well, in this low-resource setting, the risk of not applying this technology outweighs the risk of taking ages to get regulatory approval and having something there." How do you see these local needs—and this is a local need like, "We really need something here now"—versus, "We need to do this in the right way, we need to think about this in a safe way and protect people, especially people who are more vulnerable and underserved?" How do you think about this? How do you help governments think about this? How should innovators in the audience who are listening to this think about this? What a great question, and so many pieces to it.

I'll work backwards. I think it's that bit about vulnerability that always sticks in my mind when I hear the argument that there is this urgency we need to respond to that means we should, for a moment, disregard the normal rules and procedures and just get on with it because there is such an outsized benefit. I think it's a little bit bizarre, this coming from me—someone who has an academic post in AI for healthcare, someone who has worked in the field and really does believe it can be helpful. I think sometimes we assume that what these tools are going to do is going to be so profound that we found the equivalent of a parachute. Nothing is a parachute.

It is not the difference between zero people surviving and almost everyone surviving if you jump out of a plane. These things are incrementally beneficial. And, yes, that increment will be a lot larger when you're supporting a community health worker or a trained nurse in rural Congo than it will be in central London. But I am not a huge fan of moral relativism, and I think that there are safe ways for us to trial these procedures and figure out what does meet the threshold that we all know to be appropriate so that we can get it out at a national scale, rather than just trialing it on people who I don't think are necessarily being given a choice. Because when a community health worker shows up with a tablet and is collecting information and generating a prediction, are we sure that there is meaningful consent being considered here?

When you're talking to a person who sometimes doesn't even have a primary school education, let alone a secondary or tertiary education? There are nuances that make me maybe a bit more worried than others about how quickly we deploy this technology. So, that's what I really want to say as we think about how quickly we want to deploy these technologies globally. On the other piece on regulation: I think you made a great point. There's a role for harmonization, but there is also a pretty key aspect of localization here.

There are groups like IMDRF and WHO that play a key part in making sure we get the harmonization right. The analogy I like to use is that these technologies are very different from the pharmaceuticals that we've thought about for a long time. When you give someone paracetamol in London versus when you give someone paracetamol in Cape Town, South Africa, it's pretty likely they're going to respond the same way because human biology is highly conserved. You'll have seen the jokes that we share 95% of our genetics with a banana; biology is just highly conserved. There is now increasingly a recognition that you do get genetic differences, but not to the same degree that you see with software and AI as a medical device.

These technologies are inductive; they're based on the data they saw. If you train them on a white, middle-class man in North London, it's unsurprising—if you were taking pictures of that person's skin to see if they've got a cancerous mole or not—and you take it to Cape Town, South Africa, it's probably not going to work as well. You need a regulator to be asking that question, to be creating the benchmark that is representative of the local population, so you can evaluate its local effectiveness and decide, "Yes, this one; no, not that one." What we're seeing is because the technology is so innovative and because the questions around how to regulate it are so new, regulators are making really bizarre decisions. They're using pre-existing frameworks in a way that at times is comical but also really worrying. The example I'll give you is that a regulator—I shan't name which one in Africa...

go on, it was South Africa—approved an AI-based tool for diagnosing TB on a chest X-ray using the In Vitro Devices framework, which is a different type of medical device that has a very similar kind of risk classification approach, but it's a different type of device. The classification they gave it was Class 1, which is the lowest risk and is what you would give to something that is non-sterile and very low risk. The analogy is: the other thing I might give a Class 1 approval to would be, if I was bedbound in a hospital and needed to urinate, a nurse would hand me this compostable thing that I would urinate into that would then be disposed of. So, the diagnostic tool for TB—that determines whether you might go on to get the drugs that you need to treat a disease that still kills tens, if not hundreds, of thousands of people a year globally—versus the thing I urinate in? Clearly, we aren't getting this right everywhere.

A lot of time needs to be spent investing in the capacity of national regulatory authorities. I'm not saying the FDA or the UK has the right answer either—I think we're all figuring it out—but we need to work together more. Sorry, I was just going to add that you could argue that, in at least the EU and UK context, the CE mark is similar. If you're in Class 1 (the lowest class of risk), you basically self-certify. You say, "We think we're in this class," etc.

At some point, you might get called out on saying, "Actually, you're a bit more involved in the whole diagnostic process than you say." So there is an interesting thing there that also plays out. I wanted to touch on the thing you mentioned about taking something that's developed in one context and kind of dropping it into a task in another context. The medical metaphor I like using... I'm a GP trained in the NHS in the UK. If I spent some time working in Sierra Leone, or if I was going to be working in a different context, I'd have to do a lot of work to make sure that I understood what was going on in that context.

I would have to get some kind of local certification that showed, at least in the UK context, I was up to some level of competency and showed that I had some understanding, education, and work done in those contexts. Sometimes, if you're working more regularly in those contexts, you might be supervised by clinicians who are working in that context. So I feel like there's some equivalence there in terms of how regulators might or might not be thinking about it, and how we might be applying or approaching this conversation if you're bringing a doctor from one context into another. Maybe between some geographies or countries there might be some agreement that if you reach this threshold of certification, that's okay, but you would still need to do X, Y, and Z to be able to practice here. I feel like there's some regulatory similarity there.

Yeah. The regulatory nerds listening to you talk about that will immediately have gone, "What he's talking about is effective reliance practices." The UK will sign an agreement—the MHRA will sign an agreement with the US FDA and set up a reliance practice where we think that their regulatory procedures are so robust that if they approve something, we're happy to rely on that. It kind of happens in the EU as well, where you have one stringent authority that will do the evaluation on behalf of the EMA so all of the European countries can then use the drug. The point that I want to drive home is that kind of naive reliance where it's, "Yeah, yeah, your processes are good enough," only works in so many contexts. Given everything we've talked about regarding how AI and software are meaningfully different—that inductive, logic-based approach—there are really smart people in the regulatory space.

Johan Ordish, who used to lead software and AI regulation at the MHRA but has now jumped over to Roche, talks about the idea of "Enhanced Reliance." You take everything that someone else has done and go, "Okay, it met the threshold; now, what are the questions I need to ask to make sure it works in my unique context for whatever differences might exist?" The simple example might be in the US and UK: we actually use different units when we talk about the amount of hemoglobin in blood. Some people talk about grams per liter, some people talk about nanomoles. That changes how the number is structured. Sometimes it's 136, sometimes it's 13.6. Small quirks like that are important differences in how the health system is structured.

Remember, people go to a community health worker first in a lot of countries in Africa, but people go to a GP first in a lot of countries in Europe. Does the tool integrate into the health system in the same way? All of these questions about local nuances and quirks should be asked locally, but you can rely on a lot of the, "Are they ISO 13485 compliant or 62304 compliant?" If they're compliant with the ISO standard, you don't really need to ask that question again. I like that. To me, there are good takeaways for a regulatory audience, but also for an innovator who's trying to create impact in that space.

How do you think about this? How do you make sure that you're ready? How do you bake in, design, test, and benchmark yourself for being ready for those types of deployments? So, a really nice takeaway for people working in digital health companies. We've covered so much.

I want to talk about LLMs, though, because we said we'll come back to them, maybe in the regulatory context. Because if they're used in this way, they are medical devices. Where do you—what's your take on regulation of LLMs and where we're at with that? Oh my God. It's super interesting to see how the world has diverged.

In the UK, you had a blog published by the MHRA where they said a lot of the LLMs that we're talking about (that are accessed via an API—think GPT-4, think the Med-LM series that's been released by Google) fall under this grouping of things called "SOUP": Software of Unknown Provenance. It's quite hard to figure out how to make SOUP compliant with all of the standards that exist, which might sound super nerdy and niche, but it's going to be one of the critical things that we need to figure out how to navigate if we're going to get any of this stuff through the regulatory process. The MHRA's response was, "Have a go, let's see if you can do it—we're uncertain right now but we know there are going to be key issues." The FDA is just letting everyone do everything. There are questions about whether they are even going to think about LLMs as medical devices, or argue that it's not actually processing a signal and therefore doesn't fall within the scope of a medical device. We've seen five, six hundred...

God knows how many hundreds of AI-based tools go through FDA clearance now. So the FDA and the US market are way ahead of the rest of us. Then you have Australia, which said, "Hey, we're not even going to let LLMs do medical notes summarization, because we've seen all this research about the fact that it hallucinates symptoms for patients in its summaries." We know that LLMs hallucinate and confabulate. So, you've got the three key stringent regulatory authorities that have come up with different answers. Do I have the right one?

No. But where I've landed—and credit to Jennifer, who's the CEO of the Digital Medicine Society, who's doing some work on this—is that I think we've realized that there are a handful of regulatory approaches. We don't know what the right one is. I think what we're pushing towards is: don't pick a "certain" one, just pick *one*. I don't mind if your response is, "Hey, I don't get it, I don't understand it, I'm fearful, therefore no one does anything." What that does is it creates regulatory clarity.

It means, "Not in my jurisdiction; maybe next door, but not in mine." Currently, what we have is the Wild West across a lot of the low-and-middle-income countries where I spend a lot of my time working. That lack of regulatory clarity means that people are being exposed to risk because the regulator isn't forcing people to register their medical device. I think having these safeguards is the first critical step. My request would be: let's codify the three or four options that regulators have and let's beg and plead that they pick one while we spend some time figuring out which one's the best. Interesting take.

Do you agree, Shabs? I like your take where I don't know what the right thing is. I'm still navigating. For me, it's also very contextual. It depends on the task and where in the journey for either a patient or the clinician what's being done.

Therefore, I don't think it should be considered as a different thing to AI that's already being used. In a way, we should be thinking about it in a similar way: it's an intervention, and we're thinking about the use case, the intended users, the task to be done, the risks associated, the potential benefits, and what we are doing to mitigate them. What's your quality management system to be able to make sure that you're trying to do the right thing, and also trying to do the thing right? Applying that methodology and regulation to me is a vehicle that is a forcing function; it's a stick. To me, it's also valuable to approach this in the right way.

So, I guess my another question to you is: how could governments be enabled to think about the "carrot" side of things? How do you recognize the value of an organization or company who's invested? Doing things the right way is much harder, it takes longer, and it's more expensive. How do you get governments, health systems, or decision-makers to realize the inherent value of someone approaching something in that way to say, "Hey, we'll invest in you, we'll back you guys, because you are approaching this in the right way?" I want to flip it, because I think everyone is scared of regulation, whereas I see it as this opportunity. Who is going to be the first to partner with the national government to go, "Hey—the easiest way, and I shouldn't say this out loud, but I'm going to—here is the easiest way for me to get rid of all of my competition, because I'm going to convince you that you should regulate this technology.

I'm going to invest in going through the regulatory pathway while no one else will." At the end of this, you're going to give me regulatory approval because I'm going to find a way to effectively navigate the system and give you all the information you need. Suddenly, everyone else is on the outside and behind me and now has to spend the next 18 months doing what I've just done. I think there's going to be a real first-to-market winner here. The reason it scares me is because the companies with the resources to do this are the mega-entities: the GE Healthcares, the Apples, the Google Healths. Interestingly, they're the ones who are skirting it and sometimes trying to avoid the issue.

They're the ones with the disclaimers because, again, it's hard. The risk that we run is when the mega-entities show up and decide they want to do it, they're going to crowd out the local innovators that don't have the capital to necessarily engage with this process in the same way. I guess that's where you guys come in, as well—enabling those guys and creating platforms for them so they understand that this process isn't as scary as one might think. You're absolutely right, that is our role: to reduce the barriers to entry. But I take your point.

I'm also just looking at it going, "I don't understand why more people aren't excited," but maybe I'm a massive regulatory nerd. Look, I definitely agree with you in seeing the value of leaning into it and doing it the right way. It is beneficial, and the idea is that you create a better product and it actually has the impact that you intended because you clearly thought of it at the beginning. So it has a structure if applied right, but it is an investment as well. A company thinking about it as an investment that gives you differentiation and a competitive edge is a great way for innovators and founders in the audience to think about this.

Definitely a good takeaway. Well, and it opens up access to markets in a way that I don't think skirting the regulation does. If you go through the regulatory process in the UK and then you engage with NICE and get a health technology assessment, what's the likelihood that you get a clinical guideline based on your work? What's the likelihood that you then get onto the formulary? Suddenly, because we have a national procurement system, GPs could theoretically prescribe your product.

It's what Sleepio did, which is this digital therapeutic to improve the quality of sleep that went through the HTA process. Now GPs across the country can prescribe this thing. The profit and revenue-earning potential in national procurement mechanisms if you have a single-payer—and even if when you don't have a single-payer—that it opens up is so cool. If I was an innovator—and trust me, I'm not smart enough to come up with my own idea, so it's very easy for me to say this—I would be looking at that regulatory process and seeing how it opens up these opportunities, and going, "How do I convince one of my investors to give me the money to do this?" because it's costly, it's going to take time, and it's going to delay my go-to-market strategy by a few years, but the upside—sweet Jesus! That sounds like a good answer to a question which would be: "What would be your one recommendation to innovators for having an impact on underserved communities?" Do you have any others?

I'll repeat the two that I think we've covered during this conversation. The first is: engage with clinicians and healthcare workers. You will understand the problems you are trying to solve in a much more profound way and you will see solutions you wouldn't have otherwise seen. You will learn hard lessons, like the cool data set you currently have access to is fundamentally meaningless and you are going to have to find a way to create a new data set that actually addresses the task. The second piece is: as you engage with potential investors, help them understand the complexity of the problem that you are trying to solve.

There is a lot of healthcare exceptionalism in the world, and I think us clinicians walk around like we're special snowflakes, but healthcare is sometimes different, and especially when it comes to regulation, it's different. There are safeguards and they're there for a reason, but if you can find the right investor and explain to them why you're doing what you're doing—why you need to run the RCT with cost-effectiveness outcomes so that you can engage with the national procurers and get a massive government contract—the upside potential is enormous here. It starts with convincing your investor that they're going on a long-term journey, not one in which you're going to take a product to market in the next year, earn a few bucks, and then sell your product to GE. That's so useful, and there are lots of actionable things. Bal, we've covered so much.

We've gone on a journey to understand the work you've done with Digital Square. We heard great examples of people creating real impact for underserved communities and the nuances and the challenges. Surprise, surprise, we got into LLMs and regulation, of course. It's been really, really packed with insights and tangible things that people can take away. I'm really, really grateful for that.

Where can people find more about the work that you are doing, Bal, and the work that Digital Square and PATH are doing? It's very kind of you to ask, Shabs. We have a website: digitalsquare.org. Everything that we do ends up on there. We post a blog every couple of weeks, if not every week, on some different bit of our portfolio and projects and what progress we're making.

I occasionally go out and do stuff like this to talk to cool people like you about our work. Honestly, it's not about us and Digital Square. The whole idea of the initiative is that we're a consortium of partners. We're there to platform others; we're really here to drive investment into all of the communities that are driving change in the communities that are currently underserved. We want to be the impetus or the catalyst for change; I don't think we need to be the ones doing everything everywhere.

So, my ask would be: come talk to us if you want to be part of the consortium, or if you have something to share or to give. Let's figure out a way that we can help you there. There it is. We'll definitely put the links to Digital Square, the work, case studies, and the sources that you've curated and created. Bal, it's been a pleasure talking to you.

Thank you so much. I'm looking forward to Part 1532 of this, by the way, where we'll be talking to one of the companies that Digital Square and PATH have been working with—Audere. You mentioned them earlier, so this conversation has been a great segue into Part 2 of this. Bal, I thank you again for your insights and look forward to talking to Audere as well. My absolute pleasure, Shabs, and thanks for having me.

Dino is brilliant, so I'm sure it'll be an amazing conversation. Great stuff. All right, some quick reflections from the episode we've just had with Bal from Digital Square. Such a valuable conversation. We covered the challenges of bringing together government and health system thinking towards impact on the Last Mile of healthcare.

What considerations do we need to make, particularly from a safety and regulatory perspective? We heard some examples of companies who are really moving the needle on some of this and creating impact for underserved populations. We covered LLMs and the regulatory context around them, which was pretty spicy and great. Some great calls to action for innovators in terms of how to think about and approach some of these challenges—in terms of data, representativeness of data, the implementation challenges, and how to really think about the impact that you have on people's lives. To me, it also highlights—similar to previous episodes we've had—that we need to think about a whole ecosystem perspective.

If you're an innovator, what things can you be doing proactively before you deploy? How do you work with people locally? How do you work with clinicians and community health workers locally, and with implementers at the government level? How do you think about how you approach the relationship with innovators and developers, and the transformation and the value we want to create? There's lots to think about and take away into our own work.

It's been a really, really great conversation. I look forward to Part 2 of this with one of the companies that Digital Square has worked with. If you found this episode useful, then hit subscribe, follow us, and share it with others who want to widen their perspective on digital health, so that we can together create better outcomes for all. We've got many exciting guests and conversations lined up, so come and join us and break your bubble and get a truly global perspective on digital health. Thank you.

episodes.title: Bridging the gap: the last mile of healthcare
episodes.description: How do we meaningfully bridge policy and real impact at the last mile of healthcare? A conversation on digital health challenges and successes in underserved communities - covering safety, regulation, data infrastructure, community health workers, and the role of AI and large language models.
