episodes.bio: Alexandre Chiavegatto Filho is an Associate Professor of Machine Learning in Healthcare at the Department of Epidemiology, School of Public Health, University of São Paulo. He directs the Laboratory of Big Data and Predictive Analysis in Health (Labdaps), which includes a team of 30 researchers focused on developing AI algorithms to improve healthcare decisions.
episodes.guestRole: Associate Professor of Machine Learning in Healthcare, University of São Paulo
episodes.transcript:
Okay, so we're coming to the second part of this conversation and actually discussing a real-world application or example where we address some of the issues linked to Health Data poverty. I think in particular this one is really linked to the recommendation that we just talked about with Xiao around building inclusive and representative datasets and how that might enable supporting equity, discovery, and innovation in digital healthcare. So on that, I'm really grateful to have Professor Alexandre Chiavegatto Filho with us to actually discuss a little bit about the context where you are in Brazil, and we'll go into how this relates. But maybe to start with, Alex, please tell us a bit about yourself, your work, where you're based, and we'll go from there. Thank you so much.

Awesome, thank you very much for having me. It's a pleasure and a great opportunity to talk a little bit about this important issue of data diversity in machine learning for healthcare. I'm actually an associate professor of machine learning in healthcare here at the University of São Paulo in Brazil, where we have had our machine learning lab since 2017. We work mostly with structured data here, and our main goal is to see that when those algorithms start coming to Brazil, we're going to have them with high quality, high diversity, and high fairness. This way, it can improve the lives of the people where the algorithms are going to have the biggest impact, which is in remote areas of the world.

Here in Brazil, it's the more disadvantaged areas of Brazil. It's not an easy challenge to get those algorithms to work in those areas because we have many issues that we're probably going to talk about here. So it's the main goal of our lab to make sure that when machine learning transforms healthcare, it's going to be particularly useful for the people that it's going to have the most impact on. Amazing. So that's exactly, as you've highlighted, some particular areas around your work where we can talk about the challenges that you've managed to overcome and the ways that you've benefited and impacted those particular communities.

I think that's the stuff that's going to be great to get into. Maybe before we get into that, it would be good to get your perspective, particularly from your lab and maybe personally from your experience, on Health Data poverty, particularly around the biggest challenges that you're seeing in Brazil. You kind of alluded to them when you were doing your intro. We actually have decent Health Data quality. We collect pretty much universal data on every single birth here in Brazil, every single death, hospitalizations, and so on, which is remarkable for a middle-income country such as Brazil.

It's huge, right? It has very remote areas and a huge rainforest in the middle of it. So even with those challenges, we were able to collect high-quality Health Data. The issue here is that we do not have data integration. We do not know that this person that was born here is the same person that was hospitalized here and is the same person that died here.

Our health information systems are independent of each other, which is the biggest challenge for machine learning. In machine learning, we would want to have a follow-up of the patients so we can predict who is going to get sick, who is going to die, and who is going to need an important intervention and so on. So it's quite hard. We have been able to do some research by collecting our own data and collaborating with the healthcare system so we can have integrated data, but it's not that easy. I would say that the main challenge right now is that most of the studies that we have in Brazil—which is the same challenge around the world—are usually done in high-income areas.

It's usually done here in São Paulo or in Rio or the other large cities of Brazil, which leave out the remote areas. So we have been trying to reach out to those areas to try to get data and see how the machine learning algorithms perform differently in comparison to São Paulo. Yeah, and I guess that's a big link to a big part of the audience: what's the global relevance of this, and how does that relate to some of the challenges that are more "in fashion" at the moment within the EU and the US? These contexts are starting to speak much more about the inequities that are faced. At least what I'm hearing is that, particularly within Brazil, you have been having to deal with much of this for a much longer time.

These challenges are much bigger or multiplied within your context. That really resonates a lot. I think another thing that comes out in terms of a challenge and the way to overcome this is actually proactively going out to those communities and working with them to see how you can bridge that. That piece around awareness and actually going out there and doing something about it, rather than having a question mark—yes, society in general should do something about this, but it's always pointing at someone else expecting someone else to do it. Yeah, exactly.

I usually say, and I really believe this, that Brazil has the richest Health Data in the world. Why is that? It's because of our diversity. Most developed countries of the world are now becoming diverse in terms of genetics, background, and in terms of economic disparities. Brazil has had that for decades and centuries.

We have been a very racially diverse country for centuries and we are a very economically unequal country for centuries. So I usually say that the world is becoming more like Brazil. The difference is that the richest parts of the world are now starting to have diverse data, but we have a long history in Brazil of diverse data. For machine learning, this is going to be critical because machine learning is learning rules from data, which can be significantly different depending on the background of the person, the health resources that you have, the economic background of the patients, and so on. That diversity is crucial for machine learning algorithms.

In the richest countries of the world, you don't have that much diversity, so it means that the algorithm is going to miss some details there. But here in Brazil, we have the whole world inside of Brazil in every single sense. Here in Brazil, our algorithms are really able to learn about the rules that make human beings have diseases and other issues. So we do have very rich data and we're trying to see how that helps to improve the algorithms. What we have been doing a lot is training those algorithms in São Paulo, which would be like training in a rich city around the world, and then we try to move those algorithms to the other regions of Brazil.

An algorithm that works well in a developed city, in a large urban area, is making good decisions, has good predictive performance, and is working well. Let's see if it works equally well when we move to different regions and settings. We have been seeing that it doesn't work so well. This is a huge red flag for the future, even for the developed regions of the world. If you want to scale your algorithms throughout the world, it's probably not going to work so well because it doesn't work inside of Brazil.

It's the same system and the same currency, but the patients and the resources are diverse. Even in this setting, when you increase diversity, the algorithms usually do not transfer so well. So we have a lot of teachings to give to the world. I think the first thing would be that diversity improves the quality of the algorithm. The second one is that if you train the algorithm in a rich area, it's probably not going to work in more disadvantaged areas.

We have been finding a lot of things in Brazil, and I do think that we have things to teach the world as we move forward with artificial intelligence in healthcare. That's a really nice overview. Just to summarize, I think a couple of the key points there are the foundational point that diversity by design will improve algorithms, and the other is really having the proactive requirement at the beginning of your process to make sure that you're not just training this in a data-rich and socioeconomically rich environment. What effort are you making to ensure that the algorithm is going to be relevant to communities that are both data-poor and socioeconomically poorer? Absolutely.

I think there are a couple of key takeaway messages. I wanted to zoom in on a couple of things, particularly around building inclusive and representative datasets. One of the studies your team has done—and I'll share this with the audience—is predicting neonatal mortality leveraging routinely collected data in São Paulo. Please tell us more about that because I think that's another example of making sure that the dataset is powerful enough and relevant enough. Because it's routinely collected, it is potentially generalizable.

So let's hear a bit more about that. Exactly. I think we have three main challenges in getting those algorithms to work in remote areas. As I said in the beginning, remote areas are where the algorithms are going to have the biggest impact. It's going to have an impact on urban and developed areas, too, but the difference in quality in terms of clinical decisions is not going to be so great because you already have good physicians in urban areas.

The decisions of these physicians will improve, but they won't improve as much as in those remote areas where, especially in Brazil, we have some cities where we only have one physician for the whole city. That physician doesn't have anyone to send the patients to—no specialists—so the physician has to be a pulmonologist, a cardiologist, and so on. The decision of this physician is going to improve dramatically with the algorithm. Our main goal is to get those algorithms to those regions, and I think we have three main challenges for achieving this. The first one is that we need to use data that is actually collected in those regions, and here comes the "routinely collected" part.

If an x-ray improves the decision for diseases but it's not feasible to get the x-ray to the remote area, then it doesn't really matter. We need to use the variables that are actually collected on those regions. The first challenge is: are we able, with those variables already collected, to train machine learning algorithms that make good decisions that actually improve clinical decisions? The second one is: do the algorithms that we train elsewhere work in those remote areas? In large areas, you usually have more data, so you're probably going to use more data from urban areas to train those algorithms.

The algorithm is going to work pretty well in the urban area, but it's probably not going to work well in the remote areas. The third challenge is: how do we get those algorithms to the physicians in the remote areas where they usually do not have an electronic medical record? Paper records are still very common in the developing world. Surprisingly, in some contexts in the West, that's also true, particularly with exchange of information still being via fax machines. There are some similarities there that I can relate to.

Sorry, okay. So it's not that different, but I would guess it's a little bit more common in the Brazilian countryside. We have been tackling those three specific challenges to get those algorithms to work in remote areas. The first one is this: using routinely collected data. This study we published in 2021 used data that is collected for every single live birth here in Brazil, which includes information such as schooling of the mother, weight of the baby, gestational age of the mother, and so on, to see if we can predict which baby is going to die in the first month of life—what we call neonatal mortality.

We found that even using the information that every single birth collects in Brazil, we still got a pretty good predictive performance from the algorithms for São Paulo. Now we have a study moving the same algorithm around Brazil to see if it works well and what is the best strategy to make it work in remote areas. One strategy would be to just use data from São Paulo, another would be to use data from the remote areas, and another would be to use data from everywhere. We have been trying to find out what is the best combination for training those algorithms in order for them to work in remote areas. We have a few studies that should come out this year about this.

Then we also move internationally. We have a cohort of seven low- and middle-income countries around the world, and we're trying to see if we can find the same results in different countries. It's another paper that should come out soon. We are testing whether, in order to make good decisions for neonatal mortality in India, it is better to just use data from India or if it improves if we bring in different patients. Even though they are different kinds of patients than you have in India, maybe they learn something about human beings in general by having this diversity in data.

We're trying to use only the data that is collected everywhere. The WHO has five minimal indicators that the organization suggests every single country collects on every single live birth. We're using those because we want to make sure every single country is collecting them. Then we have also been moving to a machine learning technique called transfer learning, which is the fourth option. Instead of fixing on the training data, let's train the algorithm where we have more data and just fine-tune it for the remote areas.

The algorithm will learn about neonatal mortality in general, overall information about death and life, where it has a lot of data. Then we leave the fine-tuning for the specific areas. How much fine-tuning do we need? Is it going to be fine-tuning for the hospital itself? That is an option; we have some studies finding that it's better to train the algorithm with data from the same hospital, even if you have less data.

Are we going to fine-tune for the hospital, the city, or the region? Or maybe we do not need to fine-tune at all. We have a lot of scientific challenges ahead of us, which is very exciting, and we have some pretty cool results coming out. It all started with this: let's see if we routinely collect data. Even though the data is not perfect and not everything we wanted—we would like to use image data and so on—it's not the reality.

With the information that we already have, are we able to train interesting machine learning algorithms? Such a great example. It's great that you summarized the main challenges and the things that you've been doing to overcome them. I wanted to go into a couple of those points because they're super interesting. However, just to start with, one thing to flag is a universal benefit to this approach.

Another issue around the ethics of data that comes up a lot is: do the underserved communities benefit? They might get over the bridge of awareness and trust regarding how their data is going to be used, and they finally engage and say, "Yeah, I'll give my data to train an algorithm," but they never see the benefits. This is a great example of how underserved communities can actually directly benefit from having their data being used to train ML models. It's such a great example and a shining story to show that this is possible. Yeah, and we have been talking with the local government here in São Paulo, and they are very interested in adding those algorithms to their own digital system.

When the hospital inserts the information about the newborn, it would show an alert for a high-risk baby. It will show up straight away within the local government system, saying that according to the history of babies here and according to the algorithms, this baby has, for example, a 92% probability of dying in the first month. So, probably do not send this baby home; keep it under observation. It helps make good decisions that might then have a positive impact and reduce the chances of mortality or even morbidity by identifying those people. A great piece of impact.

You then went on to a great balancing tension piece. One question that often gets asked is: it's great to have localized and contextual things, but we need things to scale and be generalizable. Does it make sense to have hyper-localized ML algorithms or data if the radius of positive impact is small? But if we're thinking about the needs in healthcare, we need to be thinking much bigger. This was a great segue into the work you're doing to connect to other regions, cities, and contexts both within Brazil and internationally.

How does this fair then? Are there similar predictive dynamics within other contexts? To me, that raises a really interesting question philosophically regarding societal and digital determinants of health. How much of it is universal and how much is actually due to the local area? How granular do you want to get with locality and your unique context?

Again, it's the population health versus precision health consideration. The challenges you're facing with the strategy have lots of parallels with the challenges that health systems in general face: do we think about things at a population health level, and how do we balance that with thinking at an individual level? This is super interesting. I would separate this into scientific knowledge and practical application. For scientific knowledge, it is very interesting what you mentioned regarding whether the dynamics change for the rules that lead to neonatal mortality.

Maybe in some countries, birth weight is more important because you don't have preventive measures for it. In other countries, another characteristic is more important. The algorithms will learn that the rules are different, and it will be very interesting to understand why. What makes the dynamics change from one country to the other? This is a scientific challenge.

In terms of actual practical application challenges, I would say that we need to make sure the predictive performance is the best possible for each local area. We will be as specific as we need to be because we're trying to see exactly how specific we need to be. We're going to automatize this, so it's not going to be a huge difficulty to scale. It's going to be scalable, but within the scale, there will be fine-tuning. We are able to insert this within the algorithm and the system so it will be scalable but also precise and specific for each country.

As the algorithm moves around, it will learn how to be specific for each place. I would make those two distinctions. Both are very interesting. We want to make scientific discoveries, but in the end, we want to get those algorithms to work and have an impact on people. Absolutely.

On this point of fine-tuning, you mentioned transfer learning. Could you very quickly explain what that is and how that helps with fine-tuning or making something more specific and precise? My understanding is you've got something trained in one context—for example, São Paulo—and you're trying to apply that to a rural context. What is happening at a technical level? Given the mixed technical ability in the audience, could you summarize what transfer learning is and what impact it can have?

Transfer learning is still a very new technique, especially for structured, tabular data, which is the most common type of data collected here and around the world. The main idea—not to get too technical—is if you think about a neural network with a lot of layers of neurons, you would train the algorithm where you have a lot of data, like in São Paulo. Then you leave, for example, the last two layers of the network open to be fine-tuned in the remote areas. If you have 10 layers, the first eight layers are going to be from São Paulo. It learns the basics—the literature shows that the first few layers learn basic stuff—about the health issue.

Then you leave the last two layers open for training on the specific areas. Eight layers come from São Paulo where you have more data, and then you leave a little bit of the algorithm to be specific for the region. This is an example. We have been doing this for random forest, gradient boosting, and other common algorithms for structured data. Basically, the algorithm learns the basics where you have a lot of data, but then the details of the decision will be trained on the specific area where you want it to work.

Interesting. What kind of results have you seen? I know you said it's yet to be published, but are you able to share a sneak peek? It's still a very new area, but we have been finding some gains. It's not huge, of course.

We're already using state-of-the-art algorithms, but if we get 5% better results when you're already using state-of-the-art everything, that 5% is usually huge. We have been getting results like that. The algorithms get to be more robust and less prone to overfitting because the basics were trained with a lot of data. Exactly, not overfitting to the local context. Very interesting.

I can see that in the scaled model as well, where you have the more universal data points that are collected around the world, and then you're adding layers that are more important contextually. That seems quite exciting and helps bridge that balance we were talking about earlier. We've covered a lot. If I were to summarize, the biggest thing I see in terms of action here is the proactive effort to make sure you're reaching out to communities where data poverty is a factor. Another learning is around leveraging data you have, using routinely collected data, and making it applicable in different contexts while also keeping the impact for the initial community.

That's where techniques like transfer learning come in. The other part is: how do you make this scale and be globally relevant? That sums up the benchmarking work you've done. I will share that as well: benchmarking and working with seven other low- and middle-income countries who collect similar data points and seeing how that behaves there. Really super interesting.

Do you have any other learnings to share with colleagues based in the EU, US, or UK who don't get to see these kinds of stories much in their context? What is your call to action for them? We work mostly with technical issues, and a huge technical issue for machine learning in healthcare is going to be fairness. We must make sure those algorithms work even within the same city. We must ensure they are not working better for white residents or richer residents and so on.

How do we identify this and how do we correct the algorithm to make sure it doesn't do that? I have two PhD students working on that with data from Brazil. In such a diverse country, we have been applying machine learning to different cities and developing techniques to identify when we have an issue. Then how do we make sure the algorithm doesn't make those wrong decisions again? This is because we usually have inequalities even within the same city.

You have income inequalities, racial diversity, and so on. Even within remote areas, we try to make sure they work well. We have a bunch of other technical challenges, such as online learning, to make sure those algorithms are learning as they make decisions. How do we ensure data privacy is respected? We have been working on federated learning a lot to make sure we do not transfer patient data; we only transfer the algorithms.

So, yes, it's a very exciting field. Yeah, looking forward to reading more and following your work. How can other people follow you and keep track of the transfer learning paper and others coming out from your unit? My social media is mostly in Portuguese, but our scientific articles are in English. If you want to follow us, we have been publishing on machine learning in healthcare and have a bunch more coming out.

I'm on Google Scholar if you want to follow my page. Perfect. I can put a link into any material that's going out. Alexander Chiavegatto Filho, thank you so much for talking to us. The big takeaway for me is that the world is becoming more like Brazil.

I think you just had Carnival last week as well, so I also hope the world becomes like that. Yeah, your first suggestion was that we did this podcast last week, and I was like, "Oh no." It's our most beloved holiday here in Brazil. Absolutely, I wouldn't dream of it. But we made it. Perfect.

Thank you so much for sharing your experiences and challenges. I think this will be really useful for a lot of people. Thanks for showcasing your work and talking about your impact. Thank you very much. I hope to be able to speak to you again about the further work you've done.

episodes.title: Practical solutions to health data poverty
episodes.description: How a team in Brazil is maximising the impact of data-driven technology for underserved communities - and what the global community can learn from Brazil's approach to data diversity.

topics: Defining health data poverty: what it means and why it matters for global health
Relevance to developed nations: implications for the US, EU, and UK
In-depth analysis of a 2021 Lancet paper co-authored by Dr Liu
Real-world examples of health data poverty and its impacts
Dr Liu's views on current progress and the steps ahead
How society and the healthcare ecosystem can address these challenges comprehensively
episodes.bio:
Dr Xiaoxuan (Xiao, pronounced "Shau") Liu is an Honorary Associate Professor in AI and Digital Health at the University of Birmingham, Principal Scientist and Health Research Lead at Microsoft AI, and a Deputy Editor at NEJM AI.

She was appointed a 125th Anniversary Fellow at the University of Birmingham in August 2024 following her significant contributions to internationally adopted evidence standards and policy for AI and health. Before this, she was an ophthalmology doctor in the NHS and a Health Scientist at Apple.

Dr Liu's work focuses on the responsible innovation of AI health technologies, seeking to ensure they are safe, effective and equitable. Projects she has previously led include:

- **Improving the evidence** — developing internationally adopted reporting guidelines for AI clinical trials (SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI), and contributing to other AI reporting standards including TRIPOD+AI, STARD-AI and DECIDE-AI; as well as defining standards for NICE (the Digital Health Technologies Evidence Standards Framework), in collaboration with Imperial College London and the Alan Turing Institute.
- **Improving safety** — developing tools for assessing the safety of AI-enabled medical devices: the Medical Algorithmic Audit and CANAIRI (Collaboration for Translational AI Trials), and working directly with medical device regulators such as the MHRA.
- **Improving equity and fairness** — tackling algorithmic bias and improving the transparency and diversity of health datasets to mitigate AI-driven health inequalities, through STANDING Together.
- **Improving global health** — conducting real-world trials of generative AI and large language models to assist community health workers in resource-limited settings, in collaboration with PATH.

Dr Liu works with a range of academic, industry and policy institutions around the world. She supports the UK NIHR Incubator for AI & Digital Healthcare and the NHS AI and Digital Regulatory Services, and serves as a board member for the MHRA's AI Airlock — the regulatory sandbox for AI as a Medical Device.
episodes.guestRole: AI ethics, evaluation and regulation researcher
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to the first in a series of conversations where we delve into some of the most pressing issues concerning AI and healthcare. Of course, there are lots of these at the moment: great articles, great podcasts, great material, and great publications. However, what I see or observe in this conversation is they're very US, EU, and UK focused. While this is great, this keeps us in a bubble, and actually, if you think about it, it's actually the rest of the world outside of this where the biggest needs are and where most of humanity lives. And so the focus of this conversation is really around LMICs and underserved populations, perhaps in the geographies we mentioned, but also who's actually doing and moving the needle on these issues.

Because sometimes also that's where the conversation gets stuck: "Oh, we should do something about it," but who's actually doing something about it? And particularly from an LMIC, what can we learn? How can we learn from this? So at least as a baseline, this has a big learning for me, and I hope you as a listener will come along for the ride as well. And so I guess with that, I'm very, very excited to be talking to Xiao today.

So welcome, Xiao. This is the first part, and we're talking today in this first part about health data and poverty. Now, Xiao, you're a heavyweight in the field in general. You know, aside from your early work where I got to know you, leading the CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI guidelines for reporting of clinical trials, you've also written one of the seminal calls to action, or been part of the writing committee with a few other people, on the call to action around health data poverty, and really calling it out as, "We need to do something about this." So I'm really excited to talk to you about this, but maybe we can start with you telling us a little bit about yourself and then maybe you can go into how you define health data poverty. Thanks.

Yeah, thanks for having me. It's really exciting to be on this podcast, and what a great topic. So my name is Xiao. I'm a medical doctor by background and I'm also nowadays a full-time academic researcher based at the University of Birmingham in the UK. I have experience working across healthcare policy, regulation, some time in industry as well, and now in academia.

My research focuses on the evaluation and regulation of AI health technologies, focusing on safety, effectiveness, equity, and sustainability. So thanks so much for having me here. Pleasure. So, Xiao, that's so pertinent, especially the area of your focus. And I mean, there's so many rabbit holes we could go down with the areas that you've been researching and writing about.

But if we focus on this area in particular, how do you define, or what has the work that you've done defined health data poverty as? And why should we in our contexts in, I guess, like you know, we find our context together here as the US, the EU, the UK—kind of technically the West, as it were—why should we care about this? Yeah, maybe I can tell the story as to how we came up with the term "health data poverty" in the first place. So I was working on a review at the time. I'm an ophthalmologist by background; I was interested in eye imaging datasets.

And we did a mapping exercise looking at all the publicly available eye imaging datasets that we could find, and found that there was a huge disparity in terms of where the datasets were distributed around the world, and a heavy bias towards countries with higher resources, well-established health systems, and well-established digital infrastructure. And there were also tons of problems with the way that those datasets were documented. So when we think about the concept of health data poverty, we wrote about this in a paper in the Lancet Digital Health, and we defined it as the inability for individuals, groups, or populations to benefit from discoveries or innovations because of a lack of data that adequately represents them. So that's a bit of a mouthful, but it's really a multifaceted problem. When we talk about health data poverty, it makes us think about a lack of data, but a lack of data is only the first level of the problem.

So it might be that we have individuals or groups who aren't present in the dataset, but then the next level down is those who are present in the dataset but maybe aren't accurately represented. Maybe we get more inaccuracies and errors and misrepresentations in data representing certain groups. Like, for example, if we don't capture things like ethnicity coding at a very granular level for the whole of the Asian community, which we know is a very diverse community, what does that mean for the insights that we can derive for them? And then there's almost another level down where our definitions around things like personal attributes aren't perfect and they aren't sufficiently granular to actually represent people. So I guess what I'm saying is that health data poverty can come from a number of different routes into affecting bias in datasets, and it can be problematic for when we do research on that data, but also when we create data-driven interventions like, for example, AI algorithms and software.

Yeah, absolutely. And I think you touched on something because, at least when we initially think about this, from my perspective, we think more or index more towards that first area. And I guess at least for me, my assumption is that's linked to the concept of availability bias, and particularly with the impact you have on if that data is then used to train models which are then going to impact care; you suddenly have this propagating problem. And I guess the source of that which is being propagated digitally is just the problems that we have inherently within a society and within healthcare, and how healthcare data gathering is set up a few layers down. So there's so many levels at which this plays out.

And it's great that you talk about the ways that it goes further down in terms of inaccuracies within certain groups and the other things that you've mentioned. And I think what this plays out towards as well is that we miss a trick on potentially the benefits of certain... we talk about the promise of AI and we talk about the digital divide, and we risk whole layers of our community or parts of our community missing out even from being present in the data. And I think, I guess another reflection to me is this other more ethical layer, which is: people who then donate data are the ones who don't benefit from it because of the way society is set up, because the models are then just deployed on richer areas because that's where the money is, right? So what are your thoughts about that?

Yeah, absolutely. That kind of perpetuating cycle issue is definitely true. And then if you think about the fact that if you're interacting with digital tools and data-generating health interventions, then in effect, that problem kind of gets worse because the data that you're generating off these existing data-driven tools is going to be, again, only working or only targeted towards certain populations that are already accessing the datasets. I think the other issue to bring up is that sometimes the presence of the health data poverty issue within a dataset isn't immediately obvious. And part of that reason is we don't currently document our datasets or label our datasets in sufficient granularity or in a sufficiently transparent way.

Often you can get a dataset where you don't actually know what percentage represents what ethnicity because that information is just not recorded or it's poorly recorded. And so you can't actually make any—as a researcher or as an innovator—you can't make any judgments about how suitable is this if I want to create an algorithm that's detecting cancer for, let's say, the whole of the UK population, but I'm not getting sufficiently granular labeling within that dataset. Well, I can't actually make that judgment. So that's maybe a nice segue onto one of the projects that we've been working on for the last two years called "Standing Together," which is exactly tackling this issue—trying to bring more transparency into the limitations of datasets when we think about it with an equity lens, documenting very clearly where biases may or may not be embedded in the data and what sort of attributes we should be labeling the dataset with. So, yeah, just a little plug there on Standing Together, which is hopefully going to be published soon.

The recommendations can be found at www.datadiversity.org. We'll try and make sure that that's in the notes that follow up on this so people can follow that. So what I'm hearing then is that we need a good way to help developers or gatherers of data create an extra layer of standardization of what is good in this type of criteria as a criterion. Because I guess what it links to for me is like "Diversity by Design," where you're thinking about it at the beginning of the process rather than trying to catch your tail afterwards, and defining what is good at the outset. Or at least with the dataset you have, you can then be able to do something about it.

So making it visible, right? Making the invisible more visible in your data. I guess that resonates a lot. And I think, if we could just get into a bit more around particularly the recommendations that you have in the article—and this article was written in 2021—so maybe you could go over the recommendations? And I'd love to get your assessment, or at least from what you see and the conversations you have, on what you read and what's out here at the moment.

Where do you think we're at in terms of having moved the needle on this? What have we done well—we, the collective we—and what do you think are the key challenges that we have still left to do? Yeah, that's a big question. Well, we have done some repeated investigations into mapping different datasets across other disease areas since we wrote that original article, which was really prompted by that ophthalmology use case. So we've since looked at datasets for skin cancer; we've looked at it in COVID-19; we've looked at cardiovascular datasets; and also, what was the last one?

It was breast cancer. These problems with poor representation within datasets and poor labeling are really pervasive across lots of different areas. And we have to accept that ultimately it's not the data that's the problem; the data is a reflection of our society and also our health system. And so to an extent, you can make the data as transparent as possible, but you cannot fix the data—fix the problem instead. The dataset should be used as a tool to understand the problem.

And so then the question becomes: how do we make sure that... what are the opportunities where, a bit like a surgical sieve, those patients who are, or the communities that are within our society—where do they drop off along their health system chain, all the way up to the point at which they become a sort of data point? That includes looking at things like accessibility to care; that includes looking at things like consent to contributing data; it includes things like participation in clinical trials and other data curation efforts. It involves things like looking at how we code data, how we aggregate data, how we harmonize it. And there's many, many opportunities along that sort of life cycle for health data where we can lose people, and it's a big long-term mission that we need to be working on.

So that's a great call to action and thinking about it from a whole life cycle of data lens, even from before someone becomes a data point, and what's their journey in there. I wanted to quickly go over the four recommendations. So if I go over them briefly, people can read them, and I'll put the link here. But one was around increasing awareness within data and digital health communities. And I think that touches on: we all have a responsibility across the life cycle, not just developers but across all of society.

And if we think about just the clinical deployment context, all the parts of that. So from a developer perspective: a developer developing an AI algorithm based on a dataset—how are we proactively thinking about that? Who do we need to work with to increase that? Do we need to think about other things that we need to do? You talked about labeling and the attributions of it.

So I like this first recommendation because it helps us think about this across... and then we're also thinking about it in terms of preparing for deployment and after deployment. How are we thinking about that, and what are the second- and third-order effects and responsibilities of the health system itself to be able to make sure that this is happening? So I like the whole life cycle approach and the pre- and post-deployment quality of data. That's really exciting.

The second is transparent communication to citizens, and that bit around trust. The third is equitable digital access, so making sure that people are visible in digital format in the data. Because that's what I like: you coupled it with the gathering and provision; they're both important. And so the episode of care is the opportunity to gather the data in the right way and also use that to provision the right care, and they affect each other. And the fourth is building inclusive and representative datasets.

So I think these are really nice—a really nice summary of recommendations, and this is great. If I kind of come back to some of the points you made in your assessment, you talked about the whole life cycle lens, and sometimes I think that's what makes it hard because it's all of our responsibility. And when something becomes everyone's responsibility, it almost becomes nobody's, or no one has the impetus—who's the driving force behind this? So I think that makes it hard. And you used the medical analogy; I'll maybe use one as well.

Sometimes we talk about modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors, and this is a risk in society. I think we sometimes treat conversations like this as a non-modifiable one, like, "Oh, it's baked into society, this problem." So it's like, "Oh, we need a whole society change; we should really do something about it." It feels like we're treating it like it's in our societal genetics, whereas your call to action here is that this is assailable, this is modifiable, and it comes back to digital determinants of health. These are modifiable determinants of health. And so I guess the gap for me is: how do we flip our mindset and therefore actions that actually move the needle forward on this? Yeah, I think that's a really good point.

I mean, this is a big, complex problem that's entangled, and it's a kind of ball of string which is a collective responsibility. And I think there's an argument to be made around: in what way can we componentize all the different aspects of it and map out where the contributions that can be made are? Which stakeholders can be naturally responsible for those components? And when we actually look at it as—is it a whole system-wide change that needs to be made, or is it actually a series of small changes that brings firstly transparency and visibility to the issue, and then resources, a lot of will, persistence, and strategic thinking to all these different components within the ecosystem? And I think I will call out something, which is: we have to have community engagement in these kinds of efforts, and that does require a substantial amount of investment.

Because often those who we are trying to engage on these topics are those who already start from furthest back from the starting line in the conversation. And so we as a community need to take the extra effort in reaching out and bringing them into the conversation. And can I just check who you mean by community and "we," and who it is we need to reach out to? Yeah, so in the case of underrepresented datasets, it's those who are at a disadvantage, who have least access to healthcare, who are from minority ethnic groups, who have disabilities, who have other barriers that hamper their ability to access healthcare and participate in the conversation. Yeah, okay.

And the community—"us"—is people who are trying to implement and make the change? Yeah. And being on the developer side and the clinician side myself—particularly on the developer side and the innovator side for our listeners—what do you think are some of the tangible things that they can be doing in preparing for deployments, or maybe they've got algorithms that are out there in the field already? How should they be thinking about how to improve based on some of these recommendations? So, for example, a good one for this part of the community is building inclusive and representative datasets, or supporting the building of that, or making sure that inclusive and representative datasets are ingested by models that are being created, or creating the attributes as you said.

What are your thoughts on that? Yeah, so I think the first thing is recognizing that it's no one particular stakeholder's responsibility. And without generalizing, my experience is that sometimes there can be a perception that this equity issue is not the issue of the people developing the technology, and it's kind of someone else's problem. But actually, it's not a problem that can be solved by just one person. This is what we're talking about in terms of a shared responsibility, right?

So understanding, from a developer point of view, what your contribution to the solution or to the problem might be. And that might be because you are the one curating the dataset, but it might also be because you're not curating a dataset, but you're selecting a dataset. Or maybe you're making algorithmic choices that might bias against certain groups versus others. And there's decision-making in all of that. Being really critical around: "Who am I trying to benefit with this innovation?

What tradeoffs am I making? And who within my team is making those decisions?" And do we have unconscious biases that we may be unaware of? Being highly self-critical about it, but then also not being, I suppose, almost paralyzed to the point of not moving forward with that, because we still need innovation. And this is, as we've said, not a one-stop solution. But accepting that if we have to move forward with an imperfect solution that may still have a degree of bias—that may still have a degree of health data poverty—to then be really transparent about it.

So then others can build off your solution and make improvements. Good call to action in there: we're all part of the ecosystem; where do we fit in that life cycle? What things do we know about that we could do? And how do we challenge ourselves, uncovering our subconscious biases and putting things into place? And I think the other thing is like: this is also never done, really; it's always going to be there.

And I guess it's always an iterative process, so also not letting perfect be the enemy of moving forward, and actually taking iterative steps. So I like those; at least that's what I've taken as calls to action, particularly from the innovator side. But I think there's a lot that we can all think about. I've got a couple of other things I wanted to get into, actually. One was related to the second recommendation on transparent communications to citizens, because I think that's a really important one.

You need citizens and people in general to trust the way that their data is collected and used. And part of it is that comes from them being able to benefit from that as well. If we see the rhetoric and conversations in society at the moment, there's a big proportion of people who are on the side of opting out. And for me, that's also creating a big digital divide, or creating a section of society that's invisible from data as well. And if the opt-outers—if we classify it that way—are broadly represented across all groups and covered all across all groups, then great.

But probably statistically, they might be skewed towards one area of society, which will then still exacerbate it. So do you have any thoughts about that? Because for me, that's another counterintuitive area of data invisibility, but one that's pertinent. Yeah, and there are risks that... I mean, there are well-founded reasons, we know that there are well-founded reasons—historical reasons—as to why certain groups may choose to do that.

But we also know that it may not help the situation if we are then creating innovations based off potentially biased data. And I think citizen engagement is so important: meaningful citizen engagement in understanding what the root cause is that we have certain groups that are choosing not to opt in to share data. What are their fears and concerns? Are they based off of historical reasons, or are they based off of facts that are better ones to make a decision based on today? And what would help build that trust?

What would help build reassurance? Do we need to do more to build trust and reassurance in certain groups? And actually, maybe that's exactly what we need to do, but then explaining the benefits of being represented in the data and going from there. Yeah, and that's—at least if I was thinking of that life cycle view—who's the key contributor to that area? It feels like a governmental area of key responsibility.

But then how do you get people to engage positively in that? But I think innovators or builders also... you know, we see some of the big tech giants, who people are very skeptical about, and we see that within the NHS as well, and probably it plays out in other countries as well. So I think it goes back to: we all have a part to play in terms of making this come to a reality. Great thinking.

And I should say, sometimes it's not—the decision-making around contributing data isn't always an active decision about consenting to share data. Sometimes it's an interaction like being at the front desk of a hospital to receive care and then being unwilling to tick certain boxes because you have fear of stigmatization within the health system, and then the secondary use of that data for research or innovation. And so again, back to that data life cycle map: figuring out where the opportunities for losing people are, and then recognizing that it doesn't always relate directly to this data sharing component, and so mapping out what the concerns are at different stages. Great. Yeah, really great point.

And then as we kind of come to get your big call to action to us, I think it would be good to get your examples on maybe some either good or bad examples. So I guess, the two areas for me are: do you have any visibility on who is currently moving the needle on building inclusive and representative datasets? And maybe if you have any examples of how we can make sure the ones who donate their data—particularly those who are otherwise underrepresented and feeling the biggest acute pain of the inverse care law (I.e., the people who need care most are the ones who are less likely to receive it)—you know, with digital health and AI potentially being able to exacerbate that, but could make that better if we do it right? In that, do you have any thoughts of who needs to ensure that people who are donating their data actually receive the benefit? So, sorry, those are two big questions: firstly, who's building inclusive and representative datasets, but then a little bit about getting the benefits of the data at the end?

Yeah, so I think there's different approaches to this. There are the big efforts to collect routinely collected health data. And particularly in the UK, we have a number of Health Data Research hubs being set up, for example, by Health Data Research UK. We have internationally a number of large-scale population-level citizen health data collection efforts. I'm thinking of programs like "Our Future Health" in the UK and the "All of Us" program in the US.

And I think there are massive opportunities there to not rely so much on those who are accessing healthcare for specific needs, and understanding more—having this kind of blanket coverage across our population. And I know within those programs there's also specific efforts to try and reach these "hard-to-reach" groups, although I know there's problems with that terminology. And then I guess there are also targeted data-driven efforts which reach out to specific communities, and there are pockets of those dotted around different places. So I think in terms of your second question around how we make sure that there's benefit back to those individuals—well, there's generic practices in terms of making sure that those who are contributing data are getting feedback in terms of what the data is being used for, and having accountability mechanisms to mandate the showing of, "This is what your data is being used for," and showing that it's responsible use. In principle, there's also a different model that I've seen in the Health Data Research hubs where there is a governance structure within each data hub that involves patients and the public for triaging or assessing the data requests, and making a judgment on whether these requests and the purpose described in them will bring benefit back to patients within the national health system, for example.

Interesting. So some of these mechanisms for feedback, and just involving patients and the public in the conversation, I think are effective. That's a good call. You know, at the end of the day, I guess the intended benefit is going to be for patients, people, and the public. And I think the key challenge is making sure that benefit actually gets to everyone, including everyone in that piece.

So that's really great. And you mentioned a few examples of organizations working on building more inclusive and representative datasets, particularly on the UK side. And I guess what we'll go into next is who might be doing that within the LMIC context as well. But that's a good connection—particularly that you mentioned about routinely collected data. And so that will be a bookmark for later on, Xiao.

I guess with everything we've talked about—and we're thinking about a whole society view, but particularly I'm guessing that the main audience of listeners are builders interested in, or people interested in, digital health, maybe clinicians, maybe people on the health system side or CCIO side, maybe investors—what's a one-word message you'd give based on everything we've said today on this topic? Yeah, I think I would say: try and understand, whichever role you're in within this ecosystem, try and figure out where you can uniquely make things better or worse, and try and strive to improve that part that you can have influence over. Try and be as transparent about it as possible. Evidence your work, make it public-facing, create opportunities to be accountable so that others can judge your work, essentially, and make sound decisions around—whether they're downstream or upstream to you—how they can also respond accordingly. And try and achieve this balance of making improvements but not being paralyzed by not being able to get it perfect.

Because this is a problem that is bigger than many of us; it's entrenched, and it's at a structural and societal level. But it's all about the small changes that we individually can make. And I think that's a really, really great call to action. Particularly the bit you talked about, continuous improvement. That's a concept that's very familiar: quality improvement.

This is a part of quality; this is a part of delivering value. And if we can attach that as a part of any efforts that we already have in place rather than trying to reinvent the wheel and create something new—bake it into how we think about quality and continuous improvement—I think that's a way to get it operationalized much more effectively. And also, be very aware of what we... we all have blind spots; we all have unconscious biases. Involve diverse voices, welcome dissent, and have good conversations around that.

Great. And you talked about Standing Together, and you also mentioned the map—kind of a map of the data life cycle. Is there work or output? You talked about a publication coming soon. Is any of this connected to what you've talked about that might be coming out in the work of Standing Together, and is a map of this available so people can visualize this life cycle?

Yeah, well, I want to make it available now. We have described it at various points throughout our publications. The Standing Together paper will be coming out soon, but we do have a public-facing report that can be found at datadiversity.org. And that is an international, consensus-based set of recommendations around how we can be better about transparency of datasets, and then what you do with the limitations of datasets when you're thinking of, for example, developing an algorithm or doing a piece of research relating to that data. There are also a series of other papers that will be accompanying this, which are those dataset mapping reviews that I mentioned: in COVID, breast cancer, and heart failure.

We already have the ophthalmology and the dermatology skin cancer one published, both in the Lancet Digital Health. And yeah, those are the series of upcoming papers where we try and bring some of the evidence into this conversation. And then obviously there's the health data poverty paper as well that we mentioned at the beginning. Perfect. Thank you for sharing those resources as well, Xiao.

I think it's been great to learn from the perspective of a real expert in this field. We've managed to get a good definition; we've managed to see how far, if anything, we've come from three years ago when you published the initial call to action. We've got an understanding of what the recommendations are and how they might fit together in an overall landscape of people who are going from creating datasets to impacting people at the end, and who the people are in there and how we also all need to work together. So there's some great calls to action there, and I'll try to summarize them as well. But I just wanted to say thank you so much for taking the plunge and being the first person that agreed to speak to me about this very, very important topic.

And I think this is a really, really nice segue onto part two of this, where we'll be speaking to a professor in Brazil who has actually tried to do something about the fourth recommendation, which is building inclusive and representative datasets. So Xiao, with that, I just want to say thank you so much for a great conversation. And I think I'm certainly galvanized to go back to my organization and say, "Hey, how can we do some of these things better?" And I hope the listeners have too. Thank you so much for having me. It's been a great conversation.
episodes.pullQuote: It's not the data that's the problem; the data is a reflection of our society and also our health system.
episodes.title: Health data poverty: what can we do about it?
episodes.description: A crucial conversation on one of the most pressing issues in global digital health: health data poverty. What it is, why it matters, and how we might begin to address it.
